playbooks.name: .RDP File Created By Uncommon Application
playbooks.description: Detects a browser, email client, or chat application writing a file that ends in .rdp — programs that render web pages or messages but do not normally author Remote Desktop connection files. hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection has 2 alternative branches. The condition string ('selection') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. (A list of scalar values under a single field is different — that is intra-field membership, not a branch OR.)

The literal detection strings ('-noni -ep bypass $', 'cyzfc.dat,', 'PointFunctionCall') are rule criteria and are stated as such.

This is a literal-string indicator rule, not a behavioral one. Every non-entity-scoped question that references "these indicator patterns" carries the rule's two CommandLine branches in its own selection (Q6, Q13, Q14, Q15, Q17, Q18), so no question promises pattern filtering the query does not perform. The load-bearing artifact is the on-disk XSL/host file, which Q10 (attack:T1216.file_event) covers directly, and the in-script payload surfaces as a spawned child in Q7 (follow_on). hint_dispositions.reason: The bypass does not involve cross-process handle access or memory manipulation of another process — the signed script host executes attacker JScript within its own process via the XSL transform, then spawns ordinary children. There is no target process being opened (no GrantedAccess mask to key on), so a process_access query would have no selective signal distinguishing this rule's firing from background telemetry. The relevant evidence (host relocation + XSL drop, and any spawned payload) is covered by Q3, Q7, and Q10. No compensating attack:T1216.process_access question authored.

playbooks.name: Blue Mockingbird
playbooks.description: Fires when either of two independent command patterns runs — cmd.exe whose command line contains both `sc config` and `wercplsupporte.dll`, or wmic.exe whose command line ends in COR_PROFILER. What spawned the process that made this change, and what started that parent?
What other child processes did the same parent spawn?
What registry key and value did the alerting process write, and is that location a known persistence spot?

Were other persistence mechanisms installed on this host around the alert?
When this host has previously produced this rule's pattern, what parents and users drove it, and does the current alert fit that history?
Have other hosts produced this rule's pattern in the past week, and does the cross-host distribution look like automation or one-off activity?

What else did this account run across the environment around this time?

notes: Topology read from rule.detection directly as well as condition_topology. shape is OR_of_selections, raw condition `sc_cmd or wmic_cmd`, required_any_of [[sc_cmd, wmic_cmd]], no filters. sc_cmd is Image|endswith \cmd.exe AND CommandLine|contains|all ['sc config', 'wercplsupporte.dll'] — an intra-selection AND that is preserved as an AND in Q1 and the description. wmic_cmd is Image|endswith \wmic.exe AND CommandLine|endswith COR_PROFILER. The two selections are OR'd, so the description and Q1 use disjunctive framing.

Primary technique T1112 (Modify Registry) drives the chain skeleton because both branches converge on a registry write that is the persistence itself — a ServiceDll repoint under the service key, or a profiler variable under Session Manager Environment paired with a CLSID InProcServer32 registration. T1047 is secondary - it is the delivery mechanism for one branch only (wmic writing the environment variable), and its analytic contributed two distinct chain stages (the WMI-Activity channel view and the remote-connection view) plus the user_context dimension.

Threat-specific rule (family name in the title), so the cluster is named once in the description to tie the rule name to the behavior, and the rest of the playbook stays behavioral. The intel's incident chain (initial access through a deserialization flaw, privilege escalation via impersonation abuse, credential theft, RDP/SMB lateral movement, mining pool egress) is deliberately not transcribed. Two generalizable pieces of it survive - Q13 tells the analyst to treat a set of internet-facing application servers as a population defined by exposure, and Q18 names the worker-process-spawns-shell and impersonation-abuse routes as what a preceding detection would look like. Command values from the intel (`wmic ENVIRONMENT create name="COR_PROFILER"...`) are used as format guidance in Q1, not as an incident narrative.

Q5 (registry.registry_key_context) is KEEP_EXACT and ProcessGuid-scoped, which for this rule will frequently return nothing - a `sc config` is committed to the registry by the service control manager and a wmic environment write by the WMI provider host, neither of which shares the alerting ProcessGuid. The template is must_include and its detection was not modified; instead the context states the empty-result caveat directly, and Q6 (attack:T1112.registry_key_paths) is the host-scoped key-path question that actually surfaces the committed write. The two are complementary, not duplicates - Q5 attributes a write to the alerting process, Q6 finds the write regardless of which process committed it.

Q-vs-query agreement. Q12, Q13, Q14, Q15 and Q17 all claim the rule's pattern and all embed the rule's detection block verbatim through reflection, so the claim is enforced. Q6, Q9 and Q11 are host-scoped and claim only what their selections enforce (registry key paths, reg.exe write verbs, the persistence-tool binary list). Q16 is account-scoped with no pattern claim in its text. Q8 claims wmic.exe/WmiPrvSE.exe connections and enforces exactly that with Image|endswith. Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5 and Q10 are entity-scoped.

This rule fires specifically on a registry write to the wercplsupport service's ServiceDll value, a service-DLL hijack. Investigating that write is registry_set + process_creation + file work: what DLL path was set (Q3/Q4), which process wrote it and its lineage (Q5), whether the DLL loaded or executed (Q6), and whether the DLL is on disk (Q7). Any parallel WMI-driven registry persistence (COR_PROFILER CLSID InProcServer32) surfaces through the registry-related-modifications clustering (Q11), and any wmic.exe execution surfaces through the process-based-persistence question (Q14) — neither requires WMI-Activity channel telemetry. The template's own notes_to_llm directs skipping this question for malware-specific detections; the brief classifies this rule with filename_prefix malware and the title names a specific RAT family. A change ticket for a non-stock svchost service group is not a check that resolves this alert either way.

The alerting process is a service host started by the service control manager under a service principal, not an action a user performs interactively. There is no human behind the account to ask; the equivalent legitimacy check is the service-install record and the registered ImagePath, covered by the service-install question.

A svchost-hosted service starts at boot and on service-control demand, so its execution time carries no work-hours signal. The load-bearing timing question is when the service was registered, which the -7d service-install question answers directly from the install record.

This template asks whether the change was made via the organization's standard tooling; the alert is a service starting, not a change being made. The comparable check — whether the service was deployed by a sanctioned mechanism — is answered by the service-install record and the ServiceDll path, not by organizational recall about tooling.

notes: Rule tags no ATT&CK techniques and the brief carries an empty attack_brief, so attack_chain_coverage / dimension_coverage are empty and no attack:-sourced questions exist. condition_topology is all_AND over a single selection, so Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing (Image endswith svchost.exe AND CommandLine endswith one of the three group flags); the three CommandLine values are an OR-valued list inside that one selection, which Q1's context surfaces by asking which of the three fired.

The service-install question (Q4) is authored as `service: system` on EventID 7045, per the windows-logsources rule that Windows event-log channels are services and not categories. This is the load-bearing question for the rule: svchost -k only executes a group that a service registration created, so the install record is where the persistence mechanism is named.

Q5 (registry_set) and Q6 (image_load) are the two artifacts a svchost service registration leaves behind — the Svchost group value plus the service's ServiceDll value, and the DLL the hosted process actually loaded. Q6 is entity-scoped on the alerting ProcessGuid rather than host+Image, because svchost module-load volume on a host is unbounded; DLL loads carry Signed/Signature/Hashes on the load event, so no execution pivot is needed.

Q3 (mechanism_decode, ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY) adds the rule's CommandLine|endswith values to the host+Image selection. svchost.exe is among the most common binaries on Windows, and the template's notes direct adding CommandLine filters for common binaries rather than returning the host's whole svchost population.

Q8 (follow_on, ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY) is re-anchored from host+ParentImage to ParentProcessGuid|expand '%ProcessGuid%' per the template's notes, which prefer ParentProcessGuid when available. Host-wide ParentImage svchost.exe would return every child of every service host on the box; the alerting instance's own children are the question.

False-positive discriminator: legitimate software registers services routinely, so a service install alone is not the signal. The discriminator is the group name — msupdate, msupdate2, and alg are not stock Windows svchost groups — combined with the registered ServiceDll path and its signature status.

mutable_dispositions.notes: The analytic's 15-minute correlation horizon between request, error, process spawn, and egress is carried as the +/-15m range on the host-clustering question and stated explicitly in its context. Q9 (+4h) and Q8 (+4h) deliberately run longer than the analytic's horizon because token use against a backup service can lag the login.

No environment-specific IP list can be authored into a portable playbook. The egress question's context directs the analyst to scope on the addresses fronting this application, and the query excludes RFC1918 and loopback ranges so the remaining destinations are the externally routable ones.

These are web-request-body patterns with no process_creation field to bind to; the application's own request logs are not an ingested logsource here, so the values are enumerated in the delivery-vector context for manual review rather than injected into a query.

HTTP status-code rates are not available in any authored logsource. Rather than restate a threshold the analyst cannot query, Q3's context frames the request-log review around the source address and the injected field values, which is the actionable form of the same signal.

The allow-list is environment-coupled and cannot be authored generically. Q8's context tells the analyst to enumerate the installation's known-good application-pool children first so unexpected ones stand out, rather than embedding a filter that would be wrong in most environments.

Template default scopes host + Image|endswith '%Image%'. The rule sets no Image constraint (primary_binary is null, all_binaries empty), so an Image-scoped decode would answer a different question than the rule asks. Re-anchored on host.name + CommandLine|contains 'qlogin' — the broadest of the rule's own values, deliberately broader than the full five-value combination so that adjacent qlogin invocations (repeated attempts, the token-use call) are visible rather than only the alerting line. Image added to fields so the analyst sees which executable received the arguments. ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY, cue template — fields are curatable.
Added host.name|expand '%hostname%' alongside the ProcessGuid|expand '%ParentProcessGuid%' anchor as a scoping fallback per the field-availability guidance.

Template default uses ParentImage|endswith '%Image%'; the template's own notes_to_llm prefer ParentProcessGuid when available. Re-anchored on host.name + ParentProcessGuid|expand '%ProcessGuid%' so the question returns children of the alerting invocation specifically rather than of every execution of the same binary on a backup server that runs it routinely. Also satisfies the CommandLine-only hint by removing an Image-based scope.

skipped_templates.reason: The template counts 90 days of Image|endswith '%Image%' on the host. The rule constrains no Image, so '%Image%' hydrates to whatever the backend spawned — qlogin.exe on a CommServe host, which runs it as routine product operation. The count would therefore be large and unvarying for every alert and would answer "does this backup server run its own login utility" (yes, always), which is not a discriminator. It also contradicts the CommandLine-only hint's instruction to scope on the pattern rather than the binary. The host-history question the analyst actually needs is covered by cue_process_tool.baseline_deviation (Q15), which is scoped to the rule's parameter combination.

notes: condition_topology.shape is all_AND with a single selection and no filters. The one selection is list-valued under CommandLine|contains|all, which is an AND across the five values, not an intra- selection OR — so there is no disjunctive branch anywhere in the rule and or_valued_selections is empty. Q1 and the description both use conjunctive framing ("carries all of ... together in one invocation").

Investigative framing: this is an argument-injection authentication bypass, so the identity the resulting session holds is not the identity that authenticated. Q6 is written as the load-bearing question on that point (which identity did the login resolve to, given ' -localadmin' occupies the password position), Q2 records the launch-side account as a distinct fact from the session identity, and the full cue_user_actor pair (Q11-Q14) is emitted because the User on the alerting event will typically be the backup service account, where the user pivot degenerates and the parent-process substitute carries the answer.

The rule's parameter combination has no benign producer — an operator supplies a password to -clp, not a flag, and does not append _localadmin__ to a username. Baseline and scope questions are therefore framed as measuring prior attempts and reach, not as false-positive calibration; their contexts say so explicitly so an analyst does not read a non-zero historical count as normalisation. rule.falsepositives is "Unknown", consistent with this.

Q3's context directs the analyst to the application's own request logs, which are not an ingested logsource in this pipeline's category set; the query stays process_creation and returns the parent context that is available on the endpoint. The request-log review is flagged via answer_sources manual_review rather than promised as a query, so the "if context mentions a log source, query that source" rule is not violated — no queryable logsource is named.

cue_user_actor.clustering (Q13) keeps the template's deliberate omission of a host.name filter: the question is explicitly cross-host, so a host fallback would invert its intent. The service-principal degeneration case is handled by its paired substitute (Q14).

The backup service is stated mechanically as a credential store with broad file access in the description, because that is what sets the consequence of an administrative token being issued without a password check — not as a severity claim.

notes: Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not by trusting the decomposer. condition_topology reports shape all_AND for the bare `selection` condition; the selection's value is a SINGLE map (TargetObject|contains plus Details|contains|all), not a list of maps, so there is no hidden implicit OR. The `details_values` list ['powershell', '-command'] sits under one field with the |all modifier, which is intra-field conjunction, not a branch OR. AND framing is therefore correct and Q1 states both conditions must hold on the same event.

Rule is technique-tagged T1202 (Indirect Command Execution) and the brief's attack_brief is T1202-only, so T1202 drives the chain decomposition and dimensions. The substance of the detection is T1546.001 (Change Default File Association) — writing a file-class \shell\open\command\ handler — which is why Q3 asks which file class was hijacked and Q8 anchors on powershell.exe under explorer.exe. T1546.001 is not tagged on the rule and is not claimed in techniques[]; it informs question framing only.

EventType equality was not authored into any query. The source detection carries no EventType clause, and endpoint telemetry emits ECS event.action values rather than Sysmon SetValue literals, so none was added.

Registry deletion is not observable in endpoint telemetry (no key/value delete events), so no question asks whether the handler was removed. Reversion is judged from the key's re-modification history in Q14 (-90d, same anchor) and from whether the payload executed (Q8).

Details (value data) is present on roughly 79% of endpoint registry modifications. Every question whose answer depends on it — Q1, Q3, Q4 — states the fallback platform-neutrally (read the key on the host) rather than assuming the field is populated.

powershell.script_block_logging (Q6) is KEEP_EXACT; its detection block, fields, and service: powershell + EventID: 4104 logsource are unmodified. Only range was adapted from +/-5m to +4h, because the handler executes on the user's next file open rather than at registry-write time — a +/-5m window around the write would return 0 by construction for the very content the question asks for.

Q1, Q2, and Q3 carry frozen question-set template fields verbatim (including the process.code_signature.* columns) per validate_template_fields; Q1 and Q3 therefore share the host+TargetObject anchor and field list. They are retained as distinct questions because they serve different phases — Q1 is triage confirmation that both detection conditions hold, Q3 is the analysis-phase judgment of which file class was hijacked.

hint_dispositions.reason: The replacement is predicated on the alert being a credential-dumping command invocation, where 'which credential store was targeted' (LSASS/SAM/NTDS) is read from the CommandLine. This alert is a file write of a spyware-implant component into a protected system directory; there is no credential access command on the file event, and DevilsTongue's credential theft is in-memory harvesting of browser password stores and messaging data performed by the loaded DLL, not an LSASS/SAM/NTDS dump. The upstream client that received the exploit is also several stages removed from this system32 drop (the escalation runs in between), so a crash event does not reliably time-correlate to the file write. That upstream-execution angle is instead covered by the delivery-vector parent lookup (Q5), the patch-status check naming both CVEs (Q4), and the precursor alert sweep (Q16).

The CommandLine|contains and ParentCommandLine|contains lists are internally OR (any one value matches), which is stated in Q1 as a list of alternatives inside the one condition, not as a disjunction between selections.

Q8 (cue_parent_process.clustering) is re-anchored from the template's process_creation default to `category: file_activity`, per the template's own notes_to_llm ("consider adapting to file_event ... a file_event query scoped to the parent's Image can reveal the triggering document path"). The exploitation path for this rule runs through content written into the service's own directories and deleted immediately after evaluation, so the file event is often the only surviving artifact. Anchored on ProcessGuid|expand '%ParentProcessGuid%' plus host.name rather than the dead %file_paths%/%file_dirs% placeholders or a host-only filter. file_activity rather than file_event because the service deletes the evaluated content — the deletion event is as informative as the write. No hash is projected: file writes carry none, and the hash pivot runs dropped path -> later execution -> process.hash.*, which the context directs the analyst to follow.

Style: the rule is CVE-specific, so the affected product family and the CVE ID are named — they are the rule's own detection target and the analyst cannot check patch status without them. The investigation is framed on the generalizable pattern (an internet-facing file-transfer service spawning an interpreter it has no reason to spawn, via content written into directories it evaluates) rather than on the historical intrusion set, per style_guide §2 and §3. Specific callback addresses, file names, and the reused GUID from the reference material are deliberately omitted from analyst-visible prose: they are point-in-time indicators from one wave of exploitation, and the file, module, and egress questions surface the equivalent artifacts empirically without dating the playbook.

Q14 (cue_user_actor.clustering) keeps the template's deliberate omission of a host.name filter — the question is explicitly cross-environment, and on a clustered transfer deployment the shared service account is exactly what makes it useful. The service-principal degeneration case is handled by its paired substitute (Q15).

notes: Condition topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not by trusting the decomposer. The condition is a bare `selection`; the brief reports shape all_AND and that is genuine. The selection is a single map of field/value pairs, not a list of maps, so there is no positive-path list-form implicit OR for the decomposer to have missed. The two list values it does contain are the intra-field carve-outs: `CommandLine|contains: [/delete, /change]` is intra-field membership (fires on either token) and `CommandLine|contains|all: [/TN, \Microsoft\Windows\Defrag\ScheduledDefrag]` requires both. Q1 is therefore framed with AND across fields and with the honest intra-field "either /delete or /change" disjunction on the one field that takes it, matching what the rule actually fires on.

Rule substance kept deliberately small. Removing ScheduledDefrag disables maintenance, not security — it sits at the edge of T1562 rather than inside it, and the identical command ships in debloat scripts, VDI golden-image builds, and SSD guidance, so the false-positive population is large and the signal weak alone. No question or context asserts that disabling defrag is itself notable. The playbook is built around the surrounding sequence instead: Q9 (siblings under the alerting parent) is the load-bearing question, supported by Q17 (other persistence and configuration tooling in the window), Q10 (other scheduled tasks touched), Q7 (other TaskCache writes), Q11 (host clustering) and Q12 (prior alerts). VDI, golden-image and SSD hosts are named mechanically in Q2 and Q3 as the specific benign population.

The two mechanical reasons an operator disables defrag are stated in the description without severity language: defrag rewrites unallocated sectors and so destroys deleted-file recoverability an operator may want preserved, and the command also appears inside broader sweeps that switch off scheduled maintenance. The threat-intel reference for this rule describes an encrypted virtual filesystem living in sectors the OS believes are free; that mechanism is generalised into the first reason rather than transcribed, per the technique-focused rule guidance — the rule is tagged T1053.005 with a generic title, so no actor, campaign, or platform is named.

techniques.name: Disable or Modify Windows Event Log

attack_chain_coverage.label: registry_modification
attack_chain_coverage.description: Actor creates the MiniNt key under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control, either directly or by renaming an existing key onto the path

attack_chain_coverage.label: mechanism_identification
attack_chain_coverage.description: The registry write emulates the preinstallation environment, which prevents the Event Log service from starting — identify the control targeted and the command used

attack_chain_coverage.label: attribution
attack_chain_coverage.description: Determine which process wrote the key and what launched it — the rule carries no binary, so the writing process and its parent are the attribution spine

attack_chain_coverage.label: effect_trigger
attack_chain_coverage.description: The key only takes effect at boot; the host must restart before the Event Log service is skipped

attack_chain_coverage.label: log_gap_detection
attack_chain_coverage.description: Anomalous gap in event records with no clearing event and no service stop — the fingerprint of collection suppression rather than log clearing

attack_chain_coverage.label: post_suppression_activity
attack_chain_coverage.description: Activity the suppression was meant to enable, observable only through telemetry that does not depend on the Windows event log

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\MiniNt (rule-pinned); analytic lists Run, Services, Security Settings, LSASS as the generic monitored set
mutable_dispositions.notes: The rule pins one exact key path, so the environment-specific path list collapses to it. Every key-anchored query carries TargetObject|expand '%TargetObject%', which hydrates to that path. The generic Run/Services/Policies set is covered fleet-agnostically by the host-wide registry question.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: regedit.exe, msiexec.exe (analytic's example allowlist of legitimate registry tools)
mutable_dispositions.notes: Not injected as a query filter. MiniNt has no legitimate population, so an allowlist of registry tools cannot exonerate the write — a regedit.exe or msiexec.exe write to this key would be no more expected than any other. The parent question surfaces lineage without filtering it.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — flag unsigned executables or abnormal lineage performing the modification

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — correlation window between registry modification, service stop, and audit policy commands
mutable_dispositions.notes: Expressed as query ranges rather than values: +7d for the restart that triggers the effect (the reboot may be days later), +4h for post-write process activity, +/-1h for other tampering, +/-30m for co-occurring registry writes.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — monitored services such as EventLog or custom loggers
mutable_dispositions.notes: The targeted service is fixed by the technique (the Windows Event Log service) and is not tampered with directly — the key prevents it from starting, so there is no service-state event to query. Named in context on the what-was-disabled and protection-status questions instead.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — accounts authorized to legitimately modify audit policies or disable services
mutable_dispositions.notes: No account is authorized to create MiniNt on a running production host, so an authorized-admin allowlist has no discriminating power here. The user/host question frames account identity as attribution rather than as an approval check.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — expected administrative tools/processes to prevent false positives
mutable_dispositions.notes: Deliberately not applied. Excluding administrative tools would suppress the most likely delivery route for this key (reg.exe or a PowerShell cmdlet run by an operator). The writing process is reported, not filtered.

Recommended, not must_include. Startup-folder drops and scheduled-task XML definitions are unrelated to a key that prevents the Event Log service from starting; what ran on the host after the write is covered by the activity-after-tampering question, which is not restricted to persistence paths.

The rule pins no binary (rule.primary_binary is null), so %Image% hydrates to whatever process the operator happened to use. Recommended. MiniNt has no legitimate population on a running production host, so user recall cannot resolve legitimacy — there is no benign action a user would recall performing that produces this key. One organizational check (change_ticket) is retained to rule out imaging and bench-build workflows.

Recommended. Work-hours alignment calibrates activity that has a legitimate variant; this key does not, so the timing of the write changes nothing about the verdict. The timing that matters is the write-to-restart interval, which the restart question covers.

Recommended. The question asks whether the method matches how the organization normally makes this change; no organization has a normal method for creating MiniNt, so the comparison has no baseline. Slots spent instead on attribution (parent lineage, spawned children) and on post-write activity.

hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection has 2 alternative branches. The condition string ('selection') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. (A list of scalar values under a single field is different — that is intra-field membership, not a branch OR.)
hints_acted_on.where: Description and Q1 — both use 'either ... or' framing for the two positive branches (TargetObject equal to the MiniNt path with EventType CreateKey, or NewName equal to the MiniNt path). Q1's context tells the analyst to note which alternative fired and what each implies: direct creation is the single-command primitive, a rename onto the path indicates the key was staged elsewhere first to avoid a path-anchored detection.

notes: Primary technique T1685.001: the rule fires on the exact registry primitive that suppresses Windows event log collection. T1112 is the same act viewed as a registry modification and contributes the parent_process_analysis dimension; T1685 is the parent tool-tampering technique from the brief's attack_brief and contributes user_context.

EventType: CreateKey was dropped from every authored query. The endpoint agent emits ECS event.action values (creation, modification, deletion), never the Sysmon literal CreateKey, so an EventType equality condition would match nothing. The TargetObject path alone is specific enough — HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\MiniNt has no legitimate population on a running host — so dropping the condition costs no precision. EventType and NewName remain in Q1's frozen fields list for display.

The rule's second branch (NewName) is a key rename onto the MiniNt path. NewName is not authored as a query selector because the key-anchored queries expand %TargetObject%, which hydrates from whichever branch fired; adding a NewName clause would over-restrict the host-history and fleet-scope questions.

Approved-change framing was deliberately limited to a single question. MiniNt has no legitimate population on a running production Windows host, so 'was this authorized' has almost no discriminating power; the remaining organizational_context templates were skipped and the slots spent on attribution and on what followed the write.

Registry deletion is not observable on this telemetry, so no question promises confirmation that the key was removed. The re-modification history question frames reversion through later writes to the same path, and the protection-status question directs the analyst to inspect the host for current state.

Q10's service: security question, Q11's protection-status context and Q12's post-write activity context all state the same mechanical point in different places: after the key takes effect, absence of Security-channel records is expected rather than reassuring, and the surviving evidence is endpoint process telemetry, forwarded copies of earlier records, and other hosts.

notes: Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not from the brief's shape field alone. shape: all_AND is genuine. The positive path is a single selection with a single scalar field (ParentImage|endswith: \System32\dns.exe) — there is no list-form on the positive path at all, so the known decomposer gap (not descending into selections) cannot bite here. The only list-form is Image|endswith under the `filter` block, which sits under `not` in the condition — De Morgan turns intra-field OR membership into an AND of four negations (child is not werfault AND not conhost AND not dnscmd AND not dns). Q1 is framed conjunctively: child of \System32\dns.exe AND not in the exclusion list.

IMPORTANT for reviewers: the rule places NO positive constraint on the child process. The child appears only in a negative filter. Any child of \System32\dns.exe other than werfault.exe/conhost.exe/dnscmd.exe/dns.exe fires this rule. Q1's context and the description both say so explicitly, because an analyst who assumes the alert has already characterised the child will misread it.

T1569 is not in rule.techniques (which lists T1190 and T1569.002) but IS present in brief.attack_brief with its own all_dimensions (obfuscation_check, time_correlation, tuning_parameter, user_context). Listed under techniques[] as secondary so dimension_coverage entries do not carry a dangling technique reference.

Primary technique is T1190: the rule exists to catch the consequence of exploiting an internet-reachable service. T1569.002 is secondary — it contributes the service-execution follow-on angle (registry service-key modification, Security 4697) rather than describing what the rule fires on. The rule detects a child of the service, not a service being executed.

Q6 re-anchor recorded here as it is a template adaptation, not a mutable element: cue_parent_process.mechanism_decode's stock query is ProcessGuid|expand '%ParentProcessGuid%'. ParentProcessGuid is frequently unavailable on sigma alerts, and AND-ing host.name onto a ProcessGuid lookup does not rescue it. Re-anchored (ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY is sanctioned for this) to host.name + Image|endswith [dns.exe, werfault.exe] over -7d, which preserves the template's intent (understand the parent instance and how it came to spawn this child) while answering the rule-specific question the stock query could not: did the DNS service crash and restart. werfault.exe is included deliberately — the rule excludes it as a child, so crash evidence never raises this alert and must be pulled separately.

Q4 (initial_access.campaign_scope, position: start) is placed 4th rather than later despite being a fleet-scope question. For a wormable server-side vulnerability the 'how many DNS servers' question is triage-relevant, not a closing question, and the template's position: start agrees.

No CommandLine|contains constraint is authorable anywhere: rule.commandline_values is empty and the rule has no command-line criteria. Q5 and Q10 are therefore phrased without any parameter-filter claim ('decode its full command line', 'this same child binary'), so Q-vs-query agreement holds by construction. Q1/Q2/Q3/Q7 are entity-scoped on ProcessGuid, which auto-satisfies.

Style: CVE-2020-1350 is named in the description and in Q3/Q8/Q11 context — the rule title carries the CVE and patch status is load-bearing triage, so the ID is both sanctioned and necessary. No vendor, researcher, writeup, actor, or incident chain is named. The 'SIGRed' marketing name is deliberately not used. The wire mechanics in Q8's context (SIG record, 512-byte UDP limit, 4,096 with EDNS0, TC truncation flag forcing TCP retry) are drawn from the technical references and stated mechanically, without attribution.

The alert is honestly framed as a heuristic in the description and in Q1's context: the exploit is processed inside dns.exe over the wire and produces no process-creation evidence, so this rule observes a consequence and cannot demonstrate exploitation. Q3 (patch status / TcpReceivePacketSize) is positioned early precisely so a patched host short-circuits toward false positive or failed attempt rather than assumed compromise.

The domain-controller and SYSTEM observations are stated as mechanical facts (the DNS Server role is a prerequisite of Windows domain environments; the service runs as SYSTEM so its children inherit that context) and are used to explain why the follow-on and service-installation questions matter — not as severity claims.

user_actor pair — non-deduplicable. Both variants of both cue_user_actor pairs are emitted: Q14 (user-pattern baseline) with Q15 (parent-pattern baseline), and Q16 (user-pivot clustering) with Q17 (parent-pattern clustering). This rule fires on a user opening a document, so the alert normally carries an interactive account and the user pivot is meaningful; but the rule places no constraint on User, and a document opened through an automated conversion or preview path fires it under a service identity, where the user pivot degenerates. skipped_templates.reason: Query is host.name + Image|endswith '%Image%' aggregated over -90d, which for this rule resolves to "how often does this host run csc.exe" — a count driven by developer toolchains and server-side .NET page compilation, neither of which has any bearing on Word invoking the compiler. The rule's discriminator is the parent, not the binary. The -90d first-seen judgment for the actual pattern is carried by the reflected Q14 (user-scoped) and Q15 (parent-scoped), both of which count WINWORD.EXE -> csc.exe rather than any csc.exe use, and Q6 covers csc.exe activity on the host in the alert window.

Budget — the 8 must_include templates, the 4 non-deduplicable cue_user_actor variants and the 3 hint-driven logsource questions (application, file_event, network_connection) consume 15 of 18 slots, and the remaining 3 went to the compiler decode (Q6), the payload-execution hash pivot (Q10) and the host activity aggregate (Q18). The prior-alert sweep is the least applicable tier-3 question for this rule: this pairing is an initial-access event, so the decisive evidence sits forward of the alert (what the document spawned, what was written, what executed) rather than in earlier detections on the host, and the -24h same-rule alert count across the environment (Q13) already covers the alert-correlation angle at the breadth that matters here.

notes: Primary technique is T1203 — the rule fires on the exploitation artefact itself (the .NET Framework's C# compiler being invoked by the document handler as a consequence of the SOAP WSDL parser flaw), not on the user's act of opening the file. T1204.002 and T1566.001 are the delivery half of the same chain and drove Q3, Q10 and Q13; their parent techniques T1204 and T1566 appear in the brief's attack_brief and contribute only restatements of the same dimensions plus T1204's user_context, which Q4 covers. All five are recorded in techniques[] because all five carry an attack_brief.

Condition topology is all_AND with a single selection and no list-valued keys (or_valued_selections is empty), so Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing: both the parent image and the child image must match in the same event. No disjunctive language is used anywhere.

Q11 uses `service: application`, never `category: application`, per AGENTS.md — Application is a Windows event-log channel, and windows-logsources keys channel scoping off service:. The brief's hint text says `category: application`; the AGENTS.md channel rule overrides it, and the audit's category check reads the service name through its own fallback, so the logsource-coverage hint is satisfied either way.

CVE-specific rule, so the exploitation mechanism is described directly (the SOAP WSDL parser flaw, the document that reaches it, the compiler it invokes). No historical incident is narrated: no sender, sample hash, URL, IP or dropped filename from the reference material appears in any analyst-visible field, and the payload-execution question describes the user-writable staging pattern generically rather than the specific filenames one sample used.

Hash handling: file writes carry no hash, so no hash question is authored against Q8 or Q9. The pivot is recorded in Q10 — dropped path, later execution, Hashes projected on the process_creation event — and Q8's context states the constraint explicitly so an analyst does not look for a hash on the file write.

playbooks.name: Exploitation Activity of CVE-2025-59287 - WSUS Suspicious Child Process
playbooks.description: Detects a command interpreter or PowerShell host (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, or powershell_ise.exe) starting as the child of a Windows Server Update Services process. The rule requires the child binary to match, together with either a parent whose image ends in wsusservice.exe, or a w3wp.exe

questions.question: Is the alerting process one of the rule's shell binaries, and did it start under either wsusservice.exe or a w3wp.exe worker running the WsusPool application pool?
Does this host hold the WSUS role, and is the alerting account expected to run a shell on it?
Is this WSUS parent expected to spawn a shell, and what started the parent itself?
What web request reached the WSUS web services immediately before this shell started?
Is the WSUS role on this host patched against the known unauthenticated remote code execution flaws?
What other child processes did this same WSUS parent instance spawn?
Did this same detection fire on other WSUS servers in the environment?
What did the shell actually run, and was any of it encoded or obfuscated?
Did PowerShell script block logging capture the full script content on this host?
Were PowerShell security controls bypassed or weakened around this execution?
What modules did the WSUS parent process load in the hour before the shell was spawned?
What files did the alerting shell write, and where did they land?
Did the shell or its related tooling connect outbound from this server around the alert?
What other process activity occurred on this server around the time of the alert?
Has this account previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit its role?
Has this WSUS parent historically driven the rule's pattern, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this account do across the environment around this time?
Did the same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window, or is it isolated to this server?

attack_chain_coverage.description: Adversary sends crafted input to an internet- or network-facing application endpoint (the WSUS reporting/client/API SOAP endpoints).

attack_chain_coverage.label: error_or_anomalous_response
attack_chain_coverage.description: The request produces elevated 4xx/5xx responses or unusual methods/paths against the published endpoint, visible only in the web server access/error logs.

attack_chain_coverage.label: server_process_spawns_shell_or_loads_modules
attack_chain_coverage.description: The server process (w3wp.exe or the service itself) spawns a shell/LOLbin or loads non-standard modules — the event this rule fires on.

attack_chain_coverage.label: payload_written_to_writable_path
attack_chain_coverage.description: The exploited process drops or modifies files in user-writable paths (the T1203 analytic's file-write stage), staging tooling or collection output.

attack_chain_coverage.label: outbound_callback
attack_chain_coverage.description: Optional outbound callback from the host — collected data posted to an external endpoint, or a command channel established shortly after the spawn.

playbooks.name: Exploitation Attempt Of CVE-2020-1472 - Execution of ZeroLogon PoC
playbooks.description: Detects cmd.exe spawning a binary named cool.exe or zero.exe whose command line carries both `Administrator` and `-c`, together with either a `taskkill /f /im` payload or a `powershell` payload — the invocation form of the widely circulated CVE-2020-1472 (ZeroLogon) proof-of-concept executables. The

questions.question: Does the alerting command line match this rule — a cmd.exe-spawned cool.exe or zero.exe carrying Administrator and -c, plus either a taskkill payload or a powershell payload?
Is this user and host expected to run domain controller exploitation tooling?
What started the cmd.exe that spawned this binary, and is that grandparent chain expected?
What other child processes did the same cmd.exe instance spawn?
Decode the full invocation of the exploit binary — which domain controller, which domain, and what command was passed to -c?
What did the exploit binary actually launch after the Netlogon authentication step?
Did this host open connections to remote-service ports on the domain controller around the time of the alert?
Was a domain controller machine account changed, or an anonymous or machine-account logon recorded, around the time of this alert?
Was a service installed or did a process fault on the domain controller in the hours around this alert?
What modules did the exploit binary load, and do their signer and hash identify a known build?
What files did the exploit binary and its children write on this host?
Did cross-process memory-write or execution-hijack API calls occur on this host in the alert window?
Has this host run a binary of this name at any point in the last 90 days?
Where has this user authenticated recently?
Has this user previously produced this rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven this rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this user do across the network around this time?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window, or is the activity isolated to this host?

Host + ParentName + Image aggregation over -90d, which counts how often cmd.exe spawned this child binary on the host — a count dominated by ordinary shell use and unrelated to the setup-script constraint. Host + ParentName scoped process listing over +/-15m, whose result set is the same cmd.exe children the follow_on question already returns, minus the setup-script constraint that makes it meaningful. The alert-window neighborhood is covered by the host clustering aggregation (Q16).

Fleet-wide ParentName + Image aggregation over -24h. With the parent pinned to cmd.exe this degenerates into a fleet-wide count of one binary's executions under any shell. The reflected parent-pattern clustering (Q15) asks the same fleet-scope question with the rule's own criteria, and the reflected parent-pattern baseline (Q13) covers the longer window.

-90d host-scoped count of the child Image grouped by User. The child is whatever binary the setup script called, so this measures how often that binary runs on the host generally, not whether this pattern is routine; for a common payload name the count is high for reasons unrelated to the alert. The reflected parent-pattern baseline (Q13) counts the rule's actual pattern instead.

user_actor pair — non-deduplicable. cue_user_actor.baseline / baseline_svc (Q12/Q13) and cue_user_actor.clustering / clustering_svc (Q14/Q15) are both emitted because the setup-scripts hook runs under SYSTEM in the normal case, which is exactly the condition under which the user pivot degenerates.

skipped_templates.reason: The hook executes unattended during a post-upgrade reboot under SYSTEM, so there is no interactive user to ask. The equivalent human check — did anyone plan servicing or authorise a post-setup customization for this host — is asked by the change-ticket question (Q3) against the record rather than against recall, and Q2 asks whether the host and account fit the servicing work.

The method question ("is this how your organization normally makes this change") collapses into the change-ticket and servicing-window questions for this rule, because the only legitimate procedure that reaches this code path is image deployment or a feature update. Q3 and Q4 cover it without a third redundant ProcessGuid boilerplate question.

Its Startup-folder and Tasks-XML path list is generic, and the file-write question this rule actually needs is the one about the setup script itself. Threat-specific rule (family in title), so style_guide §2's exception permits naming FakeUpdates/SocGholish generically. The user-participant angle is treated as real evidence rather than filler: Q2 asks what site the user was on and whether an update prompt appeared, routed to organizational_knowledge / manual_review. Q9 uses file_event correlated by host.name + TargetFilename path/extension anchors rather than process lineage, because the writer of the archive is the browser and is NOT in the alerting process's ProcessGuid/ParentProcessGuid lineage - the lineage break is the point of the question. Legitimate cause is narrow but real - some genuine software updaters drive script hosts. The discriminators named across Q3 (what started wscript.exe), Q9 (where the archive came from), Q5 (what the script did), and Q13/Q14 (whether this user or this parent has ever produced the pattern) are the ones that separate an updater from a loader.

Deviation from KEEP_EXACT on masquerading.binary_origin's detection block - the template ships 'TargetFilename|contains|expand: %file_name%'. Per resources/patterns_sigma.yaml, %file_name% maps to event_data.process.name, i.e. the WRITING process's name on a file_event alert, not the written file's name. Shipping it verbatim would search for files whose path contains the writer's process name, which is not what the question asks. Substituted %TargetFilename% (which hydrates to the written file's name) keeping the |contains modifier, host anchor, -30d range and the frozen fields list unchanged. The template's process_creation-shaped assumption is the defect, not the swap.

Deviation from ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY defaults on cue_artifact.artifact_verification - re-pointed from process_creation (Image|endswith / CommandLine|contains legs, Hashes -> process.hash) to image_load, exactly as the template's notes_to_llm directs for DLL artifacts. This is the load-bearing question for the rule - a file write carries no hash or signer, so "is this the real Microsoft DLL or an impostor" is only answerable on the load event, where ImageLoaded, Signed, Signature, SignatureStatus and Hashes are populated. The Image|endswith execution leg is dead for a .dll artifact (an executable's path never ends in .dll).

Deviation from ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY defaults on cue_artifact.follow_on - dropped the 'Image|endswith|expand %TargetFilename%' leg for the same reason (a process Image cannot end in .dll) and kept only the CommandLine|contains leg, which catches explicit invocation through rundll32.exe / regsvr32.exe / installer registration. The implicit search-order load, which is the rule's actual threat model, is covered by the image_load question rather than here; the context says so, so a zero result is not read as "unused".

No hash question is asked against the file event itself. Defend populates a hash on file writes in ~0.00007% of events; the hash pivot for this rule is the load event (image_load, dll.hash), which Q9 uses directly.

No question uses host-only scoping against file telemetry. Every file_event/file_activity query is anchored on host.name plus a TargetFilename constraint, on ProcessGuid/ParentProcessGuid lineage, or on the rule's own reflected selection block. The one fleet-wide file query (cue_artifact.scope) is filename-anchored with no host filter by design.

Q4 (masquerading.true_identity) and Q7 (cue_process_tool.process_chain) share a 'ProcessGuid|expand' selection but project disjoint fields - identity metadata (Image/OriginalFileName/Hashes) versus lineage (Image/CommandLine/ParentImage/ParentCommandLine) - and answer different steps. Both retained; neither is the alert-lookup boilerplate filler.

T1036.005 is primary - the rule fires on a file bearing a legitimate system DLL's name written outside that resource's legitimate location, which is the sub-technique's definition. T1036 contributes the execution_context and time_correlation dimensions and the write-then-execute correlation window, but its analytic is process_creation/service-registration shaped and does not drive the skeleton.

Style call: the rule title carries a threat-actor designation. The style guide's threat-specific exception covers malware families, not actor names, so the designation appears only in `name:` — no analyst-visible prose names the actor, attributes it, or narrates a historical intrusion chain or targeted sector. Questions describe the observable indicator classes instead.

Q-vs-query agreement on an IOC rule: every question that references 'these hashes' is either entity-scoped (ProcessGuid) or carries the rule's Hashes|contains list verbatim via a REFLECTED template. No question claims command-line or parameter filtering, since the rule constrains no command line (rule.commandline_values is empty).

Q8's Security-channel question is scoped by host.name on codes 4624/4648/4672 rather than by the Kerberos codes named in the T1212 analytic (4768/4769/4770): those are logged on the domain controller, not on the alerting member host, so a host-scoped query for them would return nothing. 4624/4648/4672 are logged on this host and carry the same authentication-abuse and privileged-rights signal the analytic describes.

Content analysis of a SAM hive dump is a manual forensic retrieval with no log-side answer; its investigative value (which accounts/hashes are exposed, are all hives captured) is delivered by credential_target_identification (Q5) and credential_exposure_assessment (Q11), which are more specific for this credential-access rule.

The dump file name carries a random component (SAM-<random>.dmp), so filename-endswith baseline/scope queries do not generalize; the rule-pattern baselines (Q13, Q14, Q16) count the rule's actual selection instead, and the dump's cross-host spread is covered by the fleet-wide parent-pattern question (Q16).

hint_dispositions.reason: The T1003.002 registry footprint for SAM dumping is a hive READ/EXPORT, not a value write: reg save HKLM\SAM opens the hive for read (Security 4656 handle events / process_access EID10, both excluded from this endpoint telemetry), and the tool's own registry activity is key create/delete (Sysmon EID12), not the value modifications (EID13/14) that a `category: registry_set` query returns after conversion to event.category:registry. A registry_set question anchored on HKLM\SAM would therefore be a match-nothing query on the deployed telemetry. The credential-store-targeting dimension this hint aims at is covered instead by credential_target_identification (Q5), which reads the hive-export command line and names HKLM\SAM/SYSTEM/SECURITY, with the registry-read visibility gap stated in its context.

notes: Topology verified by hand against rule.detection, not taken from the brief alone: `selection` holds two fields, `Image|endswith` and `CommandLine|contains`, each with a list of SCALARS. That is intra-field membership (an OR within one field), which is the documented carve-out — the two fields still AND together. There is no positive-path list-of-maps here, so `shape: all_AND` is genuine and Q1 is framed conjunctively: image is rundll32.exe or cmd.exe AND the command line contains one of the three names. Q1's context tells the analyst which of the three matched, because the DLL branch and the batch branch lead to different follow-up evidence.

Framing: the rule detects a public adversary-emulation utility, not malware. A sanctioned detection-validation or red team exercise is therefore treated as a leading hypothesis (Q2, position start) rather than a false-positive footnote, and the fleet-distribution question (Q12) and parent-scoped fleet window (Q16) are written as evidence FOR or AGAINST that hypothesis — a planned exercise touches a defined host set in a tight window, one host alone does not.

The actor whose playbook the utility emulates is deliberately not named in any analyst-visible field. The rule fires on the emulation utility's hardcoded artifact names, which anyone can run; naming the emulated actor would assert an attribution the alert cannot support. Prose is framed on what the rule actually detects — proxy execution through rundll32 (T1218.011) and batch execution through cmd.exe (T1059.003) — and the tool name itself appears only where the rule title already carries it.

Q9 scopes on `Image|endswith|expand '%Image%'` rather than the rule's binary list: the rule constrains Image (rundll32.exe or cmd.exe), so %Image% is a faithful proxy for the alerting branch, and scoping to the branch that actually fired is tighter than querying both.
Q5 (hacking_tool.tool_specific_artifacts) keeps its KEEP_EXACT query and frozen fields list verbatim, including EventType — the template's fields list is compared exactly by validate_template_fields.

Same read-side blind spot as the process_access hint; the exposure is instead established from the dump file itself (Q1/Q5/Q18) and the exposed-account assessment (Q8). notes: T1608 (Stage Capabilities) is the rule's only tag and is a PRE-platform technique -- its attack_brief carries no Windows analytics, no mutable_elements, and an empty all_dimensions, so attack_chain_coverage and dimension_coverage are legitimately empty and no attack:{id}.{dimension} questions were authored. The behaviour the rule actually observes is proxy/tunnelling on the endpoint (T1090 / T1102 / T1572 in substance), and the five llm_generated questions carry that investigation rather than the resource-development framing.

HCM is genuine, Microsoft-signed software relaying to Microsoft-owned infrastructure, so signature and reputation questions cannot discriminate here and none were authored as a verdict path. The signer columns survive only inside the frozen universal/registry template field lists, where the question text asks for coherence between signer and key rather than for a trust verdict. The discriminators the playbook is built around are authorization (Q9), host role (Q2), and the relay namespace/tenant (Q8).

Q8 (relay namespace and tenant) is the single most decisive question in this playbook and is not answerable from registry telemetry -- HCM keeps its connection strings in its own configuration alongside the installed listener. Q5 authors the service-installation record as `service: system` with EventID 7045, not `category: system` -- channel scoping keys off service:, and a category: form would silently produce an unscoped query.

No cue_user_actor template appears in this brief, so no user-pivot / service_principal_substitute pair was authored and no always_include keys are present. User attribution on the registry event is surfaced via the frozen universal.host_user_context field list (Q2).

Style: the rule title names a malware family, so style_guide §2's threat-specific exception applies. Prose nonetheless stays technique-framed (rundll32 proxying a DLL via an ordinal/short-name export, T1218.011) rather than family-framed, because the pattern is shared across loader families and the durable substance is the technique. No writeup, vendor, or researcher is credited; no single historical incident chain is transcribed; no attribution adjectives used.

Q12 (cue_process_tool.baseline) deliberately does NOT use the template's bare Image|endswith rundll32.exe over 90d. rundll32.exe runs constantly on every Windows host, so that count answers nothing. Added a selection_writable_dir CommandLine|contains block ANDed with the host+binary scope, which is both the honest measurement and the Q-vs-query match for the question's 'DLLs from user-writable directories' claim.

Q3 (mechanism_decode) keeps the template's host+binary +/-5m scope rather than falling back to ProcessGuid. Over a five-minute window rundll32 volume is bounded, and the wider scope is doing real work here: loaders frequently invoke the same DLL more than once or chain a second DLL, which a ProcessGuid-scoped query would hide. The question makes no parameter-filter claim, so no CommandLine constraint is required.

All four REFLECTED templates (cue_process_tool.baseline_deviation, cue_process_tool.scope, cue_user_actor.baseline, cue_user_actor.baseline_svc) and cue_user_actor.clustering_svc keep their brief-composed detection blocks verbatim; only question/context wording was adapted. Any [REFLECTED REGRESSION] linter warning on these is a false positive.

cue_user_actor.baseline (Q14) is scoped on User|expand only with no host.name fallback, which the field-availability caveat would normally flag. Left as composed: the detection block of a REFLECTED template is not modifiable, and if User is unavailable the query returns nothing rather than something misleading. The parent-scoped sibling (Q15) is the compensating pivot.

The rule's CommandLine|endswith '\rundll32.exe' means the process launched with no DLL and no export argument. That is the load-bearing constraint, not the binary name — rundll32 with a DLL argument is ordinary. It was carried into the non-entity-scoped cue_process_tool.baseline query (Q12) so the 90-day history counts the argument-less form rather than all rundll32 use, which would be meaningless volume on any Windows host.

cue_parent_process.baseline (Q11) and cue_parent_process.scope (Q17) were left without the CommandLine constraint: both are already scoped by ParentName to a browser, and a browser spawning rundll32 at all is the anomaly regardless of arguments. The CommandLine field is projected in both so the analyst can tell the forms apart.

Q6's image_load query targets the browser parent rather than rundll32. An argument-less rundll32 loads no module of its own by command line, so its load list is only default system DLLs; the injected module, if it was loaded rather than mapped manually, appears in the browser's list. Manually mapped payloads leave no load event at all, which is stated in Q6's context.

A memory dump is unique per-capture data, not a redistributable binary — its hash carries no threat-intel reputation, and the file never executes so there is no execution event to read process.hash from. dedup_decisions.reason: Hash-of-execution pivot does not fit a memory dump: a .dmp is not an executable that later runs, and file writes carry no hash, so there is no execution event to read a process.hash from. Whether the dump is genuine credential material is covered by Q1/Q4 (writer + lsass target) and Q3 (still on disk for manual retrieval and hashing).

Content analysis of the file is not log-derivable — the .dmp content is raw LSASS memory, not a decodable script or config. The confirm-the-artifact angle (is this really taskmgr dumping lsass) is carried by verify_trigger_match and credential_target_identification.

A filename-only baseline of the lsass .dmp adds little over the rule-pattern baselines: cue_user_actor.baseline and cue_process_tool.baseline_deviation already answer whether this exact dump pattern has occurred for this user and on this host, and cue_process_tool.scope covers the fleet.

A 90-day baseline of taskmgr.exe alone (Image|endswith) measures ubiquitous, benign Task Manager usage and would normalize a common binary. The reflected rule-pattern baselines (cue_user_actor.baseline, cue_process_tool.baseline_deviation) count the lsass-dump firing specifically, which is the meaningful first-seen signal.

Children of taskmgr are the wrong pivot for this rule — the dump is written in-process (MiniDumpWriteDump), and post-dump handling (copy, compress, move the .dmp) is performed by unrelated processes, not taskmgr children. That activity is covered by cue_host_context.clustering and file.file_directory_context.

must_include template; its purpose is to identify the file the service executes and check its location, signature, and hash — which on a driver_load alert is answered directly and better by the load event itself. The template correlates file writes to the alerting ProcessGuid and its direct children. On a driver_load alert the ProcessGuid is the loading process (service control manager, or nothing at all for a boot-time load), which is not the process that wrote the .sys file — the write happened earlier, by an unrelated process, so the lineage correlation returns nothing by construction. The question it exists to answer (is the driver file on disk, and where did it come from) is asked directly by Q9, which anchors file writes on the alerting driver's own filename via %ImageLoaded%.

notes: condition_topology.shape is all_AND with a single selection, but that selection is a ~70-entry ImageLoaded|endswith list, so the match is disjunctive within it. Q1 and the description are framed accordingly — 'any one of' the catalogued filenames — and Q1 asks the analyst to record which name matched, since the entries range from named attacker tooling (mimidrv.sys, gmer64.sys) through hex-string sample names to short generic names a legitimate driver could carry. The 70 names are deliberately kept out of the question title and out of every query; the %ImageLoaded% placeholder carries whichever one fired.

Both of the rule's stated false-positive modes are name-collision cases (a vulnerable driver that kept its name across versions, a legitimate driver sharing a listed name). Q4 (hash/signer identification), Q2 (installed-product accounting), Q12 (deployment record), and Q13 (hash/signer drift behind the name) are the four questions that resolve them, and each says so in its context. This is the substantive difference from the hash-matching sibling rule, where the file identification is settled by the match itself.

Q1 keeps the brief template's frozen fields list ([ImageLoaded]) but re-anchors the query from ProcessGuid to host.name + ImageLoaded|endswith|expand on category driver_load: the alert is the load event itself, and the driver's identity, not a process's command line, is what the analyst is verifying. Same re-anchor applied to Q2/Q3/Q4.

Reviewer note: the rule's second branch reads `NewName: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCertDlls` — 'CurentControlSet' is a typo upstream in SigmaHQ and that branch will not match a real key rename. The either/or framing is retained as the brief's topology hint requires, and Q1 directs the analyst to note which branch fired, but in practice only the TargetObject branch is expected to fire. Not corrected here: the playbook does not modify the source rule.

Both branches use exact equality on the key path (no |endswith), so the rule matches only the literal CurrentControlSet form and only the key itself; ControlSet001/002 paths and value-level TargetObjects such as ...\AppCertDlls\<ValueName> would not match this rule as written. The mutable element TargetObject ('may vary by control set or group policy context') is noted against this, and all key-anchored questions expand the alert's own TargetObject rather than a hardcoded path.

No EventType equality condition existed in the source detection, so nothing was dropped on that account. No filter block exists either — the rule has no exclusion arm. NewName is retained in Q1's frozen universal.verify_trigger_match fields list as authored in the brief.

Q8 and Q9 anchor ImageLoaded|endswith|expand on '%Details%'. Details holds the DLL path payload for this key and is populated on roughly 79% of endpoint registry modifications; Q8's context gives the fallback (review host library loads for modules outside System32) when it is absent.

Registry deletion/cleanup is never promised: Q10 and Q13 both state that value deletion is not observable in this telemetry and point the persistence judgment at re-modification history and continued module loading instead.

A sibling playbook covers AppInit_DLLs (4f84b697). This playbook is scoped to AppCertDlls and the contexts draw the distinction where it changes the analyst's reasoning: AppCertDlls triggers on CreateProcess-family API calls rather than user32.dll linkage, has no LoadAppInit_DLLs/Secure Boot enablement gate, and — unlike AppInit_DLLs, which had real accessibility, IME and endpoint-security registrants — has essentially no legitimate population, so the questions target the DLL's identity and origin rather than whether the mechanism is in use.

Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. Both use explicit either/or framing over the two branches (TargetObject|endswith the AppInit_Dlls path OR NewName|endswith it via a key rename), with the not-filter arm (value data other than the literal (Empty)) preserved as an AND-ed exclusion. Q1's context tells the analyst to record which branch fired and states the downstream consequence: the TargetObject branch carries the DLL list in Details so the decode / on-disk / library-load questions are answerable, while the NewName rename branch carries no value data and those questions require reading the value off the host first. notes: Primary technique T1546.010: the rule fires exactly on the AppInit_Dlls value write. The rule's `filter: Details: (Empty)` is preserved as prose, not as a query clause. '(Empty)' is a Sysmon-emitted literal for empty value data and does not appear in Elastic Defend registry telemetry, so authoring it as a query filter would be inert. It is described in the description and Q1 context as the semantic exclusion it is: the rule targets population of the list, not clearing it.

Q8 (llm_generated) covers a triage question no template supplies: AppInit_DLLs is ignored when Secure Boot is enabled and when LoadAppInit_DLLs is 0, so the registration may be inert. Q9 and Q10 anchor ImageLoaded|endswith|expand on '%Details%'. AppInit_DLLs accepts a space- or comma-separated list, so a multi-DLL value will not match by suffix; both questions' contexts tell the analyst to run the lookup per path in that case, and Q9's context gives the fallback when Details is absent (~21% of endpoint registry modifications).

hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection_img has 2 alternative branches. The condition string ('all of selection_* and not 1 of filter_main_*') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. (A list of scalar values under a single field is different — that is intra-field membership, not a branch OR.)
hints_acted_on.where: Q1 question and context, and the playbook description. Both state the two-part requirement as selection_cli AND selection_img, and state selection_img itself as EITHER Image|endswith \net.exe / \net1.exe OR OriginalFileName net.exe / net1.exe — never flattened to AND. Q1's context instructs the analyst to read both fields, note which branch matched, and states the downstream consequence of each: an OriginalFileName-only match makes the binary-path question (Q12) and the other-LOLBin question (Q13) load-bearing because the file on disk was renamed; an Image-path-only match points at a repacked binary whose version resource was stripped; a both-branches match is the ordinary case and moves the investigation onto the account and the share. Q12's context restates the branch dependency so it reads standalone.

notes: Primary technique is T1021.002 (SMB/Windows Admin Shares): 'net use \\host\share /USER:acct pwd' is the native way an admin share is mounted, and its Windows analytic (share access followed by remote execution) is the chain the playbook skeleton follows. T1078 (Valid Accounts) is secondary and contributes the identity dimensions — which account, is it privileged, has it done this before. T1021 (Remote Services) appears in the attack_brief as the parent technique and contributes the command_analysis dimension; it is recorded as secondary because the rule tags only T1021.002 and T1078.

condition_topology.shape is OR_of_selections and the OR lives INSIDE selection_img, not between top-level selection groups: required_all_of is [selection_img, selection_cli] and or_valued_selections is [selection_img]. The disjunction is therefore branch-level within the binary-identification requirement, while selection_cli's three CommandLine|contains|all entries remain a strict AND. Q1 and the description preserve both halves — AND across the two selections, OR within selection_img — rather than distributing the OR across the whole condition, which would have described a rule that fires on any net.exe or on any ' use ' command line.

Sensitive-content handling: the rule exists because the password is rendered in cleartext in process telemetry, so every question is framed on the credential-exposure and remediation axis — which account was supplied, how privileged it is, where the password is stored (a person's memory versus a script's source), which servers it was presented to, and what rotation scope follows. No question directs the analyst to read, record, or reuse the password value, and Q2's context states explicitly that the value does not belong in case notes. No credential-shaped example strings appear anywhere in the prose.

Noisy-binary handling: net.exe is a routine administrative binary, so no question scopes on Image alone. Q2 (mechanism_decode) adds CommandLine|contains|all [' use ', '/USER:'] to its host+binary scope; the generic Image-scoped baseline and same_action_other_hosts templates were dropped in favour of the reflected pattern queries (Q11, Q14, Q15, Q16, Q17), which enforce the rule's full selection including the trailing-space filter. The only remaining %Image% uses are Q2 (process identity, with a CommandLine constraint) and Q12 (the alerting event's own path, ProcessGuid-scoped).

Reflected templates (Q11, Q14, Q15, Q16, Q17) keep the brief generator's detection block byte-verbatim, including the ':*\\' and '/USER:* *' wildcard entries and the filter_main_empty trailing-space filter. Only question, context and range were adapted. A [REFLECTED REGRESSION] lint warning on these is expected and is the known false positive documented for verbatim-preserved reflections — no detection block was modified, so reflection_overrides is empty.

phase_b emits "unknown template 'lolbin.historical_lolbin_baseline' in Q16". This is structural, not an authoring error: _load_template_fields() indexes question_sets/*.yaml by the presence of a `query_template` key, and reflection_kind templates deliberately carry no query_template because the brief generator composes their query from the rule's detection block. The template exists at resources/question_sets/lolbin.yaml:127 and its `fields: [CommandLine]` list is reproduced exactly in Q16. phase_b emits "REFLECTED template cue_process_tool.baseline_deviation dropped (confirm this was deliberate)". Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly: single selection, condition 'selection'. The only list-form on the positive path is a list of scalars under one field (CommandLine|contains|all), which is intra-field membership under an |all modifier — conjunctive by construction. all_AND is genuine; Q1 is framed conjunctively ("contains config, msdtc, start and auto together, and is its parent updata.exe").

Style: the rule is threat-specific (family name in title), so per style_guide §2 the family is named once, generically, in the description only. No question or context names it; the framing is the technique (T1574.001 service-side DLL search-order hijack) so the playbook survives the family name going stale.

Q6 field list includes Image although the rule has no Image field — the rule constrains only the parent and the arguments, so which utility ran the configuration (sc.exe, powershell.exe, a wrapper) is unknown at alert time and is itself an answer the question needs.

dedup_decisions.reason: Command-decode angle is covered by cue_artifact.mechanism_decode (script content) and powershell.script_block_logging (deobfuscated executed content). The process_tool variant (Image|endswith %Image% on the writer) would re-scope to the writing binary's other runs, adding no distinct analytical step for a filename-detected script drop.

Writer baseline keys on %Image% (likely powershell.exe / a shell / a server process) which is ubiquitous and noisy. cue_artifact.baseline (has THIS script name been created before on this host) is the targeted first-seen signal for a file-creation rule.

A %Image% baseline would baseline the loading binary, which for a sideload is often a common signed host process and gives low-signal volume. The targeted first-seen signal for an image_load rule is whether THIS module path has loaded on this host before, covered by cue_image_load.baseline (Q7).

A DLL module load is not a ticketed change action; legitimacy for this rule is resolved by human_recall (Q12) and timing_alignment (Q13) instead.
No standard organizational procedure governs module loads by installed software; redundant with human_recall/timing for this rule and adds no distinct coverage.

Work-hours alignment cannot make a run-as reassignment benign or malign on its own, and the timing signal that does discriminate here is whether the task fired after the change, which Q6 and Q7 measure against the trigger. Question count is already at 18.

The "is direct schtasks.exe use normal here" judgment is answered from measurement rather than policy recall by Q11 (this host's history of this pattern) and Q16 (fleet-wide distribution — scripted deployment versus one-off), which show what the environment's actual procedure is.
