Technique-focused framing per style_guide §2. The rule is not emerging_threats-tagged and its title names the application, not a malware family. The single reference is a vendor situational-awareness writeup of one 2023 supply-chain incident with named-actor attribution, a fixed installer/module hash set, and a C2 domain list; none of the attribution, the vendor credit, or the incident chain is transcribed. 3CXDesktopApp.exe is named throughout because it is the rule's detection anchor and the subject of every query.

The rule's version and hash indicators are point-in-time 2023 values, so the prose is deliberately not built around a campaign. The likeliest 2026 outcomes are an unpatched install or a version-string coincidence, and the playbook is ordered for that: Q1 separates the branches, Q10 asks how long the install has been present, and Q5 asks whether the alerting host is a patching outlier or one of many. The durable framing kept is that this is a signed, widely-deployed application whose build itself was altered — so a valid signature and normal-looking egress are the premise, not exculpatory, and the discriminators are build identity and behaviour. The reference's specific installer hashes and C2 domains are not embedded: the rule already carries its own hash list (reflected verbatim in Q6/Q11/Q12/Q13/Q15), and a fixed domain list would date the playbook while adding nothing the destination-profile framing in Q8 does not.

Q5 (fleet version spread) is llm_generated rather than reflected because it deliberately drops the FileVersion|contains constraint the rule carries — its purpose is to show which builds exist across the environment so the analyst can tell a single unpatched host from an install base on the same version. Reflecting the rule's selection would return only hosts already matching and answer nothing. Q6 (the reflected fleet_pattern query) is the complementary question and keeps the rule's selection verbatim.

Q4 and Q8 use Image|endswith|expand '%Image%' rather than pinning the literal path: unlike the parent-anchored sibling rule for this application, here the alerting process IS the softphone, so the alert's own %Image% is the correct anchor for its module loads and its egress.

Differentiation from the sibling playbook for 63f3605b (Potential Suspicious Child Process Of 3CXDesktopApp), same application: that rule is parent-anchored and investigates what the application spawned, so its skeleton is the parent_child technique set (parent_process_legitimacy, sibling_processes) plus the powershell set for decoding the child's command. This rule is build-anchored and investigates whether this install is the build the rule names, so its skeleton is identity/version triage (Q1), install origin (Q3), module identity (Q4), and build distribution across the environment (Q5/Q6). Overlapping angles were re-pointed rather than repeated: the image_load question there asks whether the parent application's modules are vendor-signed, here it is the primary evidence for the altered build and is anchored on the alerting process itself; the network question there profiles the parent's egress alongside a child launch, here it profiles the alerting process's own egress over a wider window; child processes are the whole subject there and are reduced to a single follow-on question (Q9) here, framed as 'has this progressed past build identity to execution'.

Q1 and Q3 share no scoping — Q1 is ProcessGuid entity-scoped binary confirmation of which branch matched (fields: Image, OriginalFileName, Hashes, FileVersion, Product, frozen per the universal template); Q3 is the Phase 2 host+Image scoped origin/invocation reading (fields: CommandLine, CurrentDirectory) per the mechanism_decode template's default scope, which is appropriate here because the application is not a high-volume binary like cmd.exe.

hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection_img has 2 alternative branches. The condition string ('all of selection_*') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. hints_acted_on.where: Q1 question and context use 'either the Image branch or the OriginalFileName branch' and tell the analyst to note which fired and what each implies; the playbook description uses the same disjunctive framing. selection_parent is kept as an AND of ParentImage and IntegrityLevel, and IntegrityLevel's two values are treated as intra-field membership.

notes: What the rule actually observes: not msiexec itself. It fires on the exploit's payoff — a command interpreter created as a child of Microsoft Edge's elevation_service.exe at SYSTEM integrity. The installer abuse that produces that state is upstream and invisible to this rule, which is why the host-clustering question directs the analyst at msiexec/installer activity in the surrounding window.
Q1's title omits the enumerated Image/OriginalFileName values to stay under the title-length target; the full value lists are in its context.

Q12 uses IntegrityLevel, which is Sigma-spec and converts cleanly, but its population under some endpoint telemetry is undocumented in this pipeline — the context therefore frames an empty result platform-neutrally as a possible visibility gap.

No question promises parameter or flag filtering: the rule has no commandline_values, so the decode/verification questions are entity-scoped and the baseline questions ask about frequency and parents rather than 'similar parameters'.

notes: Rule substance check against rule.detection: the rule has NO constraint on the child process whatsoever. Its entire selection is ParentImage = C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe AND ParentCommandLine|contains "-k RPCSS". It is not "an RPC service host spawned a shell/recon binary" - it fires on ANY child of the RPCSS service group. The rule's own description calls it a "long shot". Every question that would have leaned on a child-binary allowlist was reframed accordingly: the child is the analyst's judgment call, not the rule's.

Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not just condition_topology. shape: all_AND is genuine - condition is the bare string "selection", one selection block, two keys, both scalar values (ParentImage is a single string, ParentCommandLine|contains a single string). No list-form on the positive path anywhere in the rule, so no disjunctive framing is needed; Q1 uses AND framing ("ParentImage exactly ... and a ParentCommandLine containing ..."). No filters, so excluded_any_of is genuinely empty.

Primary technique T1190: the rule exists to catch the downstream consequence of remote exploitation of a network-reachable service, and its behavioral chain (request -> service process spawns child -> optional callback) is the rule's actual subject. T1569.002/T1569 contribute the service-installation and service-registry dimensions, which is what an operator who lands inside a SYSTEM service host typically does next; they do not drive the skeleton.

Q3 (patch status) is treated as load-bearing triage rather than a routine checkbox. CVE-2022-26809 was patched in April 2022, so on a patched host the exploitation path is closed and the child process has an ordinary explanation. The playbook deliberately does not assume compromise.
The RPC service runs as SYSTEM, so any child it spawns starts as SYSTEM. This is stated in Q2's context as a mechanical consequence of the parent, explicitly not as a severity signal.

Q8 and Q12 use ParentName|expand '%ParentName%', which resolves to svchost.exe - the noisiest possible parent scope, since svchost hosts most Windows services. Neither question is allowed to imply otherwise: Q8's context tells the analyst the results span every svchost instance on the host and to read ParentCommandLine to isolate the -k RPCSS children; Q12's context states that a high count establishes the binary as a normal service child without proving the RPC service group launched it. Q8 adds ParentCommandLine to the template's fields to make that separation possible (cue templates are exempt from the frozen-fields check). The long-range fleet-wide svchost scope was declined outright - see the cue_parent_process.scope dedup entry.

Q-vs-query agreement: no question claims CommandLine parameter filtering. rule.commandline_values is empty, so no CommandLine|contains filter is available to mirror. Questions are entity-scoped (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4/Q7/Q9-child branch on ProcessGuid), reflected (Q13/Q14/Q16 embed the rule's own selection), or honestly weakened to describe what the query actually measures (Q6/Q8/Q12).

Q9's DestinationPort values 135 and 445 are drawn from the referenced vendor guidance and the MSRC advisory, both of which identify the RPC endpoint mapper and SMB as the reachable paths for this vulnerability. Injected as query values per the mutable-element rule rather than left as prose.

The raw condition was decomposed by hand into three OR'd branches, each with its own internal AND and its own negated filter — (selection_svchost AND NOT filter_svchost) OR (selection_regsvr AND NOT filter_regsvr) OR (selection_anomaly_parent AND (child_1 OR child_2)) — and both fields use disjunctive "either/or" framing that preserves each branch's internal conjunction. notes: condition_topology.shape is 'complex' and the brief's prose explicitly declines to summarise, with required_all_of / required_any_of / excluded_any_of all empty. The topology was therefore derived by hand from rule.condition_topology.raw and rule.detection, not from the decomposed fields. The actual structure is a three-way OR. Branch 1 = Image endswith \svchost.exe AND CommandLine contains ALL of [C:\Users\, \Desktop\] AND NOT (ParentImage startswith C:\Windows\System32\). Branch 2 = ParentImage endswith \excel.exe AND Image endswith \regsvr32.exe AND CommandLine contains ANY of [' -s ', \AppData\Local\Temp\] AND NOT (CommandLine contains .dll). Branch 3 = ParentImage endswith \svchost.exe AND ((Image endswith \whoami.exe AND CommandLine contains ' /all') OR (Image endswith ANY of [\net.exe, \net1.exe] AND CommandLine contains ' view')). Note the two filters are branch-local, not global — filter_svchost negates only branch 1 and filter_regsvr only branch 2, so a .dll on the command line does not suppress branches 1 or 3.

Primary technique is T1055. Two of the three branches turn on svchost.exe being something other than the real service host — running from a user profile path, or spawning children the service host does not spawn — which is the residue of code executing inside a spoofed or injected service host. T1033 and T1135 are secondary: they describe the child binaries inside branch 3 only (whoami /all, net view), so they contribute chain stages, dimensions, and mutable elements but do not drive the skeleton.

The hash that matters on the svchost branch is the alerting binary's own — the question is whether the file carrying the system binary's name is that binary — and it lives on the execution event the alert already points at.

notes: TOPOLOGY — deviation from the reported shape, read directly from rule.detection. The brief reports all_AND with prose "Rule fires when selection matches; AND filter_main_wav does NOT match." I read the detection block directly because of the documented decomposer blind spot for list-form selections (TOFIX/topology_blind_to_intra_selection_or.md). Finding — `selection` is a SINGLE map with one key (TargetObject|contains '\SOFTWARE\Classes\.wav\OpenWithProgIds\'), so it is NOT list-form and carries no intra-selection OR. The list-of-maps is `filter_main_wav`, which IS list-form (two alternative maps -- TargetObject|endswith '.AssocFile.WAV' and TargetObject|contains '.wav.') and so is a two-branch OR that the decomposer never descended into.

TOPOLOGY — why AND framing was kept anyway. The list-form OR here sits under a negation (`not 1 of filter_main_*`). By De Morgan, NOT (A OR B) == (NOT A) AND (NOT B), so the firing condition is a flat conjunction of three predicates -- path contains the ProgIds prefix, name does not end in .AssocFile.WAV, name does not contain '.wav.'. The reported all_AND is therefore correct for the FIRING semantics, and "either ... or" framing would have been wrong here — it would tell the analyst a branch could fire when in fact both exclusions must be false simultaneously. Q1 and the description use conjunctive "neither ... nor" framing and enumerate all three predicates explicitly, so the negated OR is visible to the analyst rather than hidden behind a single "filter did not match" statement. This is the inverse of the warned case — a list-form selection under NOT collapses to AND, and only a list-form selection in the positive path is a branch OR.

EventType equality conditions — the source detection contains none, so nothing was dropped on that account. The EventType entry in Q12's fields list is the frozen file_activity template field and is mapped back to event.action by the playbook pipeline; it is not an equality condition.

Details availability — value data is recorded on roughly four fifths of registry modifications and is specifically absent for binary value data, which an encrypted blob very likely is. The playbook's spine is therefore the writing-process pivot (Q7) and the loader-on-disk question (Q12), not the value content. Q5 states the gap platform-neutrally and routes value retrieval to manual_review / edr_console rather than promising the query will show the blob. Value size and entropy are named in Q5's context as manual work rather than promised as a query result.

Registry deletion is not observable on endpoint telemetry. Q9 (cue_registry_key.artifact_verification) was rewritten away from the template's "verify whether the value persists after reboot or is cleaned up" phrasing and frames persistence around the value's re-modification history and the writing process instead. No question asks whether the key was removed.

Q13 (cue_registry_key.follow_on) — the template's notes_to_llm asks for the query to be narrowed to the executable named in the registry Details field. That is not possible for this rule: the value data is an encrypted blob rather than a payload path, and details_values in the brief is empty. The question was reframed honestly as "what ran on this host afterwards" with a host-scoped aggregation over +4h, and its context states that registry reads are not recorded so the consuming process cannot be identified directly.

Threat-specific rule (malware family named in the rule title), so the family name is retained in `name` as the sigma rule title requires. All analyst-visible prose is written to the technique pattern — registry-resident payload staging — and names no actor, campaign, report, or vendor.

Q6 (llm_generated) injects the rule's own detection value ('\SOFTWARE\Classes\.wav\OpenWithProgIds\') as a TargetObject|contains constraint to enumerate sibling values under the same key over -30d. It covers the multi-value split case (a payload too large for one value gets spread across several) which no template addresses, and it gives the analyst the host's own legitimate handler registrations as a comparison set for what a normal value name looks like.
No cue_user_actor cue in this brief, so no user-pivot / service-principal-substitute pair was authored and no question carries always_include.

Is this host expected to run a file-transfer server, and is the account behind this execution expected to launch command interpreters from it?
What request to the file-transfer application preceded this execution?
Is the CrushFTP installation on this host patched against CVE-2025-54309?
What other child processes did this same crushftp.exe instance spawn around the alert?
Did this same detection fire on other file-transfer servers in the estate?
What did the spawned command line actually do, and did other command lines carrying the rule's tokens run on this host in the same window?
Was the payload passed as an encoded blob or as an IEX download cradle, and what does it resolve to?
Did script block logging capture the deobfuscated script that ran on this host?
Were PowerShell security controls weakened on this host in the hour before the spawn?
Which scripting and .NET runtime modules were loaded on this host around the alert, and by which processes?
Did the spawned interpreters or transfer utilities open outbound connections after the server launched them?
Was an elevated logon or a special-privilege assignment recorded on this host around the spawn?
Has this account previously produced this parent-and-child combination, and does that history fit the account's role?
Has crushftp.exe historically driven this same execution pattern on this host or elsewhere, or is this new for the service?
What else did this account do across the environment around this time?
Did the same parent-driven execution fire on other hosts in the same window, or is the activity isolated to this host?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?

hint_dispositions.reason: T1133's application-log analytic targets VPN, Citrix or remote-access-gateway logs showing external addresses. This host's externally reachable service is a Tomcat-hosted file transfer application, whose request handling, admin console access and licensing calls are written to the product's own log files — not to the Windows Application event channel, which for a procrun-hosted Java service carries only service start/stop and wrapper errors. A `service: application` query would return installer and service-manager events unrelated to the exploitation path. notes: Condition topology is all_AND (selection AND NOT filter_main_system_user) with no or_valued_selections, so Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing: the /create switch, the "shutdown /l /f" string and WEEKLY must all appear in the same command line, and the exclusion of AUTHORI/AUTORI accounts is stated as a condition on the registering account rather than as an alternative branch.

The payload is "shutdown /l /f" - /l is a logoff, not a restart - so the timing framing is mechanical rather than urgent: the forced logoff ends interactive sessions on the host (including a live response session) and delivers the next logon, at which point logon-triggered persistence executes. notes: Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not just the decomposer output. condition_topology.shape is all_AND and that is genuine: selection's three keys all carry SCALAR values (Image|endswith, CommandLine|startswith, CommandLine|contains), so there is no positive-path list-form implicit OR the decomposer could have missed. CVE-2025-49144 is recent (published 2025-06-23, fixed in 8.8.2), so a patched-estate false positive is not the safe default the way it is for older-CVE rules in this corpus. Q3 makes the installed version an explicit, load-bearing triage question rather than an assumption in either direction.

notes: Rule substance: this is NOT .sdb shim-database installation. The detection pins TargetObject|contains '\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\AppCompatFlags\Layers\' AND Details|contains 'REGISTERAPPRESTART' — a compatibility LAYER on the Layers key, not a Custom/InstalledSDB registration. The layer makes the compat engine call RegisterApplicationRestart for the target app so Windows relaunches it after crash/update/reboot. No .sdb file and no sdbinst.exe are involved in the alerting behavior; sdbinst (Q13) and AppPatch module loads (Q14) are authored as adjacent-abuse checks of the same framework, per the ATT&CK analytic chain, not as the alerting path.

Details availability: Details is absent on ~21% of registry modifications (binary/empty value data), but not for this rule — the detection REQUIRES Details|contains 'REGISTERAPPRESTART', so the value is REG_SZ string data and is present on every alerting event by construction. Q8 (mechanism_decode) is therefore safe to build on reading Details, and its context says so.

Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not just condition_topology. condition is the bare string 'selection'; the single selection block holds two scalar |contains values (TargetObject and Details) with no list-form anywhere on the positive path and no filters. AND framing is genuine — both conditions must hold together — and Q1 is framed conjunctively ('under the Layers key AND with REGISTERAPPRESTART in its value data'). shape: all_AND confirmed, no decomposer gap for this rule.

Target application is not queryable as a placeholder. Under AppCompatFlags\Layers the value NAME is the target executable's full path, so it is embedded in TargetObject rather than exposed as its own field. Q12 (follow_on) therefore cannot filter process_creation on that path and is left host-scoped over +4h, with its context directing the analyst to read the executable path from the value name and match it in the results. Q12's question makes no filtering claim, so Q-vs-query agreement holds.

Q1/Q2/Q7 carry process.code_signature.subject_name and process.code_signature.trusted in fields:. These are raw ECS names outside the platform floor and will draw lint_ecs_field_names warnings, but the fields lists on these question-set templates are frozen (validate_template_fields hard-fails on any edit), so they are copied verbatim from the brief as required.
No cue_user_actor pattern in this brief, so no user-pivot / service_principal_substitute pair and no always_include questions. User context is carried by Q2 (universal.host_user_context).

notes: What the rule actually detects, corrected from the title: no LSASS access, no SAM/SYSTEM hive extraction, no ntds.dit. Branch 1 is a recursive quiet xcopy of a domain controller's SYSVOL replication share (credential harvesting from Group Policy Preferences cpassword and logon scripts). Branch 2 is a Sysinternals AD Explorer snapshot of the joined domain written to a user's Downloads folder as a .snp file. Both are file-collection actions; the whole playbook is framed on the technique.

Primary technique is T1552.001 (Credentials In Files): both branches collect credential-bearing or directory data out of files rather than out of process memory or a registry hive. T1003.003 (NTDS) is the rule's other tag and is secondary — the AD Explorer snapshot is offline directory data, which is what makes the tag defensible, but the rule detects no ntds.dit access, no shadow-copy creation, and no ntdsutil.exe, so T1003.003's analytic chain does not drive the skeleton. T1552 and T1003 are the parent techniques carried in the brief's attack_brief; their dimensions are covered, but T1003's LSASS/SAM analytic has no applicable surface here.

The rule title carries an attribution adjective. Per style_guide ban #4 it appears only in `name:` (which must equal the rule title verbatim) and in no analyst-visible field — the description, every question, and every context are framed on the technique. The command patterns the rule matches are generic: commodity tooling, penetration testers, backup and migration work, and any operator produce identical command lines, so attribution adds nothing an analyst can act on.

process_access is not authorable (no cross-process handle telemetry), and no windows_api_channel substitute was authored: the endorsed `endpoint.events.api` substitute covers injection-side API activity, which is unrelated to a file copy and a directory snapshot. Nothing in this playbook promises handle-level visibility into LSASS.

Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5, and Q9 share the ProcessGuid alert-lookup query. Q1/Q4/Q5 are genuine alert lookups (the analyst reads the CommandLine to verify the branch, decode the argument scope, and identify the credential store); Q2, Q3, and Q9 are organizational questions answered from engagement records, asset inventory, and Active Directory, and carry the boilerplate per AGENTS.md § 'All Questions Must Have a Query'.

notes: Hand-derived condition reading. Raw: (selection_img and 1 of selection_encoded_*) or selection_ioc. Two top-level OR branches. Branch A = selection_img AND (selection_encoded_aspx OR selection_encoded_path): ParentImage|endswith \w3wp.exe together with encoded evidence. selection_encoded_aspx is a LIST OF MAPS — an OR of two alternative field-maps (CommandLine|wide|base64offset|contains spinstall0.aspx OR CommandLine|base64|contains spinstall0.aspx), i.e. UTF-16 base64 or ASCII base64. selection_encoded_path is a single map whose one field takes a 4-scalar list — intra-field membership (OR) over the 15/16 long-form and 8.3 short-form LAYOUTS paths, and it is wide-only (an ASCII-base64 LAYOUTS path would not match it). Branch B = selection_ioc alone: CommandLine|contains over a 2-scalar list (intra-field OR) of the plaintext -EncodedCommand prefix and TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS\spinstall0.aspx — with NO parent constraint, so it fires under any parent. That asymmetry is the analyst-relevant part and is what Q1 asks them to record.

Technique-focused framing kept throughout. CVE IDs are permitted in prose and CVE-2025-53770 is named in the rule title, so it appears in the description and the patch-status question; no actor, vendor or report names appear anywhere in analyst-visible prose.

HTTP/IIS access logs are not an authorable logsource category, so three of the five T1190 mutable elements (PublicVIPs, SuspiciousPatterns, ErrorRateThreshold) are dispositioned as context on the delivery-vector question with their exact values, rather than inventing a category that the conversion pipeline cannot scope.

Question order runs start-position triage and parent/vector context (Q1-Q5), then analysis (Q6), then the chain-progression context questions (Q7-Q11), the user-actor pairs (Q12-Q15), and host/fleet breadth last (Q16-Q18). initial_access.campaign_scope carries position:start in the brief but is placed last, with the other broad-scope questions, because it answers fleet breadth rather than triage.

The false-positive discriminator for this rule is that SharePoint application pools legitimately spawn children (timer jobs, search indexing, provisioning during patch windows). That is stated in the description and is the explicit subject of Q3 (which pool served the request) and Q11 (the 90-day empirical allowed-child list).

notes: brief.hints[] is empty for this rule — no hint was acted on or declined, so hints_acted_on is omitted and hint_dispositions is empty.

The brief's condition topology is all_AND over a single selection whose TargetFilename|endswith carries three alternative values. hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection_cmd has 2 alternative branches. The condition string ('all of selection_*') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. (A list of scalar values under a single field is different — that is intra-field membership, not a branch OR.)
hints_acted_on.where: Q1 question ("does the alerting process resolve to the command interpreter by either its Image path or its OriginalFileName?") and Q1 context, which names the two alternative branches explicitly, instructs the analyst to note which one fired, and states the downstream consequence: an Image-path match needs no further binary-identity work, while an OriginalFileName match with a non-\cmd.exe Image path means a renamed/relocated interpreter and makes origin and signing load-bearing. The playbook description uses the same 'either ... or' framing for selection_cmd while preserving the AND across selection_action / selection_cli_1 / selection_cli_2.

notes: Primary technique T1070.004 (File Deletion): the rule's own detection is a delayed copy, and the reason the delay exists is almost always so a file can be moved or replaced after the process holding it exits — the deletion of the source is the technique the copy serves. T1070 (Indicator Removal) is the parent technique and contributes the broader log/registry/task cleanup dimension, covered by Q11; it is not tagged on the rule but is keyed in the brief's attack_brief and is listed here as secondary so its dimensions can be tracked.

Technique-focused rule — the rule description notes the construction is "usually used by malware", but the title and tags are generic and there is no emerging_threats tag and no threat intel in db_refs. All prose stays technique-neutral: the delay-then-copy pattern is described mechanically (ping -n burns N seconds, copy /y overwrites without prompting) with no family or campaign named.

Q6 (cue_artifact.artifact_verification) deviates structurally from its template, which anchors on %TargetFilename%. That placeholder does not resolve on a process_creation alert, and the copy destination exists only as text inside the CommandLine with no placeholder for it. The template's intent — find the artifact EXECUTING and read its hash — is preserved with two execution legs anchored on what the alert does carry: processes started by the alerting command (ParentProcessGuid) and executions out of the staging directories a delayed copy targets. The template is ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY, so re-anchoring is in scope; noted here because the divergence from the default query is larger than usual.

Q5, Q4, Q9, Q1 and Q2 all use a ProcessGuid alert lookup but project different fields and serve different tasks (rule match / overwrite target / current destination state / copy operand resolution with CurrentDirectory / identity). Per AGENTS.md this is the sanctioned alert-lookup boilerplate, not near-identical-query duplication.

questions.question: Does the script block create a scheduled task — either through the ScheduledTask cmdlets or through an Invoke-CimMethod call against the PS_ScheduledTask class?

What task does the complete script configure — its name, action, trigger, and run-as principal?
Did the task-creation commands also appear on a PowerShell command line, and which invocation carried them?
Was a task actually registered — what task name and creating account does the audit trail record?
Did a task-cache registry write record the new task's registration?
When is the task scheduled to run, and has it already executed?

Did the PowerShell session spawn follow-on activity after the script ran?
Were PowerShell security controls bypassed or weakened before this execution?
What other PowerShell script activity occurred on this host around the alert?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?
Is full script block logging enabled on this host, or is only suspicious-content logging active?
Has this user produced this task-creation pattern before, and does that history fit their role?
Which hosts have produced this task-creation pattern in the last 90 days, and is the alerting host among them?
What else did this user do across the network around this time?
Did this same task-creation pattern fire on other hosts in the same window?

notes: Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not just condition_topology. shape all_AND is genuine. The positive path (selection) is two modifiers on ONE field — TargetFilename|contains \procmon AND TargetFilename|endswith .sys — with no list-valued key, so there is no hidden implicit OR. The only list-form is Image|endswith under filter_main_process_explorer, which sits under `not 1 of filter_main_*`; by De Morgan that collapses to AND (NOT procmon.exe AND NOT procmon64.exe AND NOT procmon64a.exe). Q1 is framed conjunctively as one combination, matching condition_topology.prose.

No hash question is authored against the file event — file writes carry no hash. The hash pivot for a .sys is the driver load, not a process execution, so cue_artifact.artifact_verification (Q6) was adapted from category process_creation to category driver_load, where Hashes/Signed/Signature/SignatureStatus are populated. The template's notes_to_llm sanction this adaptation for DLL artifacts (image_load); a kernel driver is the same case one category over. Its two process-execution legs (Image|endswith / CommandLine|contains) were dropped because a .sys never runs as a process.

cue_artifact.follow_on (Q7) was likewise adapted away from process_creation. "Was this file executed after it was created" has no process_creation answer for a kernel driver; the equivalent progression is service registration and kernel load. Q6 carries the load, so Q7 carries the service registration (service: system, EventID 7045) — a distinct query and a distinct finding (how the driver was made loadable, with what start type and under what account).

The driver's Microsoft signature is the premise, not the finding — Process Monitor's driver is genuinely signed, so signature status cannot triage this alert. The playbook's weight sits on writer identity (Q1, Q3, Q4, Q13), on whether the written bytes really are the Sysinternals driver (Q5, Q6), and on whether the driver reached the kernel (Q6, Q7).

The template's query anchors network_connection on host.name + Image|endswith|expand '%Image%', which on a driver load event hydrates to the process that triggered the load (typically the service control manager), so the question would report that process's connections and mislead. No compensating network question was authored — the driver's abuse pattern is local (handle access to and termination of protected processes), not outbound. Q13 (cue_host_context.clustering) surfaces any egress tooling that ran on the host in the alert window.

Its frozen query correlates file_activity to the alerting ProcessGuid and its direct children, which for this rule returns files written by the driver-loading process rather than the driver file itself — the driver was written before the load, by a different process. Q7 (llm_generated) asks the question this template exists to ask, anchored correctly on host.name + TargetFilename|endswith|expand '%ImageLoaded%' over -7d, and returns the writing process, path, and timing.

Recommended, not must_include. hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection has 2 alternative branches. The condition string ('selection') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. (A list of scalar values under a single field is different — that is intra-field membership, not a branch OR.)
hints_acted_on.where: Q1 question text uses "either a path ending in \kprocesshacker.sys, or an import hash on the rule's list", and its context tells the analyst to note which branch matched and what each branch implies. The playbook description uses the same "either ... or" framing. Q5 (cue_image_load.artifact_verification) resolves the hash branch independently of the file name.

notes: Primary and only technique T1543 — the rule fires on the driver load, and a kernel driver reaches memory through a service entry, so the service-creation chain is the whole of the ATT&CK surface here.

The rule's two branches are not equivalent in weight. The path branch (\kprocesshacker.sys) is the ordinary case and fires on installed tooling; the import-hash branch fires on driver content regardless of file name and is the branch that survives a rename. Q1's context makes the distinction and Q5 gives the hash branch its own query.

A valid signature is expected on this driver and is not exculpatory — it is what allows the driver to load under driver-signature enforcement. Q4's context states this explicitly so the analyst does not close on the signature alone.
No cue_user_actor pattern is present in the brief, so no user-pivot / service-principal pair applies.

notes: Rule substance, verified against rule.detection, rule.description and references.db_refs: this is NOT malware self-cleanup / anti-forensics. It is the law-enforcement removal utility that was pushed to infected hosts over the botnet's own channel during the August 2023 takedown. The referenced DOJ victim-resources page states the uninstaller removed the implant and untethered the host from the botnet but explicitly did NOT remediate second-stage malware already installed. The playbook is therefore framed as a removal event rather than an attack step, with no manufactured alarm — but the two findings that do matter are preserved: (a) a genuine execution implies the host was enrolled in the botnet, so the parent process and the pre-alert history are the high-value pivots (Q4, Q14, Q15), and (b) removal covered one implant only, so second-stage residue is the durable question (Q15).

2026 realism: the takedown was in 2023 and the file plus its hashes are public, so the most likely live fire is a retained sample detonated on an analysis or test host, or an unrelated file carrying the name (the name branch places no constraint on content). Q2, Q10, Q11, Q12 and Q16 all give the analyst a way to confirm that path rather than pursue an intrusion narrative.

Q15 (llm_generated, -90d alert history) and Q14 (cue_host_context.precursor, -6h alert history) share a query structure but are deliberately both kept. The windows answer different questions: -6h covers the immediate staging that explains how the file arrived; -90d covers the dwell an enrolled host would plausibly have and is where second-stage residue — the thing removal did not address — would surface. Q15 aggregates by rule.name (distribution over time) where Q14 lists events (timeline reconstruction). Not a near-duplicate in result or intent.

Q5 (llm_generated, file_event) is anchored on host.name + TargetFilename|contains 'QbotUninstall.exe' rather than %TargetFilename%|endswith|expand — the alert is a process_creation event and carries no file name to hydrate. The literal name is the only usable anchor and keeps the query scoped beyond host.name, per the file-event scoping rule. Its context tells the analyst to substitute the alerting Image's file name if the hash branch fired under a different name, and states that file writes carry no hash so identity comes from the execution event.

Style: the rule title names the malware family, so per style_guide §2's threat-specific exception the family is cited generically exactly once, in the description. It appears in no question or context — those are framed on the mechanism (a removal payload delivered over an implant's own channel, leaving second-stage payloads in place), which survives the family name going stale. No writeup, vendor, or researcher credit; no attribution adjectives; no incident chain transcription.

Sibling rule bfd34392 (Qakbot Rundll32 Fake DLL Extension Execution) covers the loader angle for the same family. This playbook stays on the uninstaller/removal angle only and authors no rundll32 or DLL-loading questions.

Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame the disjunction faithfully as 'EITHER ... OR ...'. notes: EventType equality conditions dropped from both branches per the file/registry authoring rules — the endpoint agent emits ECS event.action values (modification/creation), never the Sysmon literals RenameKey / SetValue, so an EventType clause in a playbook query would match nothing. The branches are therefore distinguished in prose (Q1 context) rather than in query selections, and every registry query stays on category: registry_set so conversion scopes it to event.category:registry.

Q12 (cue_registry_key.follow_on) was re-anchored from the template's bare host.name +4h process_creation sweep to host.name + ParentImage|endswith '\explorer.exe'. The template's notes_to_llm ask for the query to be narrowed to the configured persistence payload, which is not knowable at authoring time (the payload path lives in the alert's value data). The trigger for this mechanism is fixed by the technique — the Recycle Bin verb command is executed by Explorer when the user opens the folder — so the parent is the narrowing available a priori. Aggregation flipped to true because a flat +4h host listing drowns in agent telemetry. The question is framed as "what did explorer.exe launch" rather than promising a payload match, so no unearned filter claim.

Q14 / Q15 use TargetObject|contains with the rule's CLSID literal instead of TargetObject|expand. Reason: the alerting event may be either branch of the disjunction, and %TargetObject% on the rename branch is the pre-rename path, which would return an empty history. The literal matches both branches and any verb name under \shell, which is what "has this key been touched before" means for this rule.

Q11 keeps the template's file_activity + ProcessGuid/ParentProcessGuid correlation unmodified. The template's notes offer a TargetFilename|contains filter when the rule pins a concrete payload path; this rule pins none (details_values is empty — the payload path is attacker-chosen value data), so no filter was added.

Q8 and Q9 share the host+TargetObject anchor by design, per registry.registry_key_context's notes_to_llm: Q8 carries the "where in the hive does this land and does the signer cohere with the key" judgment, Q9 carries the value-decoding work. Not deduplicable.

notes: Topology verified against rule.detection directly, not just the decomposer. condition is the bare `selection`; shape: all_AND is genuine. The single selection ANDs two fields: TargetObject|endswith (one scalar) with Details|contains (a list of seven scalars). The list is intra-field membership under ONE field — any-of within Details, ANDed with the TargetObject constraint — which is the documented carve-out, not a positive-path OR of selections. Q1 is therefore framed conjunctively across the two fields ("value path ends in ... AND the value data contains any one of ...") with the intra-field any-of stated explicitly so the analyst knows only one directory pattern needs to hit. No filter/not branches exist, so no De Morgan case.

Which key the rule actually pins: TargetObject|endswith \Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run — the Group Policy-backed Explorer Run key, NOT the ordinary \CurrentVersion\Run. The endswith form matches both the HKLM (SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run, machine-wide, needs admin) and HKCU (Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run, per-user) instances. FP framing is calibrated to this: the policy key is normally populated only by Group Policy and carries far less legitimate third-party software than the ordinary Run key, so Q5/Q6 ask whether a policy rollout explains the write and Q13 frames zero 90-day history as the expected state for this key. The rule declares falsepositives: Unknown, so no specific benign population was named.

Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not just condition_topology.shape. The selection has a single field (OriginalFileName) whose value is a list of scalars — intra-field membership, not a list of maps — so it is a within-field OR and the top-level structure is a genuine AND of selection with the negated filter_main_legit_names group. The rule carries no ATT&CK tags (rule.techniques is empty) and the brief supplied no attack_brief, so attack_chain_coverage and dimension_coverage are empty by construction. T1036.003 is recorded as primary on the basis of the masquerading technique set (filename_prefix 'renamed') and the detection mechanism itself — the inference is the author's, not the rule's.

No signature-verification question was authored. Renaming a file does not alter its Authenticode signature or its PE version resource, so a renamed Teams binary is still genuinely Microsoft-signed and a 'is it signed' question answers yes in both the benign and the non-benign case. The signing state is stated as the premise in the true_identity context instead, and the signature question that does carry information — per-module signer and status on the libraries the copy loaded — is asked in the image_load question.

No outbound network_connection question was authored. Teams is an Electron application whose normal operation includes continuous egress to content and telemetry endpoints, so a destination list from a renamed copy is unremarkable in both cases and would not discriminate. The loaded-module question covers the follow-on that does discriminate.

Q-vs-query agreement: no question claims parameter or flag filtering. The rule has no commandline_values, so no CommandLine|contains constraint was available to mirror; the questions that could have implied one were written to describe what their query actually measures. The '%Image%'-scoped baseline question hydrates to the renamed path, so its question text says it counts executions of that exact path and explicitly disclaims finding copies renamed to other names — the OriginalFileName-anchored reflected fleet query is what covers those.

The image_load question is sourced llm_generated rather than attack: — there is no attack_brief to source a dimension from. It anchors on host.name + Image|endswith '%Image%' in the alert window and projects the per-module signature and hash fields, which library load events populate directly.

The writer is a fixed Windows service with no meaningful per-invocation command line to decode; a process_creation decode of ScreenConnect.Service.exe surfaces only service starts. The Phase-2 mechanism decode for this file_event rule is the file-content review (cue_artifact.mechanism_decode, "what changed in the user database"), which is included as the analysis-phase decode.

The parent of a Windows service is services.exe by definition, so the upward parent chain is uninformative. The higher-value process-lineage direction — children spawned BY ScreenConnect.Service.exe (webshell/code execution) — is covered by the llm_generated child-process question, and baseline_svc pivots on the parent for historical framing.

The alert artifact is an XML configuration/database file that is not executed, so the "hash the file when it runs" execution pivot does not apply (there is no later Image|endswith execution of a .xml). The execution angle for this rule — code run via extensions/handlers after the account change — is covered by the llm_generated child-process question.

ScreenConnect.Service.exe runs continuously on any ScreenConnect server, so a host-level binary-frequency baseline is always high and uninformative. The reflected user/parent baselines count the rule's actual firing pattern instead.

The temporary XML is a transient, frequently-rewritten file, so a first-seen file baseline is not meaningful. The reflected baselines count how often this specific write pattern has occurred by user and by parent.

Generic host-activity clustering overlaps the file-write breadth (file.file_write_burst), the child-process question, and the precursor alert timeline already included; dropped for budget without coverage loss.

Startup-folder / Run-key file persistence is covered in effect by file.file_write_burst (the writer's full file activity) and file.file_directory_context (arrivals under the ScreenConnect tree, where the App_Extensions handler drops actually land for this rule).

The "was this authorized / expected" dimension is covered by universal.host_user_context, remote_access_tool.tool_authorization, and remote_access_tool.active_session_context; the four organizational_context templates would add near-identical ProcessGuid-boilerplate questions without new investigative signal. notes: condition_topology.shape: all_AND, verified against rule.detection directly — selection is a single map whose two keys (TargetObject|endswith, Details) both carry scalar values, not a list of maps. No hidden implicit OR. Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing ("both conditions must hold on the same event").

EventType is not present in this rule's detection, so no EventType equality condition needed dropping. Queries stay on category: registry_set throughout, which scopes to event.category:registry and covers all registry modifications the endpoint agent emits.

No Details|expand constraint authored in any query. The rule's Details literal 'DWORD (0x00000001)' is a Sysmon value-rendering; endpoint registry telemetry renders value data differently, so a Details equality selection would risk matching nothing. Every registry query anchors on host.name + TargetObject and projects Details as a field for the analyst to read — Q4 states the value-data availability caveat platform-neutrally.

Q7 (llm_generated) is the GPO-versus-hands-on discriminator. It does not duplicate Q6: Q6 resolves the exact writing process and its parent via the ProcessGuid pivot, while Q7 aggregates policy-management and registry-editing tooling across the surrounding window to show whether a policy-processing pass was underway at all. Q8 (fleet distribution of the same value) is the other half of that judgment.

T1685 is the rule's only technique and is primary by default. The playbook is technique-focused: CVE-2022-30190 is named once in the description as the mechanism that makes the guardrail relevant (CVE IDs are permitted), and no incident chain is narrated.

Registry deletion is not observable on endpoint telemetry. Q10 frames reversion around the key's re-modification history over +7d (range widened from the template's +15m per its own notes_to_llm) plus direct host inspection, and never asks whether the key was removed.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: 5s-2m (analytic's suggested threshold between process start and the account creation event)
mutable_dispositions.notes: The analytic's 5s-2m window is a detection-engineering threshold for correlating 4720 with its creating process. As an investigation range it is too narrow — the account-creation step here is a file write into the service's user store rather than a tool invocation, and may lag the recon command considerably. Q9 uses +/-4h and the exact 5s-2m figure is not carried into analyst prose because it would misdirect the range; the correlation itself (4720 against the alerting process and account) is what the question asks for.

The template's own guidance is to skip it for detections where change tickets are irrelevant. This rule fires on exploitation indicators (filename_prefix "exploit", falsepositives "Unlikely") — a whoami redirected into a directory the file-transfer service publishes over the internet has no change-controlled equivalent, so an absent ticket carries no information.

Asking whether the user recalls the action assumes a person behind the account. The alerting account on this rule is the file-transfer service identity in the branch that matters, and there is no person to ask. Where the parent turns out to be interactive instead, Q3 (parent identification) surfaces that directly and Q2 covers whether the account is expected on the host.

Work-hours and maintenance-window alignment discriminates authorized administration from unauthorized change. This rule matches indicator strings with no administrative analogue, so the pattern is out of policy at 2 PM Tuesday exactly as at 3 AM Saturday and the timing adds nothing. Timing that does matter — what preceded and followed on the host — is covered by Q16 and Q17.

The template compares the method used against the organization's standard tooling for the same change (deployment via SCCM, accounts via AD tools). This rule detects reconnaissance output redirected into a service's web-served directory, which is not a change any standard procedure performs by another route, so there is no procedural alternative to compare against.

Its selection is limited to Startup folders and scheduled-task XML definitions (\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\, \Windows\System32\Tasks\, \Windows\Tasks\). The file-based persistence this rule's technique actually uses is a crafted .Archive record written into the file-transfer service's own user store, which none of those paths cover; that is covered by Q9's context and by Q7, which reads what was written under the service's directories. Generic file drops by the alerting process are listed by Q6 via lineage.

Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame the disjunction faithfully as 'EITHER ... OR ...'. hints_acted_on.where: Q1 and the description. Both state that whoami is required (the AND) and that it must be joined by EITHER a Client\Common path OR a reference to C:\Windows\Temp\Serv-U.bat. notes: Condition reading. Raw: selection_whoami and 1 of selection_cmd*. One required selection AND-ed to a two-member OR group. selection_whoami is a single scalar (CommandLine|contains whoami). selection_cmd_1 is a single map whose one field takes a 2-scalar list — intra-field membership (OR) over the forward-slash and backslash spellings of the Client/Common path, not a list of maps. selection_cmd_2 is a single scalar (C:\Windows\Temp\Serv-U.bat). No selection in this rule takes a list of maps, so there is no implicit OR beyond the one the condition string states.

The rule is titled after a vendor's temporary actor designation, which is kept in `name:` because it is the rule title, and appears nowhere in analyst-visible prose. The durable statement the playbook is written around is mechanical — a command line pairing an identity check with a path belonging to an internet-facing file-transfer service means that service was driven into executing code, whoever did it. No actor, attribution adjective, vendor or report name appears in any question, context or the description. CVE IDs are permitted by the style guide and CVE-2021-35211 is named in the rule title, so it appears in the description and in Q4. Serv-U is the victim application and the detection's anchor, so it is named throughout; no analyst tooling or SIEM product is named anywhere.

The rule places NO constraint on the parent process — it is CommandLine-only (has_parent_in_detection is false in the brief). The playbook therefore treats "is the parent the file-transfer service process?" as an open investigative question (Q3) rather than as something the alert asserts, and Q1's framing is about the two command-line branches, not about a parent-child pair.

T1136.001 is the rule's only tag and drives the skeleton; T1136 is its parent technique and its analytic and dimension set are identical, so it is recorded as secondary and contributes no distinct mutable elements (its ParentProcessName / TimeWindow / UserContext entries duplicate T1136.001's and are dispositioned once). The technique tag is a slightly loose fit for what the rule matches — the pattern is reconnaissance output staging, and the account-creation step it is tagged for happens later and by a different mechanism (a crafted .Archive record written into the file-transfer service's user store, which raises no 4720). Q9 covers both the 4720 route and that gap.

Question order runs triage (Q1-Q2), then the parent and patch-state context that establishes whether the service was the execution path (Q3-Q4), then analysis of the command and its artifacts (Q5-Q8), then the persistence step the technique tag points at (Q9), then history and baselines (Q10-Q12), the user-actor pairs (Q13-Q15), host breadth (Q16-Q17), and fleet breadth last (Q18). universal.evidence_preservation carries position:start in the brief but is placed at Q6, immediately after the command is decoded, because the filenames it looks for are only known once the command has been read. persistence_scope.process_based_persistence carries position:end and is placed at Q17 with the other broad-scope host questions.

The template's own notes say to skip where the organization has no standard procedure for the action. The procedure question for this rule is specifically whether xp_cmdshell/CLR/ Agent CmdExec is the sanctioned path on this instance, which Q5 asks directly.

The T1505.003 persistence surface for a database engine is an in-process component — an extended stored procedure DLL, a CLR assembly, or an Agent job step — not schtasks/sc/reg. Q12's module-load review covers it directly. The template's sweep also lists bitsadmin.exe, which is already one of the rule's own child binaries, so it would re-surface the alerting event as its own corroboration.

Startup-folder and \Windows\System32\Tasks\ drops are not the persistence route for a database-engine implant, which lives inside the server process. Q12's module-load review is the equivalent question for this rule, and the count is at 18 with the three logsource-coverage hints acted on.

notes: The source rule's detection is not mirrorable and no question pretends to mirror it. The rule selects on `Destination|base64offset|contains` — Destination is a Sysmon EID 20 (WmiEventConsumer) field with no source in this pipeline; on the telemetry this pipeline targets it compiles onto a field that carries zero events, so the rule's own selection can never match and reproducing it in a question would ship a match-nothing query. Per the wmi authoring constraint the WMI questions are anchored honestly on EventID 5861/5860/5857 instead (Q3, Q17), and the payload-content questions (Q1, Q4) route the analyst to the consumer record via manual_review rather than promising a query-side match. No question anywhere in this playbook authors EventNamespace, Consumer, Filter, Destination-as-a-selector, Query, Name or Type in a detection block.

Queries that can actually return rows: Q3, Q5, Q8, Q9, Q10, Q11, Q15, Q16, Q17, Q18 — all host- or fleet-scoped on fields that exist on their target telemetry. Queries that cannot: Q1, Q2, Q4, Q6, Q7, Q12, Q13, Q14 — all ProcessGuid/ParentProcessGuid-anchored, and a WMI-Activity alert document carries no process identifier to hydrate %ProcessGuid% from. Those eight are frozen KEEP_EXACT question-set templates (validate_template_fields compares their fields[] exactly) plus the organizational-filler set, so the boilerplate is the required form, not a choice; their contexts are written so the analyst gets the investigative step without the query being load-bearing, and their answer_sources point at manual_review / organizational_knowledge / edr_console accordingly.

Q1's frozen field list is [Destination] and its logsource is process_creation — that combination comes from the brief's category variant for this rule and is fixed by the template-fields check. It is inert on this telemetry. The question text and context therefore direct the analyst to read the consumer's payload from the subscription object or the registration record rather than from the query result.

T1546.003 is primary: the rule fires on the content of an event consumer, which is the subscription-persistence primitive itself. T1047 is secondary — it contributes the remote-execution and network-correlation angle (Q10) and the WMI tooling command patterns (Q5) but describes WMI as an execution mechanism rather than as the persistence structure the rule targets. T1546 (parent) contributes dimensions only; its analytic is the generic event-triggered-execution correlation, already covered by the T1546.003 chain.

condition_topology.shape is all_AND with a single selection (`selection_destination`), and reading rule.detection directly confirms it: one selection, one modifier chain (base64offset|contains) over a three-item value list, no filters, no nested groups. AND framing is correct for the description and Q1 — the list inside the selection is an implicit OR over the three markers, which the description renders as the three markers being alternatives rather than co-requirements.

The three encoded markers were not injected into any query detection block. They are base64offset variants of WriteProcessMemory and the two PE DOS-stub strings, and they only exist in the consumer payload field that has no source here; putting them in a CommandLine|contains would be a different claim than the rule makes and would match nothing. They appear in the description and in Q1's context as what the analyst is decoding toward.

No cue_user_actor pattern is present in the brief (cues.primary and cues.secondary are both empty; cue_host_context is the only cue), so no user-pivot / service-principal pair was authored and no question carries always_include.

Question order follows the behavioral chain rather than strict start/middle/end template positions: the WMI registration evidence (Q3) and payload decode (Q4) are placed immediately after triage because they are the load-bearing evidence for this rule, and the organizational-context block (Q12-Q14, position: start) is placed after the technical pivots it depends on. The persistence-scope and baseline questions (Q15-Q18) remain at the end.

notes: T1588.002 is primary: the rule fires on the artefact a Sysinternals utility leaves when it runs under a name other than the one it ships with. T1588 is the parent technique and contributes nothing beyond it. Both attack_brief entries are PRE-platform with no analytics and no dimensions, so attack_chain_coverage and dimension_coverage are empty — there is no behavioural chain to decompose.

Investigative core is identity resolution, not maliciousness. The key path names the real tool while Image names the alias, and that mismatch is what the rule detects. Q1/Q3 resolve the true identity from the key and from PE metadata plus hash, Q4/Q8 establish arrival and origin, Q5/Q11 establish what the tool did, and Q2/Q13/Q14 establish whether the use fits the host's normal administration. These utilities are legitimate signed admin tools; sanctioned use is a common outcome and the questions are written to reach it as readily as the other.

No EventType condition appears in any query. The source rule has none, and endpoint registry telemetry emits ECS event actions rather than Sysmon literals, so an EventType equality would match nothing.

Every registry question anchors on the alert's own TargetObject with bare |expand (a registry alert's key path is exact), and no question promises that a key deletion can be observed — Q7 frames cleanup around re-modification history and re-execution instead.

No cue_user_actor pattern is present in the brief (the secondary cue is cue_process_tool), so no service-principal question pair applies. User attribution is instead handled inside Q2, which directs the analyst to the writing process when the registry event resolves to SYSTEM or a machine account.

Q11 adapts cue_registry_key.follow_on away from its default host-only process_creation query. The template's intent is "did the configured payload execute", which has no equivalent here — the consent key configures nothing. The nearest true follow-on is continued use of the renamed binary itself, so the query is scoped to host + Image|endswith over +4h. Distinct from Q5, which pivots on ParentImage to find what the tool launched.

What process spawned this PowerShell instance, and is that parent chain expected?
What outbound connections did this PowerShell instance make, and are the destinations external and uncommon?

What other file activity occurred in the same drop directory?

When this host has previously fired this download-cradle pattern, what parents and users drove it, and does the current alert fit?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this user do across the network around the time of this alert?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?

playbooks.name: Suspicious Microsoft Office Child Process
playbooks.description: Detects a Microsoft Office suite product (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Publisher, Visio, OneNote, Access, WordPad, or the legacy Equation Editor) spawning a suspicious child process. The rule fires when an Office binary is the parent AND EITHER the child is a known living-off-the-land binary by name (cm

questions.question: Did a Microsoft Office product spawn a child that is either a known living-off-the-land binary or runs from a user-writable staging directory?
Is this user and host expected to open Office documents that launch interpreters or system utilities?
Which Office application is the parent, and what document or macro drove it to spawn this child?
What document or email attachment triggered this execution, and where did it come from?
Which child binary ran, where does its image live, and is it signed?
What is the full command line of the child, and does it carry a remote URL, a script or DLL reference, or a proxy-execution flag?
Did the same lineage use WMI to launch or to reach remote systems around this time?
Did the child binary load a scriptlet or an unsigned DLL from an unusual path shortly after it started?
Did the child process make an outbound network connection, and to what destination?
Was a file written to a user-writable staging path around the time of the spawn, and is it still on disk?
What other child processes did the same Office parent spawn?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this user do across the network around this time?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?
Did this same detection fire on other hosts or for other users, indicating a wider delivery campaign?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?

mutable_dispositions.notes: Rule values are carried verbatim in the reflected detection blocks (Q12, Q13, Q14, Q16, Q17). Acting on the CommandLine-only hint, cue_process_tool.mechanism_decode was re-anchored from the template's host.name + Image|endswith|expand '%Image%' selection to host.name + a CommandLine|contains list of the printer-management verbs (Add-PrinterPort, Remove-PrinterPort, Get-PrinterPort, Add-Printer, Set-Printer, Out-Printer, Generic / Text Only, prnport, printui), which enumerates the whole printer-setup operation instead of every execution of an interpreter that the rule never names.

Not directly queryable. Off-hours and deployment-window framing carried in Q4's context; the -6h alert timeline (Q18) supplies the ordering evidence.

Near-identical +/-15m host process aggregation to cue_host_context.clustering. For this rule the surrounding activity that matters is the printer-setup sequence itself, which the re-anchored mechanism_decode question enumerates directly by command pattern.

Same +/-15m host-window aggregation as cue_process_tool.clustering, already dropped. The around-this-time angle is covered by cue_user_actor.clustering (+/-1h, fleet-wide by host and binary) and the -6h alert timeline in cue_host_context.precursor; a third host-window process aggregation adds volume without a rule-specific angle.

Overlaps organizational_context.human_recall for this rule — both ask whether the printer install was authorized. human_recall is the better instrument here because printer port creation is typically user-driven desk-side work that is rarely ticketed, so ticket absence carries little signal while user recall closes the documented false positive outright.
user_actor pair — non-deduplicable

skipped_templates.reason: Child processes of the calling interpreter are not the effect of this pattern. The spooler service, not the caller, performs the port write and later loads or replays the payload, so the downstream execution appears as a module load inside spoolsv.exe (Q8) and as a registry port value (Q7), not as a child process of the alerting command.

Duplicates the authorization angle already covered by human_recall (Q3) and the expected-operation angle covered by universal.host_user_context (Q2). Printer deployment procedure adds no discriminator beyond those two for a CommandLine-only pattern where the decisive evidence is the port target path.

The persistence artifact for this pattern is a spooler port registry value replayed by the service, not schtasks / at / sc / reg / bitsadmin / wmic execution. Q7 queries that registry value directly; the template's Image|endswith list would return unrelated administrative tool use with no bearing on whether a file port was registered.

Startup-folder drops and scheduled-task XML definitions are a different mechanism. The file this pattern writes lands at the port target path (typically a system directory or the spooler tracing directory), which none of the template's TargetFilename selectors cover; Q7 (port registry value) and Q8 (unsigned module load into spoolsv.exe) cover the actual artifact and its execution.

Rule is CVE-specific rather than actor-specific, so the description and contexts describe the spooler file-port mechanism (port value written by the service, replayed across restarts, loaded from a system path) without naming reports, researchers, or campaigns.
