playbooks.name: Suspicious Process By Web Server Process
playbooks.description: Detects a web server process spawning a command interpreter, reconnaissance binary, or administrative tool. The rule fires when the child binary is one of a fixed list (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, sh.exe, bash.exe, cscript.exe, wscript.exe, arp.exe, net.exe, nltest.exe, reg.exe, sc.exe, at.ex

questions.question: Does the alerting event match the rule — a web-server parent spawning one of the listed child binaries — and which parent branch fired?
Is this server expected to spawn command interpreters or administrative tools from its web-server process at all?
Is this web-server process expected to spawn this child, and what started the web-server process itself?
What web request triggered this execution?
Is the web application and server software on this host current with security patches?
What other child processes did this same web-server process instance spawn?
What exactly did the spawned command do, and was any part of it encoded or obfuscated?
Was a service installed on this server around the time of the alert, and what binary does it run?
Did PowerShell script block logging capture the full script content?
Did the web-server process load any modules around the time of the alert that are not signed by Microsoft?
Did the alerting process or its children write files to disk, and where did those files land?
Did this server make outbound connections to external destinations around the time of the alert?
Were new logons or explicit-credential logons recorded on this server around the time of the alert?
Did other reconnaissance commands run on this server around the same time?
Has this web-server process spawned this child binary on this host before?
What else did this account run across the environment around the time of the alert?
Did the same web-server parent spawn the same child binary on other servers in this window?
Did this same detection fire on other servers in the last day?

attack_chain_coverage.label: crafted_request_to_public_endpoint
attack_chain_coverage.description: T1190: adversary sends crafted HTTP/S input to an internet-facing application; T1505.003: the request reaches a page previously written into a served directory

attack_chain_coverage.label: request_error_or_anomaly_signal
attack_chain_coverage.description: T1190: elevated 4xx/5xx responses or unusual methods/paths on the public endpoint precede the successful attempt

attack_chain_coverage.label: server_process_spawns_shell_or_loads_module
attack_chain_coverage.description: The web server process spawns a command interpreter or LOLbin, or loads a non-standard module instead of spawning a child

attack_chain_coverage.label: file_creation_in_web_directory
attack_chain_coverage.description: T1505.003: unexpected file creation in web directories — the shell page itself or staged tooling written by the spawned process

attack_chain_coverage.label: module_install_then_later_execution
attack_chain_coverage.description: T1505: installation of a server module/plugin that later executes command-line interpreters or establishes outbound connections

attack_chain_coverage.label: post_execution_logon_or_egress
attack_chain_coverage.description: T1190 stage 4: optional outbound callback from the host; T1505.003: 4624/4648 authentication following shell execution

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only (custom web server directory depending on the hosting environment; no values supplied by the analytic)
mutable_dispositions.notes: The rule is product-agnostic, so no single web root can be pinned in a query — the served directory differs per product and per site. Q11 correlates file activity by the alerting process and its children and instructs the analyst to read the returned paths against this server's configured content directories, which derives the web root from the host instead of hardcoding one. Q10's context carries the same instruction for module load paths.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: php-cgi.exe, apache.exe (analytic examples); rule list — caddy.exe, httpd.exe, nginx.exe, php-cgi.exe, php.exe, tomcat.exe, UMWorkerProcess.exe, w3wp.exe, ws_TomcatService.exe, java.exe/javaw.exe identified as Tomcat
mutable_dispositions.notes: The full parent-binary list from the rule's selection_webserver_image plus java.exe/javaw.exe is injected as the Image|endswith selection of the image_load question. Also carried verbatim in Q1's context as the two parent branches. Q15 and Q17 hydrate the parent from the alert (%ParentName%), which covers renamed or wrapped server binaries the static list would miss.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only (custom server wrapper processes or renamed webserver processes may require tuning)
mutable_dispositions.notes: Addressed by hydrating the parent from the alert rather than by a static list — Q15's 90-day parent-and-child pair baseline and Q17's fleet pivot both key on %ParentName%, so a wrapper or renamed server process is handled without tuning. Named in Q15's context.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: time delta between module install and process execution (T1505, persistence delay); 15 minutes correlation horizon between request, error, process spawn and egress (T1190)
mutable_dispositions.notes: The 15-minute horizon is the range on Q6 (sibling processes) and Q14 (recon burst), and is named in Q6's context with the instruction to widen it if activity sits at the edges. The module-install-to- execution delay is covered by Q10 at +/-1h and Q8 at +/-5m, whose contexts point at the ordering (module compiled/loaded shortly before the spawn; service installed around it).

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only (list of public IPs/hostnames fronting the app)
mutable_dispositions.notes: Scopes the access-log and proxy review. HTTP access logs are not an authorable logsource category and no process_creation field carries the fronting address, so Q4's context instructs the analyst to record the public hostname or address fronting the application along with the client source address.

These match HTTP request URIs and bodies, whose only home is the web access log — not an authorable category, and no process_creation field carries them. Carried into Q4's context with the exact values.

HTTP status codes exist only in the web access log, which is not an authorable category. Stated with the exact threshold in Q4's context as the marker of the failed attempts preceding the successful one.

The analytic's example value is CI-specific and would be misleading on a product-agnostic web-server rule. Q15's 90-day parent-and-child pair baseline derives this host's actual allowed-child list empirically instead of hardcoding one, and Q2 asks the application owner for the product's documented children. Both are named as the false-positive discriminator for this rule.

dedup_decisions.reason: Brief hint: parent_process is primary. Its query is the identical ProcessGuid|expand '%ParentProcessGuid%' parent lookup already served by the technique-set version, which additionally returns ParentCommandLine — the field the rule's tomcat2 branch turns on and the one that names the deployed application.

parent_child technique set is active, so per the deduplication rules the technique set's parent_process_legitimacy supersedes the cue's mechanism_decode — same ProcessGuid|expand '%ParentProcessGuid%' query, and the technique-set version returns the parent's own parent as well.

Near-identical to parent_child.sibling_processes (both list children of the alerting parent). sibling_processes anchors the exact parent instance via ParentProcessGuid rather than every w3wp.exe or java.exe on the host, which matters here because a web server runs several worker processes concurrently and only one of them served the request.

Its query is the same host+ParentName process_creation listing as cue_parent_process.follow_on, differing only in range, and both are subsumed by the ParentProcessGuid-anchored sibling question. The cross-logsource adaptation the template suggests (file/network activity of the parent) is authored instead as the file-activity question anchored on the alerting process and its children, and as the external-egress question.

Its ProcessGuid|expand '%ProcessGuid%' → ParentImage/ParentCommandLine projection is a strict subset of the verify_trigger_match question's fields, and the "what started the parent" step it exists for is answered by parent_child.parent_process_legitimacy, which walks one level further up.

The template's own note says it overlaps universal.host_user_context and that one of the two should be dropped. universal.host_user_context is kept because this rule's discriminator is whether the SERVER spawns children at all — a question about the host's application stack — not whether a person is an administrator; the alert fires under the application-pool or service identity in the normal case, so the discovery-specific user framing would ask an unanswerable question.

dedup_decisions.dropped: none — cue_user_actor.clustering and cue_user_actor.clustering_svc both kept
dedup_decisions.reason: user_actor pair — non-deduplicable. The user pivot asks what the account did fleet-wide in the window; the service-principal substitute asks whether the same parent-and-child launch mechanism fired on other servers. This rule's parent is by definition a long-running web-server service, so the alert almost always fires under an application-pool, service, or machine identity where the user pivot degenerates into service-owned volume — the substitute is the load-bearing half, but which identity fires cannot be known at generation time.

skipped_templates.reason: replaced_by: service_persistence.service_configuration (Q8). The brief additionally records registry.registry_key_context and scheduled_task.task_configuration as Phase 2 replacements for it. The Phase 2 decode slot is filled by Q7 (powershell.encoded_command_decode) for the command itself and Q8 for the service-installation branch.
See dedup_decisions — brief hint directs dropping it because parent_process is the primary cue.

Its host+Image|endswith '%Image%' 90-day aggregation baselines the child binary alone, and every binary in this rule's child list (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, net.exe, reg.exe, sc.exe, certutil.exe) is routine on a Windows server, so the count is high on every host and carries no signal about the rule's pattern. The discriminating dimension is the parent-and-child pairing, which Q15 baselines over the same 90 days.

Its host-wide Image+ParentImage aggregation over +/-15m is answered more precisely for this rule by Q6 (children of the exact alerting worker instance) and Q14 (recon binaries on the host in the same window). On a busy web server the unfiltered host aggregation returns the application's own process volume, in which the one worker-spawned child is not visible.

Its -6h sigma-alert listing on this host is close to Q18's alert-category query, and for a rule whose entry point is an inbound web request the preceding evidence is in the access log (Q4), not in earlier endpoint detections — exploitation of an internet-facing application typically produces no prior host alert at all.

Its fleet-wide ParentName+Image aggregation is the same query authored as Q17 (cue_user_actor.clustering_svc), which is the service-principal substitute this rule requires; keeping both would ship the identical detection block twice, differing only in range.

The template's own note says to keep it for download-cradle rules where a bypass precedes the payload. This rule fires on the parent-child pairing regardless of arguments, and the -1h host-wide CommandLine|contains scan for bypass strings would answer a question about the host's PowerShell hygiene rather than about the web server spawning a child. Any bypass flag on the alerting command line is read directly in Q7, which decodes the full command line including execution-policy and AMSI arguments.
See dedup_decisions — subset of verify_trigger_match's fields, and the parent walk is served by parent_child.parent_process_legitimacy.
See dedup_decisions — overlaps universal.host_user_context per the template's own note; the universal version is kept and adapted to the server-spawns-children discriminator.

reg.exe is one of 29 binaries in the rule's child list, so this rule is not a registry rule and the registry_set-by-ProcessGuid lookup returns nothing for the other 28. When reg.exe is the child, the key and value are visible in its command line, which Q7 reads in full; Q11 covers whether a written payload exists on disk, which is the part the command line does not answer.

Same reason — the +/-30m host-wide scan for reg.exe/regedit.exe write operations presumes a registry-focused rule. For a web server the relevant "what else happened" scope is the alerting worker's other children (Q6) and the recon burst (Q14), and any reg.exe among them appears there with its full command line.

Not skipped — recorded here for clarity: this template's applicability gate (is_persistence_rule) is met and it is authored as Q11, re-framed from the registry-payload check to the general file-write correlation, because the persistence artifact for this technique is a page written into a served directory rather than a registry value.

at.exe is one of 29 binaries in the child list, and the template's query is the same ProcessGuid|expand '%ProcessGuid%' → CommandLine lookup already authored as Q7, which decodes the full command line of whatever child fired — including at.exe arguments. Shipping both would put the identical detection block in two questions.

Its query looks for children of the Task Scheduler service (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -s Schedule), which is a follow-on for rules that detect task creation. This rule detects a web-server parent, and a scheduled task is only one of many possible outcomes; the +4h scheduler-children scan would run on every alert regardless of whether a task was created.

Manual "is the task still registered" verification presumes the alert is a task-creation event. This rule fires on the parent-child pairing, so the equivalent live-state check for this technique is whether the written page is still in the served directory, which Q11 sets up.

Its ProcessGuid|expand '%ProcessGuid%' → CommandLine query is identical to Q7's, and the live service state it asks about is only meaningful when a service was actually installed. Q8 returns the installation event with the start type and the run-as account as structured fields, which answers the configuration half; the remaining live-state check is a host action the analyst takes from Q8's result.

replaced_by: powershell.encoded_command_decode (Q7), per the brief hint. Q7 is adapted to cover the non-PowerShell encodings this set exists for (certutil -decode, caret/backtick escaping, runtime string concatenation) because the rule's child list spans cmd.exe, cscript.exe, wscript.exe and certutil.exe as well as the PowerShell binaries.

Priority: recommended. Its ProcessGuid → CommandLine boilerplate adds no query value and the organizational judgment it asks for is asked more precisely by Q2, which puts the question to the application owner in the form that discriminates for this rule — does this product spawn children as part of its operation — rather than asking whether a change ticket exists for a process spawn nobody raises tickets for.

Priority: recommended. The alert fires under an application-pool or service identity in the normal case, so there is no human behind the account to ask. The equivalent — asking the team that owns the application whether this is a product behaviour — is Q2.

Priority: recommended. Business-hours reasoning does not discriminate on an internet-facing server that serves requests continuously and is reachable from any timezone. The timing question that does discriminate for this rule is whether the spawn correlates with a deployment or maintenance window, which is part of Q2, and whether it correlates with a request, which is Q4.

Priority: recommended. It asks whether the organization normally makes changes this way, which presumes the alert is an administrative change. This rule fires on a web-server process spawning a child; the corresponding procedural question — is this how this application is designed to work — is Q2.

Priority: recommended. Its +/-4h host-wide scan for schtasks/at/sc/reg/bitsadmin/wmic overlaps the rule's own child list, so on this rule it would largely re-return the alerting event and its siblings, which Q6 already shows anchored to the exact worker instance. The persistence mechanism specific to this technique — a page left in a served directory — is covered by Q11, and the service branch by Q8.

Priority: recommended. Its Startup-folder and Tasks-directory paths are user-logon persistence locations that are not where this technique persists: a web shell persists by remaining in the served web directory, which has no fixed path and is covered by Q11's process-anchored file correlation. A host-wide Startup-folder scan on a server with no interactive logons returns installer noise.

hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR among selection groups: (selection_webserver_image OR selection_webserver_characteristics_tomcat1 OR selection_webserver_characteristics_tomcat2). Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame the disjunction faithfully as 'EITHER ... OR ...'. Where a branch is shown as (A AND B), that branch fires only when A and B match TOGETHER — keep the AND; do not split it into separate OR branches. Use condition_topology.prose for an LLM-ready summary.
hints_acted_on.where: Q1 and the description. Both frame the parent as matched by EITHER a named server binary OR a java/javaw parent identified as Tomcat, and both keep the AND inside the java branches (java.exe/javaw.exe TOGETHER WITH a \tomcat / -tomcat- path, or TOGETHER WITH a CATALINA_HOME / catalina.home / catalina.jar command line) rather than splitting them. Both also state the top-level AND with the child-binary selection. Q1's context tells the analyst to record which branch matched and what each branch implies for reading the parent.

notes: Condition reading, taken from the brief's condition_topology (OR_of_selections). Top level is an AND of two things minus a filter — selection_anomaly_children (child Image|endswith one of 29 binaries) AND at least one of the three webserver selections, AND NOT the two ManageEngine ADManager false-positive filters. The disjunction is entirely on the parent side: selection_webserver_image (ParentImage|endswith one of 9 named server binaries) OR selection_webserver_characteristics_tomcat1 (ParentImage|endswith java.exe/javaw.exe AND ParentImage|contains -tomcat-/\tomcat) OR selection_webserver_characteristics_tomcat2 (ParentImage|endswith java.exe/javaw.exe AND ParentCommandLine|contains CATALINA_HOME/catalina.home/ catalina.jar). The two tomcat branches are each an AND of two conditions on the same parent and are kept intact in the Q1 framing. or_valued_selections is empty — no selection is an OR of alternative field-maps.

Technique-focused framing throughout. The rule is product-agnostic with generic MITRE tags, so no actor, campaign, malware family, vendor, report or CVE is named in any analyst-visible field; the reference is a government advisory on web-shell detection and informed the file-in-web-directory and module-load angles without being cited.

Primary technique is T1505.003 — the rule's exact behavior is a web server process spawning a shell, which is the analytic's Windows detection for a web shell, and it drives the chain skeleton. T1190 is the entry-point half of the same event (its analytic's stage 3 is this rule verbatim) and contributed the delivery-vector, patch-status, module-load and egress questions. T1505 is in the brief's attack_brief though not tagged on the rule; it contributed the module-install-then-execute stage, which Q10 and Q8 cover.

The false-positive discriminator for this rule is broader than for a product-specific sibling because the rule is product-agnostic — some application stacks legitimately shell out (build and deploy hooks, admin consoles, backup jobs, health checks), and the rule's own falsepositives entry says so. The question set is therefore built around establishing whether THIS server spawns children at all. Q2 asks the application owner, Q15 derives the answer empirically from 90 days of this parent-and-child pairing, and Q3 identifies which application the parent was serving. The two ManageEngine ADManager filters in the rule are evidence of exactly this class of false positive and are already excluded by the rule.

HTTP access logs are not an authorable logsource category, so the three T1190 mutable elements that live there (PublicVIPs, SuspiciousPatterns, ErrorRateThreshold) are dispositioned as context on Q4 with their exact values rather than converted into a query the pipeline cannot scope.

Question order runs start-position triage and parent/vector context (Q1-Q6), then analysis (Q7-Q8), then the chain-progression context questions (Q9-Q15), the user-actor pair (Q16-Q17), and fleet breadth last (Q18). initial_access.campaign_scope carries position:start in the brief but is placed last with the other broad-scope questions because it answers fleet breadth rather than triage.

notes: condition_topology verified against rule.detection: shape all_AND is genuine. The only list-form in the rule is IntegrityLevel: [System, S-1-16-16384], which is a list of scalars under one field — intra-field membership, and the two values are the label and SID notation of the same integrity level. The filter_main_razer clause sits under `not 1 of filter_main_*` with a single member, which collapses to a plain AND-NOT by De Morgan. Q1 is therefore framed conjunctively, with the two IntegrityLevel notations described as one value in two forms rather than as a branch.

The rule''s title names Explorer, but its detection does not constrain Image at all — it fires on ANY child of RazerInstaller.exe at System integrity outside the installer directory. Questions are framed around "the SYSTEM-integrity child" rather than explorer.exe so they stay true to what the rule matches; the folder-picker Explorer window is described as the dominant benign case rather than as the detection criterion.

Kept technique-focused per the rule's generic MITRE tagging. Razer is named because the parent binary is the detection anchor, not as an actor or campaign reference. The technique is publicly documented and reproducible with an inexpensive device, so the description carries a curious-user hypothesis alongside a deliberate escalation attempt.

rule.commandline_values is empty, so no question promises parameter or flag filtering. Q4's mechanism_decode is scoped host + Image|endswith and its text asks only what the child is, with no "matching this pattern" claim; the descendant question is entity-scoped on ParentProcessGuid, which auto-satisfies alignment.

IntegrityLevel appears in the reflected detection blocks as composed by the brief generator and in Q1/Q5 field lists. Its population is not documented platform-neutrally in the availability tables; if the IntegrityLevel column is empty on descendant events, treat that as a visibility gap rather than as evidence the descendants dropped privilege.

playbooks.name: Suspicious Scripting in a WMI Consumer
playbooks.description: Detects a WMI event consumer whose stored payload carries PowerShell or scripting content of three alternative forms, any one of which fires the rule on its own: either the payload combines new-object with net.webclient and .downloadstring, or it combines new-object with net.webclient and .downloadf

questions.question: Which branch of this rule did the consumer's payload match — a download cradle, or one of the standalone scripting markers?
Is this user and host expected to register WMI event subscriptions that run scripts?
What WMI subscription activity did this host's WMI activity log record, and when was this consumer registered?
What does the consumer's payload decode to, and what operation does the decoded content perform?
What did WmiPrvSE.exe, scrcons.exe, or mofcomp.exe spawn on this host, and does any of it look unrelated to a management agent?
Did any process on this host run a command line carrying the same download-cradle combination or scripting markers the rule fires on?
Did a script host or the WMI provider host load a scripting engine library on this host?
Did WMI subscription tooling or a MOF compilation run on this host around the alert?
Did the WMI provider host, the script consumer host, or a script interpreter make outbound connections close to the alert?
Did the WMI provider host or the script consumer host write any files to disk around the alert?
Does the timing of this consumer's registration and execution align with normal work hours and maintenance windows?
Was there a change ticket, maintenance window, or agent deployment that accounts for this WMI subscription?
Does an administrator or the owning team recall registering this WMI subscription or authoring the script it runs?
What other activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
Do permanent WMI event subscriptions appear across the fleet, or only on this host?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: Microsoft Word/Excel or mshta.exe spawning wscript.exe/cscript.exe
mutable_dispositions.notes: Not injected as a query filter. The named parents are the T1059.005 analytic's generic document-container path; this rule fires on a WMI event consumer, whose execution parent is WmiPrvSE.exe or scrcons.exe. Filtering Q5 on winword.exe/excel.exe/mshta.exe would return nothing related to this alert. Q5's selection carries the parents that actually apply (\WmiPrvSE.exe, \scrcons.exe, \mofcomp.exe) and its context states explicitly that the document-container form does not apply here and the parent should be judged against the agent baseline instead. wscript.exe and cscript.exe are carried in Q7's and Q9's Image lists as the script hosts a CommandLineEventConsumer can reach.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: script execution by non-admin users or service accounts
mutable_dispositions.notes: Q2's context states that both subscription registration and consumer execution commonly run as SYSTEM even when a person initiated them, so a SYSTEM attribution is not on its own evidence of an agent. Not query-injectable: the alerting event type carries no reliable actor field, and %User% cannot be pre-filtered at authoring time.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — execution outside normal business hours or patching cycle
mutable_dispositions.notes: Q11 asks whether registration and execution align with work hours and maintenance windows, and directs the analyst to read host local time rather than the collection timestamp and to distinguish a regular execution interval (automated filter trigger) from a cluster around one session. No threshold value exists to inject.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — high entropy indicative of obfuscation or encoding

Q4 covers the same ground concretely by naming the rule's own encoding markers (' -enc ', System.Security.Cryptography.FromBase64Transform, ' -decode ') and instructing the analyst to iterate the decoding and reconstruct Chr()/concatenation/backtick-escaped strings.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: vbscript.dll, scrrun.dll, or other scripting engine modules
mutable_dispositions.notes: vbscript.dll and scrrun.dll injected verbatim into Q7's ImageLoaded|endswith list, extended with jscript.dll, jscript9.dll, wbemdisp.dll and wshom.ocx as the remaining engine and object-model modules a script consumer loads. wshom.ocx is tied in Q7's context to the WScript.Shell marker the rule fires on.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: encoded or uncommon script execution patterns
mutable_dispositions.notes: The rule's own three branches injected verbatim into Q6 against CommandLine, preserving the condition topology: selection_cradle_string (new-object AND net.webclient AND .downloadstring) OR selection_cradle_file (new-object AND net.webclient AND .downloadfile) OR selection_markers (any one of ' iex(', ' -nop ', ' -noprofile ', ' -decode ', ' -enc ', WScript.Shell, System.Security.Cryptography.FromBase64Transform), all ANDed with host scope.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — varies across managed/unmanaged workstations
mutable_dispositions.notes: T1059's tuning rationale is that the expected parent set differs per environment. Q5's context makes that the analyst's judgment call — management agents produce a small repeating set of children under WmiPrvSE.exe/scrcons.exe, and the deviation criteria (command interpreter, script host, encoded PowerShell, user-writable path) are stated rather than filtered, because they are judgments and hardcoding them would be environment-coupled.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only — restrict analysis to work hours or admin maintenance windows
mutable_dispositions.notes: T1059's window element is the same rationale as T1059.005's; Q14 uses +/-15m host clustering and its context directs the analyst to measure the interval between whatever preceded the consumer and the consumer itself.

dedup_decisions.dropped: llm_generated fleet-wide repeat of the Q6 command-marker query
dedup_decisions.reason: A fleet-scoped version of the rule's cradle/marker command-line query was considered and dropped. The markers ' -nop ', ' -enc ' and ' iex(' are common enough in ordinary PowerShell administration that an unanchored fleet query over -30d returns volume without discriminating, and the fleet-level question this playbook actually needs is whether the SUBSCRIPTION recurs across hosts (a deployed product) rather than whether the markers do. Q15 answers that on the WMI activity channel instead.

hints_acted_on.hint: dimension 'parent_process_analysis' (techniques: T1059.005) is uncovered — the question selection does not include any of: [parent_child.parent_process_legitimacy, cue_parent_process.mechanism_decode, cue_process_tool.process_chain, +6 more]. Either pull in one of those templates or author a custom attack:T1059.005.parent_process_analysis question
hints_acted_on.where: Q5 — attack:T1059.005.parent_process_analysis, a custom question as the hint's second option directs. None of the named templates are present in this brief's templates[] (the brief carries only universal, obfuscation and cue_host_context), so pulling one in was not available; the custom question anchors on ParentImage|endswith \WmiPrvSE.exe / \scrcons.exe / \mofcomp.exe, which are the parents a WMI event consumer actually executes under, and carries the T1059.005 ParentProcess and T1059 ParentProcessName mutable elements.

hints_acted_on.hint: logsource 'image_load' (recommended by techniques: T1059.005) is not covered — pull in cue_image_load.* or author a custom question with `category: image_load`
hints_acted_on.where: Q7 — attack:T1059.005.tuning_parameter, category: image_load question on scrcons.exe/WmiPrvSE.exe/wscript.exe/cscript.exe loading vbscript.dll/jscript.dll/jscript9.dll/wbemdisp.dll/wshom.ocx/scrrun.dll. Acted on rather than declined per the logsource-hint default: this is the corroborating evidence path that still works on hosts not shipping the WMI activity channel, and it carries the ModuleName mutable element.

hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection_destination has 3 alternative branches. The condition string ('selection_destination') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as 'EITHER ... OR ...', and Q1's context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. (A list of scalar values under a single field is different — that is intra-field membership, not a branch OR.)
hints_acted_on.where: Q1 and the playbook description. Both use explicit either/or framing over the three branches and preserve the internal AND of the two cradle branches (new-object AND net.webclient AND .downloadstring; new-object AND net.webclient AND .downloadfile) against the third branch's any-one-of marker list. Q1's question text asks which branch matched, and its context states what each branch implies for the rest of the investigation — cradle branches put the weight on the network and file-write evidence, the marker branch puts it on the decoded payload because it is the broadest and collects the most administrative scripting. Q6 preserves the same topology in its query condition.

notes: The Sysmon EID 19/20/21 field problem, handled explicitly. This rule's detection selects on `Destination`, a Sysmon EID 20 (WmiEventConsumer) field. That field has no source in this environment, so the rule's own selection is not mirrorable in a query and no question pretends to mirror it. No question in this playbook authors EventNamespace, Consumer, Filter, Destination-as-a-selector, Query, Name or Type in any detection block. The WMI-channel questions (Q3, Q15) anchor on EventID only — 5861 permanent subscription, 5860 temporary subscription, 5857 provider load — written as the Sigma-spec name so the pipeline maps it to event.code. The rule's marker values are instead evaluated where they can actually be observed: Q6 applies them to process CommandLine, which is what the consumer's payload becomes once an interpreter runs it.

Honesty about the alerting event's own source. The alerting event may itself originate from a source this environment does not ship, and both wmi categories are channel-dependent. This is stated platform-neutrally in the contexts where it changes the reading of a result: Q1 routes payload retrieval to the consumer record or the registration record rather than to a query result; Q3 states that an empty result on a host not shipping the channel is a visibility gap rather than evidence no subscription exists, and gives the root\subscription enumeration as the fallback; Q7 states that image_load corroborates execution on hosts where the channel is not collected; Q15 states that non-shipping hosts contribute nothing to the fleet baseline, so a single-host result may reflect collection coverage rather than a single-host subscription.

The durable, observable angle is the consumer's effect, and the playbook leans on it. Q5 (children of WmiPrvSE.exe / scrcons.exe / mofcomp.exe), Q6 (the rule's own markers against process CommandLine), Q7 (script-engine loads), Q8 (subscription tooling), Q9 (outbound connections from the provider/script hosts), Q10 (file writes by the provider/script hosts) and Q14 (host clustering) are all anchored on host.name plus fields that exist on their target telemetry and can return rows. Q1, Q2, Q4, Q11, Q12 and Q13 are ProcessGuid-anchored boilerplate — a WMI-Activity alert document carries no process identifier to hydrate %ProcessGuid% from. Three of those (Q1, Q2, Q4) are frozen KEEP_EXACT question-set templates whose fields[] are compared exactly by validate_template_fields, so the boilerplate is the required form rather than a choice; the other three are organizational filler per the SO conversion constraint. All six have contexts written so the analyst gets the investigative step without the query being load-bearing, and answer_sources pointing at manual_review / organizational_knowledge / asset_inventory / safe_environment accordingly.

Q1's frozen field list is [Destination] and its logsource is process_creation — that combination comes from the brief's category variant for this rule and is fixed by the template-fields check. It is inert on this telemetry. Q1's question text and context therefore direct the analyst to read the payload from the subscription object or the registration record rather than from the query result.

category: wmi_event was chosen over category: wmi for Q3 and Q15 to match the source rule's own logsource. Both categories carry an identical add_condition (event.dataset: wmi.operational) in the playbook pipeline, so the compiled query is the same either way; matching the rule's logsource satisfies the logsource-agreement check without changing behavior.

Operation is projected (not selected) in Q3 and Q15. It is the correct Sigma-spec name for the WMI-Activity Operation attribute and is the field that carries the consumer and filter text on grids that populate it; where it is not populated it renders as an empty column and costs nothing, while EventID and host.name carry the answer. It is never used as a selector, so it cannot silently narrow a result to zero.

T1059.005 is primary: the rule fires on the content of a WMI event consumer's script payload, and the markers it matches (WScript.Shell, FromBase64Transform, the download cradle) are the VBScript/PowerShell constructs that subtechnique covers. T1059 is the parent and contributes the command_analysis dimension (Q6) and the interpreter-argument angle; it describes scripting generically rather than the script-in-a-consumer pattern the rule targets. Both are tagged on the rule via T1059.005 only — T1059 appears in the brief's attack_brief as the parent technique's analytic set.

No cue_user_actor pattern is present in the brief (cues.primary and cues.secondary are both empty; cue_host_context is the only cue), so no user-pivot / service-principal pair was authored and no question carries always_include.

No template in this brief carries reflection_kind, so no REFLECTED detection block exists to preserve and reflection_overrides is empty. The rule's detection is reproduced deliberately and non-verbatim in Q6 against CommandLine — a different field from the rule's Destination, chosen because Destination has no source here; the branch topology and every literal value are preserved exactly.

Question order follows the behavioral chain rather than strict start/middle/end template positions: the WMI registration record (Q3) and payload decode (Q4) sit immediately after triage because they are the load-bearing evidence, the execution-effect pivots (Q5-Q10) follow the chain outward from parent to command to module to tooling to network to file, and the organizational-context questions (Q11-Q13) are placed after the technical pivots they depend on. The baseline and clustering questions (Q14-Q16) remain at the end.

Which accounts may be compromised, and do any have elevated privileges?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did the acting account do across the network around this time?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?
What other activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?

mutable_dispositions.notes: Analytic gives no concrete process list (e.g., lsass.exe, svchost.exe as examples only). Realized as the credential-store-access process_access question, which surfaces SourceImage/TargetImage/GrantedAccess so the analyst sees which sensitive targets were touched without a hard-coded target list that would miss the service's own credential database.

Analytic describes a regex of suspicious CLI keywords (dpapi, credman, mimikatz) as a tuning example, not fixed values. Realized as the decode-the-child-command question, which directs the analyst to identify reconnaissance, output redirection, download, and credential-store keywords in the actual command line rather than filtering on a fixed list.

dedup_decisions.reason: user_actor pair — non-deduplicable; both emitted (subject-pivot Q13 and launch-mechanism-pivot Q14). Serv-U typically runs as a service account, so the parent+binary substitute is load-bearing.
user_actor pair — non-deduplicable; both emitted (subject-pivot Q15 and launch-mechanism-pivot Q16).
parent_process is primary (hint) — parent cue subsumes process_chain. Parent origin is covered by parent_child.parent_process_legitimacy (Q3).

replaced_by credential_access.credential_target_identification (hint). The child binary is too common (cmd.exe/powershell.exe) for Image-scoped mechanism decode, and the rule carries no commandline_values to tighten with; the entity-scoped credential_target_identification (Q5) provides Phase 2 decode.
host+parent.name+Image baseline subsumed by cue_user_actor.baseline_svc (Q14), which pivots on the same parent.name+Image pairing across host and environment.

hint_dispositions.hint: logsource 'image_load' (recommended by techniques: T1548.002) is not covered — pull in cue_image_load.* or author a custom question with `category: image_load`
hint_dispositions.reason: The image_load recommendation derives from the broad T1548.002 analytic that also covers Rundll32/COM-object DLL-loading UAC bypass paths. That child-process signal is covered directly by the auto-elevating-binary launch question (Q7), the flagged-location execution question (Q8), and the elevated-action question (Q9). hint_dispositions.hint: logsource 'process_access' (recommended by techniques: T1548.002) is validator-blocked as a category, but a partial substitute exists — author against the Defend behavioral API channel instead — `logsource: {product: windows}` with selection on `event.dataset: endpoint.events.api` and `process.Ext.api.name` (WriteProcessMemory/QueueUserAPC/SetWindowsHookEx). hint_dispositions.reason: process_access covers the memory-injection UAC-bypass variant (injecting code into a trusted process to inherit elevation). The shell\open\command hijack this rule detects does not inject - it plants a class-key command so an auto-elevating binary or a file open SPAWNS a high-integrity child process. The elevation is observable as process_creation (auto-elevating binary in Q7, flagged-location child in Q8, High/System integrity processes in Q9), not as cross-process API calls. No WriteProcessMemory/QueueUserAPC surface is part of this chain, so no behavioral-API question was authored.

hint_dispositions.hint: logsource 'security' (recommended by techniques: T1548.002,T1546.001) is not covered and no template family exists — author a custom question with `category: security`
hint_dispositions.reason: The security recommendation maps to Windows Security EventCode 4672 (special privileges assigned to a new logon) and 4688 (process creation), both signalling that a process ran with elevated privileges. Under this environment's endpoint telemetry that same elevated-execution signal is captured natively by the High/System IntegrityLevel process_creation question (Q9) and the auto-elevating-binary launch question (Q7), which are the Defend-observable equivalents. A separate `category: security` question would query a channel this pipeline does not reliably scope for these events, so the elevation angle is kept in process_creation.

notes: Condition topology is all_AND (selection AND none of the three filter groups), so Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing — key path contains the trust path AND ends in \Path AND the writer is not an Office application or the Click-to-Run updater AND the directory is not a known Office template path.

EventType equality conditions were not carried into any query. The rule's detection has none, and the endpoint telemetry emits ECS event actions rather than Sysmon literals, so an EventType clause would match nothing. EventType appears only in the frozen fields projection of registry.registry_value_persistence_check (Q11), where it is a display column, not a filter.

Registry value deletion is not observable in this telemetry, so no question asks whether the Trusted Location entry was later removed. Q14 (key write history over -90d) frames cleanup as a re-modification question instead, and Q12 answers whether the grant was exercised.

The trusted directory itself lives in the registry value data, which is not recorded on every registry modification event. Q1, Q7, and Q8 therefore tell the analyst to read the Path value from the key directly when it is absent from the event, rather than assuming it is present or treating the directory as unknowable.

%ParentProcessGuid% is never authored against this alert — it is not a field of a registry event and hydrates to NODATA. Parent attribution goes through the writing process's own start event (Q3, ProcessGuid-anchored), and the children question (Q4) expands the ParentProcessGuid FIELD with the alert's own %ProcessGuid%.

cue_registry_key.scope (Q16) was broadened from TargetObject|expand: '%TargetObject%' to TargetObject|contains: 'Security\Trusted Locations\Location'. ADAPT_STRUCTURALLY permits it and the exact-key match would have been near-useless: the key path embeds a per-host Location index and Office application, so an exact fleet match would miss the same trusted directory registered at a different index. The broadened query answers the question the analyst actually needs — is this a rollout — and the question text promises exactly that.

cue_registry_key.follow_on (Q12) was adapted from a bare host-scoped process_creation query to one filtered on Office parents. The template's guidance is to narrow the generic query to the specific mechanism; here the grant's effect is macro execution inside an Office application, so Office child processes are the observable that the grant took effect.

cue_host_context.clustering (Q15) was adapted from process_creation to registry_set per the template's own note for registry rules, keeping the aggregation structure and swapping the projection to TargetObject+Image.

The two ECS-named signer columns (process.code_signature.subject_name / process.code_signature.trusted) on Q1, Q2 and Q7 are frozen question-set template fields — validate_template_fields hard-fails on any edit to those lists, so they are copied verbatim despite falling outside the authoring floor.

playbooks.name: Unsigned Module Loaded by ClickOnce Application
playbooks.description: Detects a process running from the ClickOnce application cache (\AppData\Local\Apps\2.0\) loading a module that is unsigned or carries an expired signature. ClickOnce deployments inherit the reputation and signature of their published host application, which makes them attractive for trusted-code ex

questions.question: Does this event match the rule's criteria — a process running from the ClickOnce application cache loading a module that is unsigned or has an expired signature?
Is this user and host expected to run this ClickOnce-deployed application?
Does the user recall installing or launching this ClickOnce application?
Is this application a documented, sanctioned deployment in this organization?
What other modules did this ClickOnce application load, and did any come from its deployment directory unsigned or under a system-library name?
What are the signing details, hash, and threat-intel reputation of the flagged module?
How was the ClickOnce application launched, and with what command line and working directory?
What process spawned this ClickOnce application, and is that parent chain expected?
When was the flagged module written into the ClickOnce deployment directory, and by which process?
Were autorun or DLL load-point registry values modified on this host around the module load?
What child processes did the ClickOnce application spawn after loading the module?
Did the ClickOnce application make outbound network connections around the module load?
Has this module been loaded on this host before, and by which processes?
When this host has previously loaded unsigned or expired-signature modules from ClickOnce cache paths, what programs and users drove it, and does this alert fit that history?
What other activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
Were files dropped to persistence locations on this host around the alert?
Have other hosts loaded unsigned or expired-signature modules from ClickOnce cache paths in the past week?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?

hint_dispositions.reason: The T1133 'application' analytic targets VPN / Citrix / remote-access gateway logs showing external logons — the External-Remote-Services interactive-access pattern. This rule's detection is purely process_creation: dns.exe spawning an unexpected child via memory-corruption RCE (the SIGRed pattern), not an interactive remote logon. There are no gateway-application events corresponding to this trigger, so an application-logsource query would return activity unrelated to what fired the alert. The relevant external-reachability check (the inbound DNS request that reached the service) is covered by the delivery_vector question.

A failed-logon query would surface noise unrelated to the DNS RCE trigger. The campaign_scope question correlates the actual detection across DNS servers, and the precursor question surfaces any prior alerts on the host, which together carry the cross-host and timeline signal the security analytic was meant to provide.

questions.question: Which file did dns.exe delete, and is it something other than the DNS debug log?

Is this DNS server patched against known DNS Server remote code execution flaws such as CVE-2020-1350?
Was an administrator performing DNS maintenance that would explain this deletion?
What category of file was deleted, and does it look like log cleanup, tool self-cleanup, or routine rotation?
Did the deleted file exist or execute on this host before it was removed, and is it recoverable?
What other files did dns.exe write or delete around the alert?
What was written to System32, NETLOGON, or SYSVOL on this host recently, and by which processes?
What modules did dns.exe load around the deletion, and were any unsigned or from unusual paths?
Did dns.exe spawn any child processes around the deletion?
Is the deleting process the legitimate System32 dns.exe launched by services.exe, or a masquerading binary?
Did dns.exe restart around this time, consistent with a service crash and auto-recovery?
Did dns.exe make outbound connections to non-DNS ports or unusual destinations around the deletion?
Was a new Windows service installed on this host around the deletion?
Were persistence tools run on this host in the surrounding window?
What other process activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
When this host previously produced this pattern, dns.exe deleting a non-log file, what drove it?

attack_chain_coverage.description: The in-service code stages a payload (executable into System32, script into NETLOGON/SYSVOL) and/or cleans up logs and tooling — the deletion is the visible edge of this

attack_chain_coverage.label: persistence_and_followon
attack_chain_coverage.description: The foothold is made durable (new service, scheduled task) and follow-on activity — child processes, outbound C2 — proceeds from the trusted service context

mutable_dispositions.notes: T1133's external-remote-services analytic models VPN/RDP logon-time anomalies, which do not apply to a DNS-service exploitation rule. The nearest applicable check — whether a maintenance window explains the activity — is folded into the human_recall administrator-maintenance framing.

T1133 intends this as an approved-external-IP allowlist for remote access; reframed for this rule as the known-upstream-resolver comparison in the dns.exe outbound-connection question — non-resolver destinations are the deviation.

Geographic allowlisting of remote-access sources is not meaningful for a server-side DNS exploitation rule; the equivalent signal here is a non-DNS-port or non-resolver outbound destination, covered by the network question.

Failed-logon counting belongs to the T1133 remote-access-authentication model, which is a mismatched mapping for this file-deletion rule; no logon-threshold tuning applies. Host-role expectation carries the tuning judgment instead.
Correlation window linking the deletion to surrounding activity — expressed as the +/-15m host-clustering range and the +/-1h module/network/service windows.

dedup_decisions.reason: dns.exe is a service launched with a static service invocation; its command line has no operational arguments to decode. The Phase-2 'what did it actually do' analysis is carried by cue_artifact.mechanism_decode (what file was deleted and whether it is cleanup vs evidence destruction), which is the meaningful mechanism for a file_delete alert.

'Does this host run dns.exe' is uninformative — a DNS server runs dns.exe continuously, so the count is always high and non-discriminating. The rule-pattern host baseline (has dns.exe deleted a non-log file here before) is the targeted first-seen signal and is covered by the reflected cue_process_tool.baseline_deviation.
Host-wide process clustering duplicates cue_host_context.clustering (same process_creation host-scoped +/-15m aggregation). Kept the host-context version.

Service-principal degeneration: dns.exe runs as SYSTEM, so %User% is a system/machine account and the user-scoped rule-pattern count collapses to the fleet-wide count already provided by cue_process_tool.scope. Neither identity axis discriminates for this rule (see clustering decline).

The parent-mechanism substitute assumes a discriminating launcher; for a Windows service the parent is always services.exe, so ParentName-scoping adds no constraint and the reflected query reduces to the fleet-pattern count. Host-pattern (baseline_deviation) and fleet-pattern (scope) reflected questions already cover the rule-pattern baseline.

Under SYSTEM the user network-wide clustering returns unbounded agent-telemetry noise (the template's own note). No compensating user-pivot authored because user identity does not attribute behavior for a SYSTEM service; process/lineage/network axes (children, modules, outbound connections) carry the same-window scope instead.

Parent-scoped same-window fleet clustering reduces to a fleet count because the parent is services.exe (non-discriminating for a service). The coordinated-rollout signal it targets is covered by cue_process_tool.scope (fleet-wide rule-pattern count) without the illusory parent constraint.

'Has this file been seen before' anchored on the deleted TargetFilename overlaps with cue_artifact.artifact_verification, which already looks backward for the file's prior existence/execution; the recovery-and-prior-existence framing is the more actionable form for a deletion.

Generic Startup-folder / Run-key drop check is less relevant to a DNS-server exploitation than the System32/NETLOGON/SYSVOL drop paths this rule's intel calls out; file.file_directory_context re-anchored on those specific directories covers the file-drop persistence angle for this host role.

The template resolves the delivery vector from the parent process, but dns.exe's parent is deterministically services.exe, so the query is uninformative. The actual delivery vector for DNS-service exploitation is a crafted DNS message over the network, addressed by the dns.exe outbound-connection question and the patch-status question (which CVE was reachable).

hint_dispositions.hint: logsource 'application' (recommended by techniques: T1133) is not covered and no template family exists — author a custom question with `category: application`
hint_dispositions.reason: The T1133 analytic's application logsource is VPN/Citrix/remote-access-gateway logs showing external IP logins — a mismatched technique mapping for a rule that detects code executing inside the DNS Server service via memory corruption, not remote-access-gateway authentication. No gateway telemetry is relevant. The closest application-log analog, dns.exe crashing and restarting, is covered via process_creation restart detection (the service auto-recovery question).

hint_dispositions.hint: logsource 'security' (recommended by techniques: T1133) is not covered and no template family exists — author a custom question with `category: security`
hint_dispositions.reason: Acted on as Q14 (attack:T1133.security): a service-installation question using the sanctioned product:windows + service:security + EventID:4697 form. Reframed from T1133's 4776/4625 remote-access authentication intent toward the rule's actual persistence pathway — code inside dns.exe registering a new service directly (which may not spawn sc.exe), per the DNS-exploit service-registration pattern.

dedup_decisions.reason: parent_child technique set is confirmed — parent_process_legitimacy performs the same ParentProcessGuid lookup and additionally projects ParentCommandLine, which is what names the script, package, or crashed process behind the parent. The more specific version wins.

Same investigative step as parent_child.sibling_processes (what else did the parent launch), and the technique-set version is the more precise form — ParentProcessGuid pins the exact parent instance, whereas the cue's ParentName scope matches every instance of a service host or updater on the host and would drown the answer.

Hint says parent_process is primary. The template's ProcessGuid|expand '%ParentProcessGuid%' lookup is byte-identical in intent to Q3 (parent_child.parent_process_legitimacy), which is already present with a wider field projection.

The parent-constrained baseline (Q8) is the meaningful form of the same question, and the reflected user/parent baselines (Q11, Q12) cover the rule's full pattern.

user_actor pair — non-deduplicable. Q11/Q12 (baseline + baseline_svc) and Q13/Q14 (clustering + clustering_svc) pivot on different identity dimensions (subject vs. launch mechanism) and degenerate under different conditions; both variants are emitted per AGENTS.md.

hints_acted_on.hint: cmd.exe: too common for Image-based scoping — use CommandLine patterns for mechanism_decode
hints_acted_on.where: Q5 — cue_process_tool.mechanism_decode re-anchored from host.name + Image|endswith \cmd.exe to ProcessGuid|expand '%ProcessGuid%'. The rule has no commandline_values to filter on, so the template's other sanctioned fallback (ProcessGuid scoping) was used. The same hint drove dropping cue_process_tool.baseline (see dedup_decisions) and the rule-pattern scoping of Q9.

hints_acted_on.hint: parent_process is primary — drop cue_process_tool:process_chain
hints_acted_on.where: cue_process_tool.process_chain dropped (see dedup_decisions); the parent lookup is covered by Q3 (parent_child.parent_process_legitimacy), and the parent cue supplies Q7, Q8, and Q10.

notes: condition_topology.shape is all_AND (single selection), so Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing — the child must end in cmd.exe AND the parent must end in one of the 24 listed binaries.

Because cmd.exe is the most common binary on Windows, every non-entity-scoped question carries the rule's parent constraint: Q8/Q10 via ParentName + Image, Q9 and the three reflected user_actor queries via the rule's full selection, Q7 via the parent's own Image. The only unconstrained views are the deliberately broad host-context aggregation (Q15) and the user-clustering pivot (Q13), which are aggregate scans by design.

cue_parent_process.clustering was adapted to network_connection scoped to the parent binary on the alerting host. Its default process_creation form (host.name + ParentName) would have produced a third near-copy of the sibling-processes query; the network view is the distinct angle the template's notes call for, and it is the one that separates an updater fetching a package from a parent receiving content elsewhere.

Technique-focused rule (generic title, single T1059 tag, no emerging-threat tag) — no actors, campaigns, or reports named. The single reference is a vendor documentation page with no fetched content in the brief, so it contributed nothing beyond the rule's own logic.

The high-value pivot is the redirect target file: Q7 correlates file writes by ProcessGuid lineage (never %file_paths%/%file_dirs% — dead fields; never host-only against file telemetry), Q8 asks whether any later command line referenced the staged temp path, and Q9 looks for egress from non-system binaries in the same +4h window. Staged discovery output only matters to the technique once it leaves the host.

Q-vs-query agreement: every question claiming a pattern filter carries a matching CommandLine|contains constraint (Q5, Q6, Q8, Q10, Q17) or is entity-scoped via ProcessGuid / ParentProcessGuid (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q7), which auto-satisfies. notes: Topology verified by reading rule.detection directly, not just condition_topology. shape: all_AND is genuine — `selection` is a single map whose TargetObject|contains value is a list of SCALARS (intra-field membership, an OR within one field, which stays AND at the selection level) ANDed with TargetObject|endswith: \EulaAccepted. questions.question: Did wfc.exe run, either by Image ending in \wfc.exe or by reporting an OriginalFileName of wfc.exe?
Is this user and host expected to compile and run .NET workflows with the Windows SDK Workflow Command-line Compiler?
Where does the wfc.exe that ran live, and is that path the expected Windows SDK install location?
What did wfc.exe compile and run? Decode its full command line and identify the XOML or source file it was given.
What process spawned wfc.exe, and is that parent chain expected for a workflow compile?
Did wfc.exe spawn a script host or proxy-execution binary such as powershell.exe, cmd.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, wscript.exe, or mshta.exe?
Did files appear in user-writable or atypical paths around the time wfc.exe ran, consistent with a compiled payload being written to disk?
Did wfc.exe load any unsigned or user-writable DLLs?
Did wfc.exe or its child processes make outbound network connections shortly after the compile?
Has this user previously produced the rule's pattern, and does that history fit their role?
Has this parent process historically driven the rule's pattern on this host or across the environment, or is the parent new for this activity?
What else did this user do across the network around this time?
Did this same parent-driven pattern fire on other hosts in the same window — i.e., is this a coordinated automation rollout, or is the activity isolated to this host?
What other activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?
When this host has previously fired the rule's wfc.exe pattern, what parents and users normally drive it, and does the current alert fit?
Have other hosts fired the rule's wfc.exe pattern in the past week, and does the cross-host distribution look like consistent automation or one-off activity?

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: Hashes|contains: 4,432 values (1,304 SHA1=, 1,303 SHA256=, 1,257 MD5=, 568 IMPHASH=) — the rule's entire selection
mutable_dispositions.notes: Not injected, and the reason is list size rather than a mapping problem. Driver loads carry hash and signature data directly, so the file's 90-day history on this host answers the baseline and the verification questions in one result rather than two near-identical ones. Q6 keeps the richer projection and its context asks both readings (first-time load versus recurring, and one hash and signer versus several).

Its query is a 90-day process_creation aggregation scoped to host.name + Image|endswith '%Image%'. On a driver load event %Image% hydrates to the process that triggered the load — typically the service control manager or a service host — so the result would measure how often that process runs, which is constant on every Windows host and says nothing about the driver. The history that matters for this rule is the driver file's, which Q6 provides on the load event's own logsource.

Its query also scopes process_creation to host.name + Image|endswith '%Image%', which on a driver load hydrates to the service control manager or a service host rather than to a tool with arguments worth decoding, and the rule has no CommandLine values at all (rule.commandline_values is empty). The Phase 2 decode is split between Q7 (the replacement — the structured 7045 service record, which is where a driver load's mechanism actually lives) and Q5 (cue_image_load.mechanism_decode — the load event's path, signer, and hash on the alert's own logsource).

Recommended, not must_include, and its judgement is already made twice in this playbook with more to work from — Q3 asks for the change record or maintenance window directly, and Q4 asks the person whether they ran the software. A kernel driver load also has no meaningful working-hours signal of its own: drivers load at boot and whenever their product starts, so the load time reflects the host's uptime rather than a person's choice of hour. Dropped to keep the question count within range while retaining the organizational checks that name a product or a person.

Recommended, not must_include. Its framing ("is this method of making changes consistent with your standard procedure") targets rules that detect a person invoking command-line tooling; this rule detects a kernel load, and the equivalent judgement — whether driver-installing software belongs on this host's build and reaches it through the normal deployment route — is asked directly by Q2 (host and user expectation) and Q3 (change record). Dropped to keep the question count within range.

hints_acted_on.where: Q7 — service_configuration kept as the Phase 2 mechanism question (KEEP_EXACT query, service: system + EventID 7045 + host.name, frozen fields ServiceName / ImagePath / StartType / AccountName), adapted to ask what the driver's service registration recorded rather than what an sc.exe command line said. cue_process_tool.mechanism_decode dropped; see skipped_templates.

hints_acted_on.where: Q11 (attack:T1543.003.tuning_parameter) — registry_set question on host.name + TargetObject|contains '\CurrentControlSet\Services\' AND Details|contains '.sys', +/-4h, projecting TargetObject / Details / Image / User. Covers the registry route to driver registration, which leaves no 7045 record when the service key is written directly.

hints_acted_on.hint: logsource 'security' (recommended by techniques: T1543.003,T1068) is not covered and no template family exists — author a custom question with `service: security`
hints_acted_on.where: Q12 (attack:T1068.time_correlation) — service: security question on EventID 4672 + host.name, +/-1h around the load, projecting SubjectUserName / SubjectLogonId / PrivilegeList. Covers the privilege-use stage of the T1068 analytic (which names EventCode=4672) and establishes which account held the rights that made the load possible.

notes: Topology verified against rule.detection directly, not from condition_topology alone. The condition is a bare 'selection' and the selection's value is a single map with one key (Hashes|contains) whose value is a list of scalars — intra-field membership, not a list of maps, so there is no hidden branch OR. shape all_AND is genuine and Q1 and the description use flat framing.

Selector-conversion check, since driver_load hash rules have been mis-read as match-nothing before: this rule's 4,432 values carry all four algorithm prefixes (SHA1, SHA256, MD5, IMPHASH), and the hash break-out plus the driver-load mapping route each prefix to its own ECS hash field, so the rule converts and can fire — the SHA256 and MD5 branches against the driver file's hash, the IMPHASH branch against its import hash. Which branch matched is not recoverable from the alert, and it does not change the investigation: every entry on the catalogue is a driver whose content is known, so the questions turn on the file's provenance and use rather than on which digest matched. No question mirrors the list — see the rule_hash_literals disposition for why.

Primary technique T1543.003 — the driver reaches kernel memory through a service entry, and its analytic is the only one whose Windows log sources (7045, the Services registry key) describe observables this rule's alert can be correlated against. T1068 is tagged and secondary: it supplies the privilege-use stage and the time_correlation dimension, but its analytic describes exploitation generically and drives no chain stage before the load. T1543 (the parent) contributes the parent_process_analysis dimension only.

Triage is framed around identifying which product legitimately bundles the driver rather than around assuming compromise. The catalogue this rule draws on is roughly four-fifths vendor-signed drivers with exploitable primitives — hardware utilities, firmware flashers, anti-cheat components — so a valid signature is expected and is not exculpatory. The discriminators the questions push on are the install path, the registering service, the writing process, the parent lineage, and whether the product belongs on this host's build.

The field_inventory.md line 'Hashes -> dll.hash.sha256' under image_load describes only the BARE-Hashes case (ecs_fix_process_creation's own comment marks the combined-string case as broken out above) and does not reflect this transform; reading it as covering prefixed values is what produced an earlier, incorrect decision to omit these values.

dedup_decisions.reason: The alert is a driver load with no acting tool binary of its own — an Image|endswith '%Image%' 90-day process_creation baseline would resolve to the service control manager, which runs constantly on every Windows host and answers nothing. Historical presence is covered by cue_image_load.baseline (Q13), which baselines the driver on this host over the same 90 days and adds the hash/signer drift check.

skipped_templates.reason: replaced_by: service_persistence.service_configuration, and the brief hint says the same. The template's host + Image|endswith '%Image%' process_creation pivot has no acting binary to decode on a driver_load alert, and rule.commandline_values is empty so there is no command line to decode at all. The mechanism record for how the driver reached the kernel is the structured 7045 service data (ServiceName / ImagePath / StartType / AccountName) in Q5, with the load event's own path/signer/hash in Q3 and Q4.

must_include template, but its purpose — identify the file the service executes and check its location, signature, and hash — is answered directly by the load event on a driver_load alert. Its default query anchors process_creation on ParentImage|endswith '\services.exe' and reads the hash off an execution event; a kernel driver never runs as a process, so that query returns this host's unrelated user-mode service starts and never the driver. The template's own notes direct re-anchoring on the rule's file when the rule carries one; that re-anchor is already Q3 (load path plus Signed/Signature/SignatureStatus) and Q4 (Hashes plus published-release comparison), with Q9 for the file's origin on disk. Adding the template on top would restate those three with a strictly worse anchor.

Its frozen query correlates file_activity to the alerting ProcessGuid and its direct children. On a driver_load alert that ProcessGuid is the loading process (service control manager, or nothing for a boot-time load), which is not the process that wrote the .sys file — the write happened earlier, by an unrelated process, so the lineage correlation returns nothing by construction. The question it exists to ask (is the file on disk, and where did it come from) is Q9, anchored on host.name plus TargetFilename|endswith|expand '%ImageLoaded%' over +/-4h.

recommended, not must_include. The informative timing axis for a driver is boot-time auto-start versus a deliberate mid-session load, and that is read from the service start type in Q5 and the service's current state in Q8 rather than from a work-hours comparison. The remaining authorization judgment is asked against concrete records by Q2 (host role, account expectation, and any lab designation or approval record) and Q12 (user recall), and the immediate temporal context by Q16's +/-15m window. A 3 AM versus 2 PM comparison adds nothing for a driver that researchers exercise at whatever hour they are working.

recommended, not must_include. The 'is this how changes are normally made' comparison needs a legitimate counterpart procedure to compare against; the only ones that apply here are driver installation via a software-deployment package and sanctioned research on a designated host, both of which are asked more directly and against a record by Q2 (host role, account expectation, lab designation) and Q12 (user recall). Retaining it would put a third approved-practice question with the same answer in front of the analyst.

recommended, not must_include; dropped for slot budget at the 18-question ceiling to make room for Q15 (the import-hash fleet sweep), which answers a question no other question in this playbook can reach — whether a RENAMED copy of this driver has loaded elsewhere, the case the rule's second detection branch exists for. Its own axis (a documented approval, lab designation, or training window) is the weakest of the three authorization questions here and the most redundant: Q2 asks the same thing against asset inventory and the owning team, and its context was extended to name the lab-designation / training-window / approval record explicitly so the documentary form is not lost; Q12 asks the person directly. A change ticket is also a poor instrument for this rule specifically — HEVD is exercised interactively by a researcher, not deployed through a change-controlled package, so the absence of a ticket carries little signal either way.

recommended, not must_include. Its Startup-folder and scheduled-task-XML selectors cover a persistence family unrelated to a kernel driver, which persists through a service entry rather than a drop into a startup location. The file-drop dimension for this rule is covered precisely by Q9 (the driver file's own write event, anchored on its filename), the service-registration dimension by Q5 and Q6, and the cross-mechanism sweep is retained by Q18 (process_based_persistence).

notes: condition_topology.shape is all_AND with a single selection, but that selection is a LIST of two maps, which is an OR in Sigma: the rule fires on ImageLoaded|endswith '\HEVD.sys' OR on Hashes|contains one of two IMPHASH values. The decomposer only reads the condition string and so reports all_AND. Q1 and the description are framed disjunctively (either branch, and record which one matched) to match the real semantics.

Both branches of the rule are reachable, by two different anchors. The %ImageLoaded% anchor reaches the ALERTING driver whatever it was called (on a name-branch fire it hydrates to HEVD.sys; on an import-hash-branch fire it hydrates to whatever name the renamed driver carried), which covers the load path, signer, hash, host baseline, and same-name fleet distribution. The rule's two IMPHASH values are additionally injected verbatim in Q15, which drops the name constraint to reach HEVD by content under ANY name across the fleet — the renamed-copy case the hash branch exists for, and the one thing no %ImageLoaded%-anchored query can see, since a renamed driver on another host shares neither name nor alert with this one.

This rule is threat-neutral, not threat-specific: HEVD is a training target, not malware. The playbook is written so the legitimate case (a researcher, a student, a CTF or lab host) is a first-class outcome rather than an afterthought — Q2 establishes the host's kind before anything else, and Q11 tests for the debugger/toolchain corroboration that the legitimate case predicts. No named actor, campaign, or malware family appears in any analyst-visible field.

Q1 keeps the brief template's frozen fields list ([ImageLoaded, Hashes]) but re-anchors the query from process_creation + ProcessGuid to driver_load + host.name + ImageLoaded|endswith|expand; see mutable_dispositions for the full rationale. Q2 (universal.host_user_context) and Q8 (service_persistence.service_current_status) keep their KEEP_EXACT process_creation + ProcessGuid queries unchanged — their fields ([host.name, User] and [CommandLine]) exist on the process_creation event, so they remain internally coherent as alert-lookup / organizational questions and needed no deviation.

playbooks.name: Vulnerable WinRing0 Driver Load
playbooks.description: Detects the load of the WinRing0 kernel driver, matched either by an import hash of D41FA95D4642DC981F10DE36F4DC8CD7 or by a file name ending in one of the known WinRing0 variants. WinRing0 is a legitimate open-source driver that gives a calling user-mode process direct hardware access — CPU model-s

questions.question: Which driver file loaded, what is its full path, and does its hash match the WinRing0 import hash the rule names?
Is this host expected to run hardware-monitoring, overclocking, or benchmarking software that loads this driver?
Was the software that loads this driver deployed under a change ticket, maintenance window, or documented approval?
Which process triggered the load, from what path, and what signer and signature status does the driver carry?
Does the driver file's hash match a published build of this driver, and which process loaded it?
Which process wrote the driver file to disk, when, and to what directory?
What process triggered the driver load, and what spawned it?
What service was installed on this host around the driver load, and what image path and start type did it register?
Does the Security log record a service installation on this host around the driver load, and which account performed it?
What service registry entries were written on this host around the driver load, and do any point at the driver file?
Is the driver still loaded and its service still registered, and under what account does it run?
Has this driver loaded on this host before, and under what processes?
Is this driver loading on other hosts in the environment?
Did any other kernel driver load on this host around this one, and were any of them unsigned or unfamiliar?
Did this host connect out on ports commonly used by mining pools around the driver load?
What other activity occurred on this host around the time of the alert?
Did other detections fire on this host in the hours before this alert?
Were other process-based persistence mechanisms installed on this host around the driver load?
