Not injected as a query branch. The rule constrains the file name and import hash and says nothing about the path, so an ImageLoaded|contains ['\Users\', '\Temp\'] filter on Q4 would drop the alerting event whenever the driver loaded from a program directory — the exact case the analyst needs to see to close the alert as installed software. The element is realized as the path judgement Q4 names (a product's own installation directory versus a temporary, AppData, ProgramData, Public, or randomly-named path), Q1 projects the full ImageLoaded for it, and Q10 applies the same judgement to the registered ImagePath value.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only (a temporal window to correlate Start key changes with service creation — the analytic states no numeric value)
mutable_dispositions.notes: Realized as the question's +/-4h range, the same window Q9 (service-installation audit) uses, so Start-value writes and service creation land in one comparable frame. Q10's context names the correlation explicitly (a Start value changed within hours of the load ties the two together). No threshold to inject.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: .sys files loaded by sc, the Registry, or ZwLoadDriver
mutable_dispositions.notes: The alert's own logsource is the element. Conversion scopes category driver_load to event.category:driver, so every driver_load question here (Q1, Q4, Q5, Q12, Q13, Q14) is already constrained to kernel driver loads by construction; an ImageLoaded|endswith '.sys' branch would filter nothing and would drop the rule's own \WinRing0.dll and \WinRing0x64.dll name variants. The three load routes the element names are each covered against the logsource that records them — the sc.exe route by Q18's persistence-tool sweep, the Registry route by Q10, and the resulting load itself by Q4.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only (raise alerts for unsigned binaries registered as services — no literal values)
mutable_dispositions.notes: No values to inject, and the element inverts for this rule — WinRing0 is validly signed, and the signature is what carries it past driver signature enforcement, so Q4's context states that a Valid status is expected and settles nothing. Q4 still projects Signed, Signature, and SignatureStatus (a renamed copy under an unexpected signer is information), Q5 carries the hash-versus-signer judgement the element's intent reduces to here, and Q14 applies the element as written to the second-driver follow-on, where an unsigned driver loading after this one is the result to pursue.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only (regex for uncommon service names, e.g. svhostx, winhelp — the analytic gives illustrations, not a list)
mutable_dispositions.notes: The illustrations are examples of a naming judgement, not values a query can enforce; injecting 'svhostx' or 'winhelp' as literals would match nothing outside the analytic's own text. Q8 projects ServiceName and Q9 projects ServiceName/ServiceFileName so the analyst performs the comparison on the host's real service names, and Q10 surfaces the registered subkey name. Q8's context frames the comparison against the monitoring or benchmarking products installed on the host.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: rationale only (list of non-administrative processes starting service management tools — the analytic enumerates none)
mutable_dispositions.notes: No literal process list in the analytic. Q7 (cue_process_tool.process_chain) resolves the loading process's parent, and its context names the discriminator — a script host, Office application, remote-management agent, or unfamiliar binary driving service management versus services.exe, a vendor installer, or explorer.exe.

mutable_dispositions.notes: KEEP_EXACT query deviation, per TOFIX/universal_verify_trigger_match_has_no_driver_load_variant.md. universal.yaml carries variants_by_category for image_load but none for driver_load, so the brief composed verify_trigger_match from the base process_creation query while rewriting its fields list to the rule's detection_fields (ImageLoaded, Hashes) — a process_creation event carries neither, so the composed query could not answer its own question. The query was re-anchored on the alert's own logsource following the image_load variant's pattern. The frozen fields list is unchanged. The rule's own literals are deliberately NOT added to the selection: the rule fires on the file-name branch OR the IMPHASH branch, and an ImageLoaded|endswith [WinRing0 names] filter would return nothing for an IMPHASH-branch fire, which is precisely the renamed-driver case the triage question most needs to display. %ImageLoaded% hydrates to the alerting file's own name and covers both branches. Same resolution as published driver playbooks 10cb6535, 05296024, 2c4523d5, 39b64854.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: category: process_creation + ParentImage|endswith '\services.exe' -> category: driver_load + host.name + ImageLoaded|endswith|expand
mutable_dispositions.notes: KEEP_EXACT query deviation, taken under the template's own notes_to_llm instruction to adapt the anchor to the rule. The template's default lists service starts under services.exe so a hash can be read from the execution event, because a service binary is normally a process. A kernel driver never runs as a process, so that query returns unrelated user-mode service starts and no hash for the driver. The driver load event carries the driver's hash directly (unlike a file write, which carries none), so the query was re-anchored on the alert's own logsource. The frozen fields list [Image, Hashes] is unchanged and both fields are populated on driver load events — Image is the loading process, Hashes the driver's own hash.

Acts on the brief hint "File paths derived from CommandLine — do NOT use the %file_paths% placeholder". The rule has no CommandLine values (rule.commandline_values is empty); its only file reference is the driver path. Q6 anchors file_event on host.name + TargetFilename|endswith|expand '%ImageLoaded%' over -7d, which is scoped beyond host.name as the file-event scoping rule requires. No dead placeholder is used anywhere in the playbook.

dedup_decisions.reason: Within-phase overlap resolved in favour of the technique set, per the dedup rule. Both questions ask whether the loaded module is a known-legitimate file by hash and signing status, and against this rule's alert both would query driver_load scoped to host.name + ImageLoaded|endswith|expand '%ImageLoaded%' — the same query twice. service_persistence.service_binary_analysis is the more specific version for a rule whose module is a driver registered as a service, and Q4 (cue_image_load.mechanism_decode) retains the full signature projection the cue template contributed.

Its query is a 90-day process_creation aggregation scoped to host.name + Image|endswith '%Image%'. On a driver load event %Image% hydrates to the process that triggered the load — typically the service control manager, which runs constantly on every Windows host, so the historical count answers nothing about the driver. Q12 (cue_image_load.baseline) provides the baseline the question intends: the 90-day history of this driver loading on this host, aggregated by loading process.

skipped_templates.reason: "replaced_by: service_persistence.service_configuration" (brief hint). Independently correct here — the template decodes command-line arguments, and rule.commandline_values is empty; on a driver load event its host+%Image% scope would decode the service control manager's command line. The Phase 2 decode for this rule is the driver load itself (path, signer, status, hash, loading process), carried by Q4 against the alert's own logsource, and the service-registration decode is carried by Q8.

Its frozen query correlates file_activity to the alerting ProcessGuid and its direct children, which for this rule returns files written by the driver-loading process — not the driver file, which was written before the load and generally by a different process (an installer or whatever staged it). Q6 (llm_generated) asks the question this template exists to ask, anchored correctly on host.name + TargetFilename|endswith|expand '%ImageLoaded%' over -7d, and returns the writing process, path, and timing. Q11 covers the "is the file still on disk" half by directing the analyst to check the alerting path on the host.

Recommended, not must_include. The load is machine-initiated — this driver loads when its consumer tool or its registered service starts, not as a step a person performs and remembers, so "do you recall doing this" has no action to name. The judgement it exists to reach for this rule is whether a person deliberately put driver-loading software on the host, which Q3 (organizational_context.change_ticket) asks at the approval level and Q2 asks at the role level, while Q6 (the file's writing process) and Q7 (the loading process's parent) answer it from evidence by naming the product rather than relying on recall.

Recommended, not must_include. Working-hours framing does not discriminate for this rule — the driver loads whenever its service or consumer tool starts, including at boot on an unattended host, so an out-of-hours load is the normal case for legitimately installed monitoring software and carries no signal. Q3 (change_ticket) covers the maintenance-window half of the question against the deployment rather than against the load, and Q16 (cue_host_context.clustering) supplies the temporal context that does discriminate — what else ran on the host in the same window.

Recommended, not must_include. Its question — is this method of making changes consistent with how the organization normally works — has the same answer as Q3 (organizational_context.change_ticket, was the software that loads this driver deployed under a change ticket or documented approval) for a rule whose subject is a driver loaded by an installed product rather than a change made with built-in administrative tooling. Keeping both would put two approved-practice questions in front of the analyst with one answer between them.

Recommended, not must_include. Its TargetFilename branches cover Startup-folder drops and scheduled-task XML definitions — a persistence family unrelated to a kernel driver, which persists through a service entry and its registry keys rather than through a file in a startup location. The file-drop dimension for this rule is covered precisely by Q6 (the driver file's own write event) and the registration dimension by Q8, Q9, and Q10; Q18 (persistence_scope.process_based_persistence) retains the cross-mechanism sweep.

notes: Primary technique is T1543.003 (Windows Service) — the rule's subject is a kernel driver, which the sub-technique's analytic names directly ("privilege escalation via driver installation or CreateServiceW usage", ".sys files loaded by sc, Registry, or ZwLoadDriver"). T1543 (parent) is secondary and contributed the parent_process_analysis dimension and the RegistryPathList element; its chain is the same service-creation chain at lower resolution and does not override the sub-technique's.

The security-logsource hint literally reads "author a custom question with `category: security`". Q9 is authored with `service: security` instead. `security` is a Windows event-log channel, not a Sigma category — windows-logsources keys channel scoping off `service:`, so `category: security` produces an unscoped query and trips the category linter. The hint's intent (Security-channel coverage of the T1543.003 service-installation analytic, EventCode 4697) is fully met. EventID 4697 populates SubjectUserName as user.name under `service:` mapping, so the bare field name is used.

condition_topology.shape is all_AND over a single selection (prose "Rule fires when selection matches"), so there is no top-level branch to frame disjunctively. The selection itself is a two-member list — an IMPHASH match OR a file-name match — which is an OR the decomposer does not reach inside. Q1 and the description are framed on that inner disjunction ("either an import hash of ... or a file name ending in ...") because it changes what the analyst does: an IMPHASH-branch fire means the driver was renamed.

Q14 (other drivers loading on this host) and Q12/Q13 (this driver's host history and fleet distribution) are not deduplicable despite sharing the driver_load logsource. Q12 and Q13 are anchored on %ImageLoaded% and answer "is THIS driver normal here / elsewhere"; Q14 deliberately drops that anchor to surface OTHER drivers in a +/-4h window, which is the documented BYOVD follow-on — the ring-0 primitive used to load a second driver that signature enforcement would block. Driver load volume per host is low enough that a host-only scope over four hours is readable.

Q15 (mining-pool ports) is authored llm_generated rather than from an ATT&CK dimension. It exists because this driver has two distinct legitimate-and-illegitimate consumer classes, and separating cryptomining use from kernel-access use changes both the remediation and the scope. The port list is a bounded, honest filter — the question names ports, the query filters on ports, and the context states that pool traffic over 443 is invisible to it.
No template in this brief carries reflection_kind, so no REFLECTED detection blocks exist to preserve or override.

Every other question in the playbook anchors on a file name ('%ImageLoaded%' or the rule's five literals), so a renamed copy of a known driver build — precisely what the hash branch exists to catch, and what Q1's context tells the analyst a hash-branch match under an unlisted name means — would otherwise fire the rule and then be uninvestigable. 18 entries is above the ~10-entry mirroring threshold AGENTS.md sets as the point where mirroring becomes a judgement call; mirrored anyway because the values are a closed catalogue of published builds rather than a pattern list, the branch is unreachable by any other anchor, and 'Hashes|contains' with prefixed values converts cleanly (see notes on the pipeline's hash break-out items).

Acts on the brief hint about %file_paths%. The rule has no CommandLine values (rule.commandline_values is empty); the only file reference is the driver path. Q5 anchors file_event on host.name + TargetFilename|endswith|expand '%ImageLoaded%'. No dead placeholder is used anywhere in the playbook.

dedup_decisions.reason: Its query is a 90-day process_creation aggregation scoped to host.name + Image|endswith '%Image%'. On a driver load event %Image% hydrates to the process that triggered the load — typically the service control manager or a service host — so the result measures how often that process runs, which is constant on every Windows host and answers nothing about the driver. Q14 (cue_image_load.baseline) provides the baseline the question intends: the 90-day history of this driver loading on this host, aggregated by loading process.

skipped_templates.reason: 'replaced_by: credential_access.credential_target_identification' in the brief. Its query also scopes process_creation to host.name + Image|endswith '%Image%', which on a driver load hydrates to the loading process rather than to a tool with arguments worth decoding, and the rule has no CommandLine values at all. The Phase 2 decode is split across Q10 (the replacement — the loading process's own command line via ProcessGuid) and Q3 (cue_image_load.mechanism_decode — the load event's path, signer, and hash against the alert's own logsource).

Its frozen query correlates file_activity to the alerting ProcessGuid and its direct children, which for this rule returns files written by the driver-loading process rather than the driver file itself — the driver was written before the load, by a different process, and needs no install step to be usable. Q5 (llm_generated) asks the question this template exists to ask, anchored on host.name + TargetFilename|endswith|expand '%ImageLoaded%' over -7d, and returns the writing process, path, and timing.

The data_staging_exfil set was selected by the rule's 'collection' tactic, but the collection this rule detects is network packet interception, not file archiving. The template's query anchors file_activity on host.name + Image|endswith|expand '%Image%', which on a driver load hydrates to the service control manager or a service host, so the question would report that process's file writes and mislead. The collection scope for this rule — which traffic the operator selected — is covered by Q10 (the loading process's filter/port arguments) and Q13 (the host's actual egress around the load).

Same %Image% hydration problem as data_staging_exfil.data_scope, and there is no archive to trace: intercepted traffic is not written to an archive file by the driver. The destination axis that applies here is the network one — where diverted traffic went — which Q13 (attack:T1599.network_destination) covers on network_connection, and Q11 covers for the remote-access ports specifically.

The template asks the analyst to look for -p / -hp / --passphrase archive flags in the triggering command line. The rule has no CommandLine values and the alert is a kernel driver load, so there is no archive and no password flag to find. Q10 already re-displays the loading process's command line for the argument analysis that IS relevant here (packet filters, ports, redirect targets).

hints_acted_on.where: Q8 (attack:T1557.001.security) — service: security question on EventID 4697, driver service registration, projecting ServiceName / ServiceFileName / SubjectUserName. Q9 (attack:T1557.001.smb_relay) — second service: security question on EventID 4624 LogonType 3, covering the SMB relay half of the technique's analytic (inbound NTLM logons after the load).

hints_acted_on.hint: 'Condition uses OR *inside* a selection: selection has 2 alternative branches. The condition string (''selection'') names the selection once, but its value is a list of maps, which Sigma evaluates as an OR of alternative field-maps — the rule fires when ANY ONE branch matches, not all of them. Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame this as ''EITHER ... OR ...'', and Q1''s context should tell the analyst which branch fired. Do NOT flatten it to AND. (A list of scalar values under a single field is different — that is intra-field membership, not a branch OR.)'
hints_acted_on.where: Q1 question text uses "either a path containing one of the five divert-driver file names, or an import hash on the rule's list"; Q1 context tells the analyst to note which branch matched and states what each implies (name branch identifies the build including rebrands; hash branch under an unlisted name means a renamed driver). The top-level description uses the same either/or framing. The five-name list under ImageLoaded|contains and the eighteen-value list under Hashes|contains are each intra-field membership within their branch, not further branches.

notes: Primary technique T1557.001 — the rule's references and the driver's documented abuse both center on redirecting SMB/authentication traffic into a relay, and it is the only tagged technique whose ATT&CK brief carries Windows-platform analytics and log sources. T1599.001 is tagged and contributes the network_destination dimension via its parent T1599, but its analytics are Network-Devices-platform and empty; it drives no chain stage of its own.

The rule's hash branch is observable and is mirrored verbatim in Q16. Prefixed Hashes values are not passed through as-is — sigma_so_pipeline.yaml's 'hashes_break_out_field' item (type hashes_fields, valid_hash_algos includes IMPHASH, drop_algo_prefix False) splits a prefixed Hashes|contains value into per-algo pseudo-fields, and 'hashes_driver-load', gated on category driver_load + product windows, maps fileIMPHASH to dll.pe.imphash. The 'Hashes -> dll.hash.sha256' row in _meta/field_inventory.md describes the BARE-Hashes case only and does not reflect the break-out transform; reading it as the prefixed case leads to the wrong conclusion that the IMPHASH branch cannot match. It can, and it does.

Triage is framed around identifying which product bundled the driver rather than around assuming compromise. WinDivert is a legitimately signed, widely bundled open-source framework, and three of the five file names the rule enumerates are vendor rebrands of it, so a valid signature is expected and is not exculpatory. The discriminators the questions push on are the install path, the companion library's loading process, the writing process, and whether that product belongs on this host's build.

Keeping both would ship two questions with the same query.

A 90-day count of csrss.exe / svchost.exe / rundll32.exe execution on the host measures nothing — every Windows host runs all ten of these writers continuously, so the answer is a large number on every alert. The reflected host baseline counts the rule's actual firing pattern on this host instead, which is the discriminating version of the same intent.

Same query as the kept question — process_creation, host.name + ParentImage|endswith '%Image%', fields Image and CommandLine. renamed_binary_activity is the technique-set version of the same child-process pivot and carries the lineage-coherence framing this rule needs.

Same query as the kept question — process_creation aggregation scoped to host.name over the alert window. The host-context version aggregates by Image and ParentImage rather than Image alone, which surfaces novel parent-child pairings the flat version hides.

skipped_templates.reason: The template's REQUIRED ADAPTATION had no input — this rule pins no directory anywhere in its detection (the writers are matched by basename and the targets by extension; the only paths present are inside the four known-good exclusion filters, which are the opposite of the directory to investigate). The template's own note sanctions the two available outs — drop, or re-anchor on the extension pattern. The extension re-anchor was rejected: the rule's extension set includes .exe, .dll and .txt, and a -7d host-scoped aggregation over every write of those three on a host is the unanchored file-volume aggregation the scoping rules prohibit against ~16M/day file telemetry. Directory context is instead carried by the write-burst question, whose context directs the analyst to read where the writer's other writes land relative to the alerting file's directory.

hints_acted_on.hint: Condition uses OR among selection groups: (selection_generic OR selection_special). Q1 (verify_trigger_match) and the playbook description must frame the disjunction faithfully as 'EITHER ... OR ...'. Where a branch is shown as (A AND B), that branch fires only when A and B match TOGETHER — keep the AND; do not split it into separate OR branches. Use condition_topology.prose for an LLM-ready summary.
hints_acted_on.where: Q1 and the top-level description both use "either ... or" framing over the two selection groups. Each branch is stated as an AND of its two legs (writer basename AND target extension) rather than split, and the four filter_main_* exclusions are named as cancelling conditions. Q1's context tells the analyst to note which branch fired and what each implies — the session/logon branch is self-contained since those binaries have no file-writing role, while the dllhost/rundll32/svchost branch leans on the file's content and execution history because those binaries write files routinely.

notes: KNOWN BUG deviation — masquerading.binary_origin (Q4) ships "TargetFilename|contains|expand: '%file_name%'", but %file_name% maps to {event_data.process.name} in resources/patterns_sigma.yaml, i.e. the ACTING process's name. On this file_event rule that hydrates to the writing binary (svchost.exe, rundll32.exe, ...) and the query becomes "find files whose path contains 'svchost.exe'" — it converts, returns ~nothing, and reads to the analyst as "this file has no prior history on this host", the exact inverse of the truth. Substituted '%TargetFilename%' with |endswith|expand, which per AGENTS.md hydrates to the alert's file NAME. The rest of the query, the host.name anchor, the -30d window, and the frozen fields list are untouched. See TOFIX/file_name_placeholder_maps_to_writing_process.md; precedent 13c02350.

What the rule actually detects is narrower than "a LOLBIN drops a payload". Every writer it lists is a non-LOLBIN Windows process with no file-authoring role in the extension set given — csrss, lsass, smss, wininit, winlogon, sihost and RuntimeBroker do not write scripts or executables at all, and dllhost, rundll32 and svchost do so only in the narrow known-good cases the four filters carve out. The discriminator is the writer/extension pairing, and the two readings it admits are (a) code running inside a genuine system process (injection or a hijacked COM/service host) staging a file under that process's trusted identity, or (b) a separate process borrowing a system binary's name. Q3 (true_identity) is the question that splits those two readings, which is why it sits early.

cue_host_context.clustering was kept on category process_creation rather than adapted to file_event per its template note. On file telemetry the template's host.name-only selection is precisely the unanchored aggregation the file scoping rules forbid (~16M events/day, ES circuit breaker); on process_creation the same selection is bounded and answers the question the template intends. The writer's file activity is covered by the ProcessGuid- anchored write-burst question instead.

No hash question is authored against the file event — file writes carry no hash (0.00007%). The hash pivot runs through the artifact_verification question, which anchors on the written file executing and reads the hash from the process event.

attack_chain_coverage.label: indirect_launcher
attack_chain_coverage.description: A user or service launches an indirection utility; for this rule the utility is the WSL interop path, and the launcher is visible on the Windows side as the alerting process's parent.

attack_chain_coverage.label: secondary_execution
attack_chain_coverage.description: The indirection utility spawns a secondary program/command — here the Windows binary carrying the \\wsl.localhost working directory, plus anything else driven from the same session and anything the binary spawned in turn.

attack_chain_coverage.label: network_and_file_effect
attack_chain_coverage.description: The utility or its child opens outbound network connections and touches the filesystem. The analytic's SSH-config precursor (%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\config) is the ssh.exe variant of T1202 and has no WSL analogue; the generalizable step is file and network activity attributed to the indirectly launched process.

mutable_dispositions.notes: The analytic's 10-30 minute correlation window between the indirect launcher and the spawned child/network activity is stated verbatim in Q5's context and realised as its +/-15m range, which sits inside that band. Q6 (+4h children) and Q8/Q9 (+/-1h network and file effect) extend the same correlation past the band deliberately — a staged payload does not always act inside 30 minutes.

The element is a tuning list for permitting indirection utilities on admin hosts and jumphosts. This rule is not utility-pinned — it keys on the working directory, so wsl is the only member of the list it can ever match and injecting the other two would match nothing. Realised instead as the fleet-scope question, whose cross-host distribution is the practical basis for deciding which hosts are permitted to use interop; Q2 carries the host-role half of the same judgement.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: powershell.exe, cmd.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, mshta.exe, msiexec.exe, curl.exe, bitsadmin.exe
mutable_dispositions.notes: All eight values injected into Q7's Image|endswith selection (pwsh.exe added alongside powershell.exe to cover the cross-platform build, which is the one a WSL user is likelier to reach for). Not injected into Q6 (cue_process_tool.follow_on), which must stay open to any child; Q7 is the dedicated high-risk-utility pivot and projects CurrentDirectory so interop-launched instances separate from ordinary ones.

The element is a severity-raising rationale (standard/interactive user on a workstation versus a server or CI agent), not a queryable value. Realised in Q2's context, which turns it around for this rule - interop on a developer workstation is the expected case and interop on a server or a general office endpoint is the one to explain. Q14's role framing carries the identity half.

No concrete CIDRs are given - known-good egress ranges are environment-specific and cannot be authored into a portable query. Realised in Q8's context, which directs the analyst to judge destinations against the egress the host's role explains rather than against a fixed list.

dedup_decisions.reason: Query is host.name-scoped process_creation aggregation over +/-15m, identical to cue_host_context.clustering in logsource, scope and range; the host_context version projects Image+ParentImage where this one projects Image alone, so it is a strict superset and the pair would have produced near-identical results.
user_actor pair — non-deduplicable
dedup_decisions.kept: cue_user_actor.baseline + cue_user_actor.baseline_svc, and cue_user_actor.clustering + cue_user_actor.clustering_svc. Both pairs emitted per AGENTS.md. Interop normally runs under the interactive user who owns the distro session, so the user pivots are usually meaningful for this rule, but a scheduled or pushed automation using wsl.exe would fire under a service principal and degenerate them - which is exactly the case the parent-scoped substitutes answer.

hints_acted_on.hint: logsource 'file_event' (recommended by techniques: T1202) is not covered — pull in cue_artifact.* or author a custom question with `category: file_event`
hints_acted_on.where: Q9 — attack:T1202.file_artifacts, a `category: file_event` question scoped by ProcessGuid to the indirectly launched binary, covering the filesystem half of the T1202 analytic's "correlate ... file access ... and network connections from the utility or its child". Anchored on ProcessGuid rather than host.name because Defend file volume makes a host-scoped file query a circuit-breaker risk, and because moving a payload across the WSL/Windows filesystem boundary is attributable to the specific process.

hints_acted_on.hint: logsource 'network_connection' (recommended by techniques: T1202) is not covered — pull in cue_network_endpoint.* or author a custom question with `category: network_connection`
hints_acted_on.where: Q8 — attack:T1202.network_activity, a `category: network_connection` question scoped by ProcessGuid to the indirectly launched binary, covering the network half of the same analytic chain step and carrying the DestCIDRs mutable element's tuning rationale in its context.

notes: condition_topology.shape is all_AND (single selection), so Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing — a Windows drive-letter Image AND a CurrentDirectory containing \\wsl.localhost must both hold.

Telemetry reality drove the authoring. This pipeline is Windows-scoped, so WSL's Linux side is not observable — no process events for what ran inside the distro, no Linux shell history. Every question is framed on what the Windows side actually records: the interop launcher lineage, the launched binary, its arguments, its children, and its file and network effect. The blind spot is named platform-neutrally in the description and in Q4/Q8/Q9 rather than being papered over with questions promising evidence the environment cannot produce.

Technique-focused authoring. T1202 is the only tagged technique and the rule keys on a behavior pattern (interop as an execution proxy), so no actor, malware family, vendor or report names appear in prose. references.sigma_refs is "Internal Research" and db_refs is empty, so there was no intel to draw on regardless.

The rule pins no binary — primary_binary is null and all_binaries is empty, because the selection matches any drive-letter Image. %Image% therefore hydrates to whatever fired and may be a very common binary. cue_process_tool.mechanism_decode (Q3) accordingly carries the rule's CurrentDirectory|contains clause alongside the template's host+Image scope, per its notes_to_llm allowance for adding filters when host+binary scope would be too noisy. This narrows the result to interop-launched invocations of the binary, which is the template's "full operation" intent for this rule, and keeps it from degenerating on a cmd.exe or powershell.exe alert. cue_process_tool.baseline (Q10) deliberately keeps the unfiltered host+Image scope — its question asks whether the binary itself is normal on the host, which is a different question from whether the interop launch path is normal, and the reflected host-pattern baseline (Q11) already answers the latter.

Q5 (llm_generated) exists because the rule's real unit of analysis is a distro session rather than a single execution: listing all Windows processes on the host carrying a WSL working directory in the alert window reconstructs the command sequence issued from the Linux side, which is the closest observable proxy for the shell history this pipeline cannot see. It is distinct from Q3 (pinned to the alerting binary) and from Q7 (pinned to the high-risk utility list, unpinned on working directory).

Is this host or user expected to run executables out of C:\ProgramData\DRM or C:\Windows\Temp?
Is this execution part of an authorized penetration test or red team engagement?
Is this parent expected to spawn this child, and what started the parent itself?
What other child processes did this same parent instance spawn?
What was the full command line and working directory of the alerting binary?
What capability did this binary invoke, and does the command line name a service, module, or injection target?
What files did this process write after it started, and did any land in a staging or system directory?
Which modules did the alerting process load from outside the standard system and program directories, and are they signed?
Was a service registry entry created or modified on this host that points at a binary under C:\ProgramData or C:\Windows\Temp?
What was written into C:\ProgramData\DRM or C:\Windows\Temp on this host, and which process wrote it?
What else executed from C:\ProgramData\DRM or C:\Windows\Temp on this host, and how soon after the staging writes did those executions run?

mutable_dispositions.notes: The rule's own CommandLine|contains values are embedded verbatim in every reflected query (Q11, Q12, Q13, Q15, Q18) by the brief generator, so the baseline, parent-history, and fleet-scope counts measure this export pattern rather than generic rundll32 volume. Also carried in Q1/Q4/Q6 question text.

mutable_dispositions.specific_values: DLL entrypoint / export-name arguments to rundll32
mutable_dispositions.notes: Rationale-level for this rule — the rule already pins the two export names; Q6 directs the analyst to resolve the DLL path and trailing arguments.
Q7 walks the parent chain; Q7 context names explorer.exe / Office / script-host / services.exe parents as the discriminating cases.
Reflected parent_pattern queries (Q13, Q15) scope the rule's pattern by ParentName, giving the parent-history and fleet-parent views directly.
Correlation windows are carried as question ranges — image_load at +/-5m (Q8), network at +1h (Q9), host clustering at +/-15m (Q16), children at +4h (Q10).
Environment-specific baseline list cannot be authored into a query; Q8 surfaces ImageLoaded plus signature and hash so the analyst can compare against what rundll32 normally maps here.

The port list is carried in Q9 context rather than a DestinationPort selection — pinning the query to those ports would hide a controller on any other port, and the loader making any outbound connection is the finding.
The rule already pins the signed proxy binary; Q8 inverts the angle and checks the signature status of what that signed binary loaded.
Environment-coupled allowlisting is not authorable into a portable query; Q9 asks the analyst to judge the destinations returned.
Q6 context directs the analyst to note whether the DLL path resolves to a user-writable or temporary directory; Q5 covers what the loader wrote.
Q2 and Q12 cover role expectation and the user's 90-day history of this pattern; Q14 covers network-wide activity for the same account.

dedup_decisions.reason: Query is host.name-scoped process_creation aggregated by Image over +/-15m — near-identical to cue_host_context.clustering, which aggregates the same window by Image plus ParentImage and is therefore strictly more informative. Within-phase duplicate.

Image-scoped 90-day count of rundll32.exe on the host measures Windows' own use of the loader (installers, control-panel applets, shell verbs) and returns high volume with no bearing on this rule. The reflected baseline_deviation template answers the same "is this routine here" question against the rule's actual export pattern.
user_actor pair — non-deduplicable
dedup_decisions.kept: template:cue_user_actor.baseline + template:cue_user_actor.baseline_svc (Q12/Q13) and template:cue_user_actor.clustering + template:cue_user_actor.clustering_svc (Q14/Q15) both emitted; user-pivot answers 'is this identity routine', parent-pivot answers 'is this launch mechanism routine', and the user pivot degenerates under SYSTEM

notes: Primary technique T1218.011: the rule's Image anchor is rundll32.exe and the CommandLine values are DLL export names, so proxy execution through the signed loader is what fires. T1059.003 is secondary — shell invocation is a downstream capability of the payload rather than the trigger, and it drives the follow_on and host-clustering questions.

attack_brief also carries the parent techniques T1218 and T1059. Their dimensions are a subset of the two tagged techniques' dimensions and are covered by the same questions; dimension_coverage is keyed to the rule's own tags.

condition_topology.shape is all_AND (single selection, no or_valued_selections), so Q1 and the description use conjunctive framing: image ends in rundll32.exe AND the command line contains one of the export names. The CommandLine|contains list is an intra-field value alternation, not a selection-group OR.

Threat-specific rule (malware family in the title, filename_prefix apt), so naming ZxShell generically in description/context is permitted per the style guide. Kept to behavior — export-driven loading, shell/proxy/service-manipulation handlers, ping-delay self-delete — with no attribution and no historical incident chain.

cue_process_tool.follow_on re-anchored from host + ParentImage|endswith|expand '%Image%' to ParentProcessGuid|expand '%ProcessGuid%' per the template's notes_to_llm ('If ProcessGuid is available, prefer using ParentProcessGuid for precision'). rundll32.exe is a high-volume loader on Windows hosts; the Image-scoped form would have returned children of every unrelated rundll32 in the window.

Q9 uses host + Image|endswith rather than ProcessGuid scoping: network telemetry for the endpoint subset is process-linked, but a +1h controller channel is worth seeing across any rundll32 on the host, and the extra rows are cheap to read against the port/address columns.
